sources.title: Ryan Hoover on launching, consumer startups and his Product Hunt regrets
sources.originalTitle: How to launch and grow your product | Ryan Hoover of Product Hunt and Weekend Fund
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover covers how to approach a launch on Product Hunt, why to stay narrow and write like a human, and what he would change (monetize sooner, stay vertical, delegate). He also shares how he generates startup ideas, why consumer is hard, and why momentum matters.

principles.text: Decide why you're launching first; customer acquisition is only one possible goal (recruiting, fundraising, feedback, morale).
principles.quote: why are you launching and a lot of people default to things like customer acquisition oh i want to acquire customers but sometimes that's actually not it's not useful

principles.text: Write launch copy like a human, the way customers or friends would describe it, not like PR.
principles.quote: they tend to write like a pr person and not like a human

principles.text: Start with a narrow audience; it makes the product, messaging and go-to-market easier, and you can expand later.
principles.quote: generally the easier it is to build a great solution for those people because now you can actually hone in the product experience the messaging and everything to serve exactly those people

principles.text: Start generating revenue earlier, even by giving it a slice of focus, and resist expanding horizontally before the core community is served.
principles.quote: we should not have tried to expand horizontally we should have just focused entirely vertically and served the tech community

principles.text: Momentum compounds in both directions, so protect shipping energy early on.
principles.quote: momentum is reflexive in that you know high momentum leads to more high momentum low momentum leads to more low momentum

principles.text: A consumer company needs a unique insight; find ideas via a problem journal, niche communities, and behavior or technology shifts.
principles.quote: i think it's really hard to build a consumer company without some sort of unique insight maybe impossible

sources.title: Ryan Hoover on Product Hunt's growth flywheel, community vs audience, and small-fund investing
sources.originalTitle: Ryan Hoover on Growth Flywheels, Building Communities, Helping Founders, LP Investing
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt grew from a tiny email list into a launch platform through a maker-driven flywheel, Twitter-graph replication and borrowed UX. He also covers why communities differ from audiences, why human psychology outlasts technology shifts, and how he runs a small, collaborative, generalist fund.

principles.text: Design flywheels where each user's activity brings in more users, then tune the spin speed or conversion.
principles.quote: how do you build these flywheels where the more people engage, the more it either grows or drives more engagement back to the site.

principles.text: Ship a crude MVP in minutes to validate demand; small nudges of organic interest are enough confidence to keep going.
principles.quote: Took 20 30 minutes to set up, shared it on Twitter and then that gave me like enough confidence to realize, okay, there's something here to to explore.

principles.text: Borrow familiar behaviors and language instead of inventing new ones; being too cute hurts comprehension.
principles.quote: we're not going to reinvent the wheel like what behaviors and actions and language do people already understand like up votes people understand what that is

principles.text: Replicate the existing social graph at signup so notifications about people users follow drive high engagement.
principles.quote: we use Twitter because we're like, "Okay, we can replicate the graph." Like everybody on tech is already on Twitter.

principles.text: Let your best users promote you by giving them permission to promote themselves; it boosts authenticity and SEO.
principles.quote: we were giving them permission to promote themselves to promote us. So it was really a win-win.

principles.text: A community is members connecting with each other, not an audience listening to you; start with utility, not 'join a community'.
principles.quote: there's a big difference between an audience and a community and people like mix them up.

sources.title: How Ryan Hoover launched Product Hunt as an email list and grew its first community
sources.originalTitle: Communicate with Users, Build Something They Want - Ryan Hoover of Product Hunt
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains how a non-technical solo founder validated Product Hunt with a 20-minute email list, grew it from an audience built over years plus manual maker outreach, and later added monetization via Ship. He also covers distributed teams, giving up work as a founder, and engaging users directly.

principles.text: Validate ideas with no-code tools before building. Email, Typeform and Stripe can prove demand fast.
principles.quote: there's a lot of ways that you can validate ideas or build products without really coding anything product on it was an email list in the beginning

principles.text: Charging money is the ultimate demand test: if people pay, they clearly want it.
principles.quote: you can put like type form and stripe together and actually collect money that's the ultimate test

principles.text: Email is a malleable MVP: you can change copy daily and see if people open and click.
principles.quote: it's also very malleable so every single morning or every day when you send that email you can change the copy you can try different things whereas when you put something in code it's a lot harder to change

principles.text: Communicate with your audience and involve them; it raises the odds you build something people want.
principles.quote: the more you can communicate with your audience make them feel involved in the process and get feedback from them the higher chance you are in building some that people want or a good product ultimately

principles.text: Do unscalable outreach to pull early users in, then productize it once it works (maker invites became a bot).
principles.quote: I would every morning go on Twitter and like search for their Twitter username and say hey Jill your product is is over here people are talking about it do you want to join in answer questions and like 80% of the time they'd say yes

principles.text: As you grow a team, give up work and hire people you let operate autonomously, even if it feels less productive.
principles.quote: you're used to doing all the work in the beginning but as you grow a team you alternately have to give up work and it might feel like you're being less productive and less effective

sources.title: Ryan Hoover on Product Hunt: from side project to YC, and lessons on launches, monetization and focus
sources.originalTitle: Ryan Hoover on Product Hunt's Acquisition and Lessons Learned About Launches with Dalton Caldwell
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover recounts how Product Hunt grew from an email list into a YC company, why he raised money, and what he'd change (monetize earlier, avoid expanding to other verticals too fast). He also shares his view on what makes launches work.

principles.text: Do manual outreach to get a growth flywheel going; messaging makers drove them to join and share, bringing more traffic.
principles.quote: I found out that when I messaged them they would join the conversation they would share and that would drive more traffic to the site and so there's a nice flywheel effect

principles.text: Frame a startup as a side project first; build what you would want to use rather than overthinking markets.
principles.quote: change your frame of mind think about it as an experiment or a side project and when you put your your frame of mind of like a side project first you you start to you sort of settle most people start to settle in well what would I want to build or what would I what could I use

principles.text: Make some revenue early to extend runway, even if small, rather than waiting until funded.
principles.quote: we should have dedicated a little bit of time and focus on revenue and in the beginning before we were funded

principles.text: Expanding to new verticals too fast fails if the core community is still tied to the original one; go deep instead.
principles.quote: we tried to expand too quickly in the beginning we didn't properly build like a core solid like Gaming Community

principles.text: Treat funding as if runway isn't infinite; redesigns are often a trap that won't move numbers much.
principles.quote: you should treat it like you don't and truthfully there's some things that that I I prioritized on the team because I wanted it myself like some redesign work that we did which redesigns are often times a trap

principles.text: Launch advice: clear imagery and tagline, test with people who don't know you, and speak like a human not a marketer.
principles.quote: make sure the imagery is really clear the tagline is really clear um you know Bounce It Off a few people that don't know you or don't know about your product and speak like a human not like a marketer

sources.title: How Ryan Hoover launched Product Hunt: build an audience first, launch constantly, share openly
sources.originalTitle: How to Launch Your Next Project /w with Product Hunt's Ryan Hoover
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt began as a half-hour email list, grew through a five-day site build and a hand-picked beta, and then joined Y Combinator. He shares launch lessons: build an audience before the product, use plain language, launch continuously, and share openly instead of hiding your idea.

principles.text: Build an audience before you build the product; distribution is the hard part now.
principles.quote: in some ways it's like flip it around think about how do you find an audience and build an audience before you actually build a product is how we think about it

principles.text: Start with 100 people who love it, reached personally, not thousands on day one.
principles.quote: you don't need thousands of people on day one you just need hundred people who love what you're building and a great way to do that is just being very community focused and like very personable with those people

principles.text: Launching is continuous: email list, beta, site, then every new feature.
principles.quote: you're always launching so we launched the email list in the beginning then we launched the beta then we launched a website

principles.text: Use simple, clear language; test copy on strangers before launch.
principles.quote: it just comes down to like simple clear language I think generally does best when it comes to communicating an idea

principles.text: Share openly and get feedback instead of guarding your idea.
principles.quote: I think it's more advantageous to share and get feedback and talk to people rather than be secretive

principles.text: Position around the underlying human need, such as saving time, not the feature category.
principles.quote: it's the underlying need which is saving time or saving money or solving loneliness

sources.title: Ryan Hoover on building Product Hunt: audience-first distribution, community flywheels and habit-forming product design
sources.originalTitle: Ryan Hoover on Startup Growth Hacks, Products, Silicon Valley Success | Product Hunt | TRS 130
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt started as a simple email list and a Reddit-style MVP built over a long weekend. He argues distribution is now the hardest part of building a startup, so audience and community matter most. He also covers habit-forming product design (the Hooked model), what he looks for as an early-stage investor, and why people from gaming make strong product builders.

principles.text: Ship the simplest MVP and don't reinvent the wheel; innovate only where it matters (content and community).
principles.quote: we felt like that wasn't where we need to innovate really it was about the content the community and that's what was important

principles.text: Building is getting easier; the real startup risk is getting users and attention, and that will only get harder.
principles.quote: the risk isn't can they build it it's actually can they get users and can they get attention

principles.text: Build an audience before or alongside the product to derisk distribution, and reuse it across future projects.
principles.quote: he had guaranteed distribution from day one like he drisk the hardest part of building a company especially in consumer social which is distribution

principles.text: Turn an audience (one to many) into a community (many to many) so users create the content and the product runs without you.
principles.quote: if you can transfer that audience into a community it's actually dramatically more powerful and more scalable than just a pure kind of audience play

principles.text: Design habit loops (trigger, action, variable reward, investment), keep action friction low, and aim for internal triggers over external notifications.
principles.quote: your product has at some point it almost should never have to rely on external triggers ideally and instead rely entirely on internal triggers

principles.text: Writing and content build trust and authority, and that trust converts into product conversions over time.
principles.quote: when you create create some content and people find it of value and they learn from it they now trust you more and that trust can be transferred into like let's say conversions for your product

sources.title: How Ryan Hoover built Product Hunt: tight-knit community first, simple V1, roadmap led by users
sources.originalTitle: Building From Scratch with Ryan Hoover
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt started as a simple newsletter and let user behavior drive the roadmap, why community products should start with a small passionate kernel, and how he now evaluates startups by asking what has changed. He also shares advice for aspiring investors and experiments in community-driven investing.

principles.text: Community products should start with a small, excited group, not everyone; that kernel grows into something bigger.
principles.quote: You just want like a really tight-knit group of people who are really excited about what you build. And then that kernel can grow into something much bigger.

principles.text: Don't over-engineer V1 by being too clever with systems and flywheels; prove the core value prop first.
principles.quote: you can also become paralyzed and like over engineer a product if you think if you think you're too if you're like too clever basically.

principles.text: Start with the easiest possible format, then let user behavior and feedback make the roadmap obvious.
principles.quote: the road map sort of just like fell out. It was just like almost obvious um based on what people were doing, the feedback we were receiving.

principles.text: Productize behaviors users already invent on their own (like makers commenting on their own launches) to unlock engagement loops.
principles.quote: why don't we actually productize that and make it clear that this person made the thing or these people made this thing so that people in the community could identify those people.

principles.text: Ask 'what's changed?' (behavior, technology, regulation) to judge whether a new product has a why-now.
principles.quote: Is there a consumer behavior shift? Is there a technology shift? What's changed in this world to enable this this new thing to emerge?

principles.text: The initial insight should be contrarian; after product-market fit, customers lead you to obvious next steps.
principles.quote: as you get that flywheel going and like as product market fit exists, you're able to be led by the customers into things that feel very obvious.

sources.title: Ryan Hoover on running Weekend Fund: backing platform shifts, community as defensibility, and monetizing Product Hunt
sources.originalTitle: Product Hunt's Ryan Hoover on raising Weekend Fund, new markets, creating communities | Angel S3 E8
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains his generalist angel thesis (early rounds, platform and behavior shifts like voice), how community can add defensibility to a product, and how Product Hunt finally made money with a single promoted slot. He also covers valuation discipline, portfolio size and building remote teams.

principles.text: Community is not for every business, but layered on a core product it builds real defensibility.
principles.quote: you can build you can build a really strong business and defensibility by building community on top of your core product and core offering

principles.text: Back founders building today for a nascent future shift in platform or consumer behavior.
principles.quote: looking for people who are building for platform shifts and consumer behavior shifts in other words like who's building something really interesting today that's super nascent for a future that they're imagining

principles.text: Build community authentically and early by talking directly with users and acting on their feedback.
principles.quote: they have a Facebook group and they're super early but they use this Facebook group and speak with their community and get feedback from them in a really authentic way

principles.text: Monetize a community without breaking trust: sell only slots for products the community already validated.
principles.quote: it's always products that were posted before in the past you can't launch a new product and then pay to be in the spot so this way it's always something that's been essentially validated or uploaded by the community

principles.text: Valuation matters at early stage: a high pre-launch price demands a huge exit to move the fund.
principles.quote: when you look at the economics of a 50k check in a 35 mil pre-launch company you know this company's got to be three billion four billion dollar exit for to be really meaningful

principles.text: Be in the hub city to build relationships, but build the team remotely.
principles.quote: founders be here incur the brunt of the cost of living and the insanity but build your team remote

sources.title: Going from product to investor: Ryan Hoover on building communities, backing founders and Weekend Fund
sources.originalTitle: Going From Product to Investor - with Product Hunt Founder Ryan Hoover
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover talks about how Product Hunt began as a simple newsletter, how he seeded its community, and how he now invests at Weekend Fund. He covers what he looks for in founders (insights, team fit for the risk), how he sets terms, and his cautious but open view of consumer social.

principles.text: Ground a product in a real problem for a specific user; building the product alone isn't enough without positioning and distribution.
principles.quote: fundamentally a product is is a solution to a problem uh at its core and so I think it's useful um as like sophisticated as like we like to think we are sometimes it's used to like ground yourself and be like okay what problem am I solving and for whom

principles.text: A good product needs a holistic view: positioning, marketing, and distribution, not just great building.
principles.quote: theoretically you could build the best product in the world but if no one knows about it there's no distribution if it doesn't resonate with people they won't try it and it just won't go anywhere

principles.text: Start with the smallest MVP (a newsletter) and keep the core loop stable; more features don't automatically make a product better.
principles.quote: the very beginning was a newsletter so it wasn't even a committee or a site but it was just a newsletter of products that me and Friends found

principles.text: Design a community like a welcoming house party: seed it with respected people and personally invite early members.
principles.quote: communities are sort of like like parties in a sense

principles.text: As an investor, look for founder insights: after a call you should learn something counterintuitive you didn't know.
principles.quote: when we come away with like oh I didn't know that or aha or wow that's counterintuitive I didn't expect that like those are the types of things that we're looking for

principles.text: Evaluate founders on how well their team's skills match the biggest risks, and judge early products by the decisions behind them, not polish.
principles.quote: we care less about like what it looks like today but actually more of the decisions that went into what they have today and where it's going

sources.title: How Ryan Hoover builds a small, product-minded VC fund: LP base, scouts, and secrets
sources.originalTitle: How Ryan Hoover Is Rebuilding VC From Scratch
sources.outlet: How I Invest Podcast and Ryan Hoover
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains how Weekend Fund runs as a set of product experiments: a $21M fund with 360 LPs, a non-exclusive scout program, and Rolodexer for intros. He covers fund construction, winning deals as a small non-lead check, and backing founders with a secret or traction.

principles.text: Treat a fund like a product: build leverage that works while you sleep and run many small experiments, most of which fail.
principles.quote: I love building products that can scale infinitely that can provide value or help people while I'm sleeping.

principles.text: Use your audience as a distribution asset: search followers at target companies and DM warm intros for a 30-50% acceptance rate.
principles.quote: the conversion rate, I'd say 30 to 50% of people accept an introduction from those those outbound requests.

principles.text: Stay a small, non-lead check so founders can always make room, and avoid the awkward middle ground.
principles.quote: not being a lead, and not getting stuck in that middle ground where you're not a lead, but you're also having to write a 750k check

principles.text: Use low-pressure messages ("no response needed") and stay helpful without being distracting; a net-negative investor hurts your reputation.
principles.quote: the worst thing you could do as a founder is bring on an investor who is net negative. And word gets around, reputation matters.

principles.text: Extend your reach with a non-exclusive scout program run in a shared channel, so everyone sees deal flow and perspectives.
principles.quote: We don't require exclusivity.

principles.text: Look for founders with a secret or traction; if neither is visible, dig into what you don't understand.
principles.quote: I want to back a founder that has a secret or has traction.

sources.title: How Ryan Hoover built Product Hunt from a newsletter and launched Weekend Fund
sources.originalTitle: Ryan Hoover of Product Hunt and Weekend Fund on Starting, Building, and Investing (EP 167)
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover traces his path from entrepreneur parents in Eugene to Product Hunt, then to investing via Weekend Fund. He covers validating a side project before committing, raising VC money only with a clear need, investing where you have an edge, and turning fund LPs into a community that helps founders.

principles.text: Start with a need: find a problem people will pay to solve and fill it.
principles.quote: he had this saying of like find the need and fill it and fundamentally like that's what kind of businesses are it's like find a need that people are willing to like pay for essentially

principles.text: Start as a tiny side project (a newsletter) and let organic response tell you whether to build more.
principles.quote: it gave me enough confidence that people people were responding positively i got more subscribers just organically

principles.text: Don't raise money for its own sake; know exactly what you need it for.
principles.quote: a lot of people today get infatuated with like the process of fundraising without even thinking about like well what do i need it for

principles.text: VC money commits you to building a big company, so delay the decision until you have conviction.
principles.quote: when you raise vc capital specifically it means that you gotta go big you know you're not looking for like a 10 million exit um you need to build a big company

principles.text: Building for a community you belong to gives you attention and an edge when raising.
principles.quote: we were building for the tech community so like that's a huge advantage when it comes to raising like you're already capturing the attention of investors and people in tech

principles.text: Give founders many capable, financially aligned supporters instead of just capital.
principles.quote: founders will benefit from having as many people around the table that are financially invested in their success as possible who are capable and excited to support and help

sources.title: How Ryan Hoover grew Product Hunt from a tiny email list into a community-led product
sources.originalTitle: 67. Ryan Hoover of ProductHunt: Start with community
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt began as a 20-30 person curated email digest, validated at ~400 subscribers, then became a site built in three weeks of weekend work with a friend. He covers seeding a community manually, designing for quality (invite-only, real identity), hiring and delegating, leaning on mentors, and why people should tinker.

principles.text: Start as a cheap experiment; validate with an email list before building a site.
principles.quote: it was an experiment so it wasn't that I was jumping off a bridge and investing a whole lot of uh you know money or or time it was it was all just a side project

principles.text: Seed a community with a core group of like-minded enthusiasts so early content is useful and welcoming.
principles.quote: it was a core group of people who were all product enthusiasts

principles.text: Design product mechanics (invite-only, real identity, no brand accounts) to protect community quality from trolls and marketers.
principles.quote: we want producton to be a place where you see the person you see the face and you see the name of the person you're talking to

principles.text: Do unscalable manual outreach early: personal emails and tweets build trust and spread the network.
principles.quote: in the early days it's sometimes the best way to get things started especially with the community because people want to they want some sort of like they see they really recognize it when it's a human behind an email

principles.text: Early members set a community's culture, and it is hard to change later.
principles.quote: the people that that start off in the community they're they're oftentimes the one that set this set the the course for the culture long term

principles.text: Build relationships out of curiosity before you need them; they pay off in fundraising and press.
principles.quote: I wasn't building those relationships with an intent to like turn it into a like selfish value for myself but it just ultimately turned out that way

sources.title: How Ryan Hoover grew Product Hunt from an email list to 200K monthly uniques
sources.originalTitle: Learn How Ryan Hoover Transformed the Startup Ecosystem with Product Hunt's Explosive Growth
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains how he validated Product Hunt as a cheap email-list experiment, then grew it through writing-built credibility, Twitter login, a daily email habit loop, exclusivity, and building in public. He also covers personal outreach, community events, and why he avoids paid acquisition.

principles.text: Test ideas with the cheapest possible MVP, like an email list, before building a real product.
principles.quote: I'm not an engineer so you know one I couldn't build a Ruby on Rails app from from front to back myself and frankly I I shouldn't waste my time trying to build something that complex to prove out an idea

principles.text: Build an audience before the startup. Distribution is harder than building, so de-risk it early.
principles.quote: the hardest thing for most startups is not really building the product it's it's one figuring out what people want so building something people want ultimately but then two breaking through the noise

principles.text: Qualitative signals like unprompted praise can matter more than subscriber counts when validating early.
principles.quote: people would go out of their way to email me and they would in person tell me hey that product and email is cool and I enjoy it I read it every day

principles.text: Use external triggers like email and notifications to bring users back and form a daily habit.
principles.quote: oftentimes you need some sort of external trigger some way to bring that person back and for us email is a great way to do that because it's inner inbox people read their email all the time

principles.text: Reset the feed daily so there is a fresh digest and a reason to return, avoiding an overwhelming feed.
principles.quote: each day the board resets essentially so the list of products on the page it starts Anew and it's kind of a way to reinforce that daily routine of coming back

principles.text: Look at who signs up and personally reach out to influential users like reporters and investors to build relationships.
principles.quote: look and see who's signing up for your product whether you're building just an email list or you do have like some sort of registration like on Twitter it's kind of frankly stupid if you're not looking and seeing who's signing up

sources.title: Ryan Hoover on micro-fund investing: new startup status symbols, AI tailwinds, follow-ons and selling early
sources.originalTitle: All Star Investor Panel! Sophia Amoruso and Ryan Hoover | E2158
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover joins Jason Calacanis and Sophia Amoruso to discuss emerging-manager fundraising, rising valuations, and how startup signaling has shifted to revenue and social reach. He shares how Weekend Fund decides follow-ons, why they sold part of a winner for early DPI, and why improving foundation models change how AI founders should think about timing.

principles.text: Revenue is now the status symbol for startups, ahead of who backed you, and it signals to funds.
principles.quote: revenue is is the new status symbol uh beyond just raising. Now raising still matters. Like if you get you know brand name firm backing you that still matters but that's that's secondary to revenue at this point.

principles.text: Social, especially video demos, is the new launchpad; the algorithm lets no-name founders get seen.
principles.quote: Now you have an algorithm, it heavily incentivizes videos for like demos and you know this is changing a lot of how founders are sort of playing the status game and and showing off what they're building

principles.text: On AI, models improve beneath you, so win by capturing users now and being in position when models get good enough.
principles.quote: it's almost more about being in position and capturing users so that when the foundational models and AI is good enough to solve the problem that you're you're promising then you're there

principles.text: Judge a follow-on as if you were a fresh investor at today's valuation, with what you now know.
principles.quote: if we believe in this company like all things being equal, even if we're not an investor, would we invest in this company at this valuation today knowing what we know now?

principles.text: Take liquidity on a big winner early; selling a slice returns capital to LPs while keeping most of your upside.
principles.quote: I think it's wise for early stage funds maybe after 5 6 7 you know 8 years in their positions to start thinking about liquidity and take 20 30% off the table.

principles.text: Stay price-aware: pass when valuations are extreme with no objective proof points, but don't miss the best company.
principles.quote: we do pass on deals sometimes when the valuation seems extremely high and it's like pre-launch and there's not a lot of like objective proof points.

sources.title: How Ryan Hoover built Product Hunt in 4 days: email-seeded community and shipping fast
sources.originalTitle: EP60: Hear how Ryan Hoover built Product Hunt in 4 days
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt began as a Linky Dink email list, was validated by unprompted feedback, then built as a simple Hacker News-style site over Thanksgiving. Growth came from personal one-to-one emails, an inner circle of early contributors, and founders sharing their own listings.

principles.text: Validate an idea with a throwaway version first; unprompted praise is the signal to build.
principles.quote: it was at that point where I was like okay I'm not the only person that likes this clearly other people do

principles.text: Copy a proven pattern and keep V1 tiny so it can be built in days.
principles.quote: not reinvent the wheel but just create some sort of Hacker News type of uh Community for products

principles.text: Speed beats perfection: ship something people can touch and react to rather than stagnating.
principles.quote: making a decision quickly is better than stagnating

principles.text: Start a community with friends and like-minded people, and let early members shape the product.
principles.quote: that's the best way to start the communities like friends and people that are like-minded

principles.text: Recruit early users with personal one-to-one emails, and make referrals easy with copy-paste intros.
principles.quote: I like that Personal Touch the Personal Touch matters a lot

principles.text: Brief early adopters before a public launch so they feel inside the process and amplify the announcement.
principles.quote: people like to kind of be a part of behind the scenes um process that goes on behind and they also want to read that article

sources.title: How Ryan Hoover launched Product Hunt as an email list and built its community
sources.originalTitle: Product Hunt CEO Ryan Hoover on Building a Community | Please Hold Episode 4
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt began as a no-code email list MVP, grew into a curated, invite-only community, and why a PM background and authentic social presence helped. He also covers early monetization via job posts, support via Twitter, and distribution value for startups.

principles.text: Validate an idea with the simplest possible MVP, like an email list, before building anything.
principles.quote: I was forced to think okay how can I build like an MVP uh very quickly to see if people actually care about this like I do so started off as an email list

principles.text: Traction often comes as a series of small signals, not one magic moment.
principles.quote: there wasn't one magical moment where it was like wow this is like a thing but it was several data points and pieces of feedback from people

principles.text: Seed a community by hand and invite-only so it doesn't get swamped by self-promotion, with a common bond among early members.
principles.quote: when building a community in the very beginning you want some sort of common bond to some extent

principles.text: Do things manually first, then productize once the process works (e.g. manual onboarding became an invite system).
principles.quote: it was completely manual I would email them ask them to like CC that person on an email and then I would just manually like on board them

principles.text: Product management is strong preparation for being CEO because it trains cross-functional communication, sales and recruiting skills.
principles.quote: the communication skills that you learn and how you navigate different aspects of the business as a product manager is super applicable to being a CEO

principles.text: Building a personal audience and authentic brand beforehand seeds the first community and keeps a company feeling human.
principles.quote: the writing that I did and and sort of the connections I made through Twitter to some extent that was the that was really the MVP for producton

sources.title: How Ryan Hoover built Product Hunt: email list first, community and daily habit as the moat
sources.originalTitle: Triangulation 188: Product Hunt Founder Ryan Hoover
sources.summary: Early (Feb 2015) interview where Hoover explains how Product Hunt grew from a curated email list into a voting community, via quick-and-dirty copying of proven patterns, a daily-habit email, and an open API. He stresses community over tech, habit triggers, and not being afraid to remind users you exist.

principles.text: Start with a tiny, scrappy version (an email list) and borrow familiar patterns instead of inventing new ones.
principles.quote: We didn't want to create something entirely new that people would have to try to learn to understand and people in the technology world understand up voting. We simply just built something quick and quick and dirty

principles.text: Traction beats the idea: early proof of use is what made investors and YC see the value in a simple concept.
principles.quote: if it wasn't for the traction itself that moment they probably wouldn't have accepted us into y commentator

principles.text: The product's real value is the community around it; clones copy the function but fail without the people.
principles.quote: most of them don't succeed they build the product it works functionally but to really succeed you need to build a community around it

principles.text: Design for a daily habit: a daily email plus day-split site layout builds a routine.
principles.quote: the design of the site is encouraged to build this daily habit that's one of the reasons why we split things by day it's intended to give you kind of this daily uh routine

principles.text: Use external triggers like email; don't be afraid to remind users you exist, as long as each message provides value.
principles.quote: without reminding people you exist even if your product is awesome I think I think just a lot of people just don't remember to come back and I think people need to be maybe more aggressive with that

principles.text: Choose a single core metric tied to the value you create for others: traffic driven to listed products.
principles.quote: we choose our single metric is how much traffic are we driving to these products right that's kind of our our core metric

sources.title: How Ryan Hoover launched Product Hunt in under a week by cutting scope and leveraging his audience
sources.originalTitle: Interview: Ryan Hoover of Product Hunt on How Product Hunt was Launched in Less than 1 Week |...
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt started as a small email list, then became a real product built in about five days with only the bare minimum features. He also covers how a pre-built audience seeded the community and how blogging, cold emails and cross-posting drove early distribution.

principles.text: Ship the smallest possible version fast to get feedback from a small early-adopter group.
principles.quote: our entire goal was to build something quickly and get it to that early adopter like 20 30 people and get starting getting feedback as quickly as possible

principles.text: Be strict about scope: cut features to the bare minimum and lean on existing tools like Twitter login.
principles.quote: we had to be really strict on what features we wanted to include what features we could realistically include and we really cut it down to the bare minimum

principles.text: Validate an idea with a lightweight manual version (an email list) before building a real product.
principles.quote: I initially created essentially an email list with with maybe 20 or 30 Founders and investors that I knew

principles.text: A launch rides on audience and trust built over time through blogging and relationships.
principles.quote: if we tried to launch product hunt six or nine months ago it wouldn't have it wouldn't be where it is today

principles.text: Cold emails work when you hand over a complete, relevant draft and a short, genuine pitch.
principles.quote: if you're going to cold email to get a guest post give them the full the full draft complete it and give them a short description of why it's important

principles.text: Cross-post content everywhere relevant for more distribution; different topics win on different platforms.
principles.quote: if it's relevant to the community and you're posting it um in the right place on medium for example then why not uh why not post it everywhere

sources.title: Ryan Hoover on vertical job marketplaces, marketplace risk and community building
sources.originalTitle: MFM x Trends - Ryan Hoover of Product Hunt Breaks Down the Biggest Opportunities He Sees
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains why vertical job marketplaces (Pattern, Marketer Hire, Toptal-style) are a big opportunity. He shares how he evaluates startups: find the biggest risk, solve the hard side of a marketplace first, avoid paid-acquisition dependence. He also defines what a real community is and why it scales better than an audience.

principles.text: Vertical job marketplaces can serve talent and employers better than horizontal job boards, and the category is both impactful and lucrative.
principles.quote: if you really build a company around like a very specific vertical, you can ultimately serve both the supply and demand, the talent and the people looking to hire that talent much better than you would typically with like a horizontal job board.

principles.text: Find the biggest risk in a company and the unique ability to solve it; assume everyone has tried everything, so something must have changed.
principles.quote: I also make an assumption that everyone has tried everything. And so, either something has to have changed, whether it's like a consumer behavior shift or technology shift, and that founder or that team also has to have some sort of like unique ability to like solve for the biggest problem or risk.

principles.text: In a marketplace, solve the hard side first; focusing only on the easy side just delays failure.
principles.quote: marketplace models the risk of these is when people focus on the easy side of the market and ultimately you need both to work, but if you focus only on the easy side, you never get the hard side and you like delay the hard side in a sense, then you're almost like delaying failure.

principles.text: Avoid businesses reliant on paid acquisition: paying for talent makes CAC vs LTV fragile to algorithm changes and new competitors.
principles.quote: when you have to pay for talent, you start to run into really hard challenges with CAC versus LTVs and like all these other like variables which can like like get thrown out of whack if Facebook changes their algorithm or if another competitor comes in and throws a bunch of money in the space.

principles.text: Start with a community before the product: it gives you a launch audience and insight into what to build.
principles.quote: starting off with a community and building something for them or building an audience of some sort is super valuable because it'll give you two things. Like one, it'll give you an audience for when you launch the thing. And two, it'll hopefully give you a lot of insight into like how you can build a great product for those people.

principles.text: A real community needs interaction among members, a sense of belonging, and utility; communities scale beyond what the founder can create alone.
principles.quote: by definition, a community requires people in that community to interact with each other. It really isn't a community unless they're interacting in some form or another. Two, community is really about a sense of belonging of some sort.

sources.title: How Ryan Hoover built Weekend Fund: small, collaborative, non-lead funds and a three-tier LP raise
sources.originalTitle: 01: Ryan Hoover (Weekend Fund) |  "101 Guide For Emerging Fund Managers" | 1947 VC
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains how he built Weekend Fund from a $3M first fund to a $21M third fund using a diversified, non-lead, small-check strategy. He also walks through his three-stage LP fundraising sequence, when to start deploying and when to start raising the next fund.

principles.text: Write checks big enough to matter to the fund but small enough to leave room for other investors, so you collaborate instead of elbowing people out.
principles.quote: I think it's actually better to deploy Capital that's meaningful for the fun but still leave plenty of room for other people and other co-investors and become more of a collaborative player

principles.text: Venture is power-law driven, so build a portfolio with enough shots on goal to catch the one or two companies that return the fund.
principles.quote: at the end of the day you know it's power law so it's like going to be one company two companies that really you know drives a majority of the returns and we wanted to have enough shots at bat to find those companies

principles.text: Raise LPs in sequence: your trusted network first, then referrals from existing LPs, then an open community raise.
principles.quote: I break it into three categories of people that we reached out to um and in this actual sequence as well so Step One is people in your network that you know that you trust that trust you

principles.text: Make LP referrals easy by asking existing LPs for introductions to specific kinds of people and handing them a ready-made blurb to forward.
principles.quote: basically you want to decrease the friction to make it easy for them to take that action and what we found is like really good results

principles.text: A community LP round of small checks (capped at $10K) can build a network of operators and founders who feed deal flow, help the portfolio and assist with diligence.
principles.quote: our goal with that was was not necessarily to raise money we already basically reached our Target but it was really to build more this network of strong operators and Founders as LPS who could be a source of deal flow

principles.text: Keep funds small: a very large first fund forces long institutional fundraising when you could just start deploying a smaller one and raise bigger later.
principles.quote: I'm very much a pro small funds personally for a bunch of reasons

sources.title: Ryan Hoover on starting out: ship small, join communities, hire to fill gaps
sources.originalTitle: Acadium Stories #18: Ryan Hoover — Advice for starting out in your career
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt grew from a 20-minute email list experiment into a company, and why building in public, prioritizing by metric impact, and hiring specialists matter. He also gives career advice: create things online, join communities, skip over-planning, and ask for help.

principles.text: Treat an idea as a cheap experiment: put something on the internet instead of writing a business plan.
principles.quote: you can't you know write a 20-page business plan and you know just uh you know think your way into a company uh you really just need to build and create

principles.text: Build something useful and fun for yourself; the intrinsic motivation helps you push through hard times.
principles.quote: maybe just build something that seems useful for yourself and that seems fun and that's a really good way to one hopefully build something that you and many other people might like

principles.text: Build in public: transparency doubles as content marketing and gets feedback before you write code.
principles.quote: it was great content marketing frankly if you just look at it purely from a content perspective people were thirsting for authenticity

principles.text: Prioritize features by the one metric they target and estimated impact; skip marginal gains and chase 2-5x bets.
principles.quote: you should primarily be working on the things that you know probably won't work but might have a two three five x kind of impact on the business

principles.text: Close skill gaps mainly by hiring specialists, and ask investors and mentors for help earlier.
principles.quote: the biggest leverage that you're gonna have is building a team and ultimately as you scale to you you hopefully hire more specialists and experts in areas that you are not

principles.text: Early in a career: create things online, join communities without transactional networking, and pick a rocket-ship company.
principles.quote: year four that might introduce you to your future co-founder your future investors to maybe some insight that you didn't know before

sources.title: Ryan Hoover on product flywheels, community-led building, and launching clearly
sources.originalTitle: Fireside Chat (Ryan Hoover, Product Hunt, CEO & Founder and Yuri Ageev, ProductSense, Founder)
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover shares lessons from his early PM mistakes and from building Product Hunt. He covers involving the community before building, designing growth as a flywheel, spotting opportunity in platform and behavior shifts, adding structure to startup teams, and launching with plain messaging instead of selling the vision.

principles.text: Share mockups with your community early to get feedback and make contributors feel they shaped the product.
principles.quote: we'll send in like an envision mock-up to the community and say hey what do you think about this thing that we're building with some context and details and just solicit advice feedback

principles.text: Map your product as a flywheel and fix the highest-friction step to drive growth.
principles.quote: the more efficient that flywheel works the more people that do each action the the lower our friction between each action the better the system works

principles.text: Validate demand cheaply with a fake-door test before building, such as a button that only counts clicks.
principles.quote: we just put the button there and counted the clicks so it was a little bit of a Wizard of Oz test but it proved out that people wanted to log in with Google

principles.text: Avoid chasing trends you have no founder-market fit for; build what you are equipped to build.
principles.quote: trends could be a trap where people get attracted to this trend and they start building a product that they have no business building

principles.text: Startups benefit from structure: domain ownership, titles and team leads beat a fully flat organization.
principles.quote: a lack of titles and a lack of kind of structure and a hierarchy can actually be a really bad thing even first of all startups

principles.text: Launching is continuous, and customer feedback should inform your decisions, not dictate what you build.
principles.quote: the goal isn't for their customer to tell you what - bill it's for the customer to inform your decisions of what to build

sources.title: Ryan Hoover on becoming a product manager: empathy, side projects, and communication
sources.originalTitle: Product Management Interview with Ryan Hoover, Product Hunt Founder
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover recounts learning product management on the job at Playhaven and what skills mattered: empathy, humility, verifying assumptions with data and customer talks, and over-communicating with engineers. He also argues side projects and blogging are the best way to prove product skill without a PM title.

principles.text: Empathy for customers and teammates is the core product manager skill; understand their day-to-day and how they are measured.
principles.quote: I think part of it is empathy is the recurring theme that probably every single p.m. would would say at some point

principles.text: Stay humble: treat your assumptions as probably wrong and verify them with customers and data.
principles.quote: you have to also realize that your assumption is probably not correct as confident as you are so it's good to have confidence but also to verify those assumptions

principles.text: Start from usage data to form hypotheses, then take them into customer conversations to validate.
principles.quote: you start building these hypotheses around why they're using some things and whether or not using others and you can take that information with you when you go talk to customers

principles.text: In customer interviews, explore the problem space first and only show your idea or prototype near the end.
principles.quote: we start with not here's this cool idea aren't you gonna love it that's a bad way of understand what they actually need but we do start exploring questions around that space

principles.text: Without PM experience, prove your process and ability to execute by shipping a side project, newsletter, meetup or podcast; no code required.
principles.quote: you do is demonstrating your process your ability to execute

principles.text: Cultivate a mindset of experimentation and curiosity; skills accumulate from repeated experiments.
principles.quote: I think it's sort of having the right frame of mind and being open to experimentation and curiosity and continually doing that over time that you'll you'll learn things without realizing it

sources.title: Build an audience first: Ryan Hoover on how writing seeded Product Hunt
sources.originalTitle: Building a startup? Build an audience, first.
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover argues founders should build an audience before (or alongside) building the product, via blogging, podcasting, newsletters or meetups. He says an audience helps with recruiting, user acquisition and research, and that his own writing and newsletter became the seed of the Product Hunt community.

principles.text: Build an audience yourself first, before looking for co-founders or customers.
principles.quote: Build an audience yourself first.

principles.text: Use content and community formats (blog, podcast, newsletter, meetups) to build that audience.
principles.quote: You can do this by blogging, podcasting, starting a newsletter, hosting meetups, etc.

principles.text: An audience makes recruiting possible when you are pre-product and pre-traction.
principles.quote: When you’re pre-product + pre-traction, it’s difficult to convince anyone (technical or not) to join.

principles.text: Acquisition is hard before and after launch, so de-risk it early with an audience.
principles.quote: Acquisition is difficult pre AND post-product. Sooner you can de-risk this the better.

principles.text: Audience-building doubles as customer development and shows who you are building for.
principles.quote: Audience-building leads to customer development and a better understanding of who you’re building for.

principles.text: A relatively small audience can be the seed that launches a product; Product Hunt would have been DOA without his.
principles.quote: These projects helped build relationships and an audience that became the seed of the Product Hunt community, and while relatively small, it established a platform. Without this, Product Hunt would have been DOA.

sources.title: How Ryan Hoover validated Product Hunt in 20 minutes with a Linkydink email group
sources.originalTitle: The 20-Minute MVP
sources.summary: Ryan describes prototyping Product Hunt with an existing link-sharing tool instead of building an app, gaining 170 subscribers in two weeks. He argues an MVP exists to learn and test assumptions, and gives a three-step framework to run before writing any code.

principles.text: An MVP is for learning, not building: it exists to validate or invalidate assumptions.
principles.quote: The purpose of an MVP is to learn, to validate and invalidate assumptions. There are almost always faster ways to do this than building a product.

principles.text: Don't assume an MVP must be coded; use existing tools to test the idea first.
principles.quote: Entrepreneurs often assume an MVP needs to be “built.”

principles.text: List your assumptions, then test the riskiest one first with cheap tactics.
principles.quote: With your riskiest assumption in hand, brainstorm ways to validate or invalidate that assumption quickly.

principles.text: Use landing pages, Wizard of Oz tests and customer interviews to get feedback before building.
principles.quote: Use landing page tests, Wizard of Oz experiments, customer interviews, and other tactics to gather feedback from your target audience.

principles.text: If an assumption is invalid, rethink the idea and audience; if valid, test the next riskiest assumption.
principles.quote: If you’re lucky enough to be right, congratulate yourself and test the next riskiest assumption.

principles.text: Early traction relies on an audience and network earned over years, not overnight.
principles.quote: Successful companies don’t start up overnight; they are founded upon years of experience and help from others that must be earned.

sources.title: Email-First Startups: why starting with email validates ideas fast
sources.originalTitle: Email-First Startups
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover argues that launching a startup as an email product is a lightweight way to validate an idea. Email is fast to build, forces focus, creates habits, reaches everyone, and later feeds web or mobile offerings. He cites Timehop, iDoneThis, Thrillist, AngelList and Sunrise as examples.

principles.text: Email-first products let you validate ideas faster than building a full website or app.
principles.quote: Generally it’s faster to build an email-first product than a full website or mobile application. The sooner you can get your product into customers hands, the sooner you can learn what does and doesn’t stick.

principles.text: Email is asynchronous, so you can fake functionality with manual processes before automating.
principles.quote: Email is largely asynchronous, allowing room to fake functionality with manual processes (see Wizard of Oz experiments).

principles.text: Email's limits force you to stay focused on one narrow use case instead of feature creep.
principles.quote: Email doesn’t afford feature-creep. Email-first products are limited, forcing you to be succinct and focused on particular use case.

principles.text: Email can become part of users' daily habits because people check it several times a day.
principles.quote: We check our email several times a day. If done right, email products can become a part of users’ daily habits.

principles.text: Email works for everyone, regardless of device or operating system, making it a ubiquitous channel.
principles.quote: Everyone users email and email doesn’t discriminate against devices or operating systems.

principles.text: A reliable email channel makes up-selling and cross-selling to web or mobile products easier.
principles.quote: Up/cross-selling to web or mobile offerings is easier when there’s a reliable channel for communication.

sources.title: How Product Hunt made its first dollar: Ship, Deals and Promoted Products
sources.originalTitle: How we made our first dollar at Product Hunt
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains why Product Hunt delayed monetizing to focus on community growth, then launched three revenue lines (Ship SaaS, Deals, Promoted Products) that booked over $250K in weeks. He stresses focus, charging for things that fit the community, and reinvesting revenue to keep building.

principles.text: Every startup needs a focused goal early, because each to-do item displaces another.
principles.quote: There’s no right way to startup but every team needs a focused goal, especially in the beginning. After all, everything on a startup’s to-do list ultimately takes the place of something else.

principles.text: Delay monetization to grow the community first; it's a valid choice, not the only right one.
principles.quote: Some startups choose to make money on day one while others choose to prioritize things differently.

principles.text: Build paid products from community feedback and observed needs, with a small dedicated team.
principles.quote: On September 14 we introduced Ship, a toolkit to help makers build awesome products, inspired by the community’s feedback and learnings supporting thousands of products launch every year.

principles.text: Formalize behavior the community already does (like offering discounts) into a paid offering.
principles.quote: We wanted to encourage this behavior and give the Product Hunt community access to discounted and exclusive deals, so we launched a paid offering to host and promote these deals directly on Product Hunt.

principles.text: Diversify revenue across several offerings once the first one is growing.
principles.quote: Although Ship is growing nicely, we understand the importance of revenue diversification, so we expanded into a few other offerings.

principles.text: Be thoughtful about what you charge for, and reinvest revenue so you can keep building long term.
principles.quote: If done right, generating revenue and achieving profitability will ensure that we can continue building forever and ultimately lead to a better product as we reinvest capital into the platform.

sources.title: How a job rejection at Monkey Inferno led to Product Hunt LIVE VIDEO
sources.originalTitle: From Rejection to Product Hunt
sources.summary: Ryan tells how he was turned down for an Entrepreneur-in-Residence role by Shaan Puri, stayed in touch, and two years later partnered with Shaan's team (Blab) to launch live video on Product Hunt LIVE. The lesson is about relationships, transparency and reframing "no".

principles.text: Never burn bridges: staying in touch after a rejection can seed future partnerships.
principles.quote: This is a great example of how important it is to never burn a bridge in Silicon Valley (or anywhere, really). Product Hunt LIVE VIDEO is happening because we stayed in touch and genuinely liked each other.

sources.title: The community trap: utility must come before community
sources.originalTitle: The community trap
sources.summary: Ryan argues "community" is an overused buzzword and that founders chase it before they have a product people actually need. Drawing on Product Hunt's early community building, he says utility is what brings people in, and community is what retains them and spreads word of mouth, but only after utility exists.

principles.text: Community is secondary to utility, for every company.
principles.quote: But community is secondary to utility.

principles.text: People don't want to join a community; they want something that solves a problem or gives clear value.
principles.quote: No one wants to join a community. They want utility – something that solves a problem or provides clear value to their life.

principles.text: Utility gets people in the door; community keeps them there and brings their friends.
principles.quote: Utility brings people through the door, while community keeps them at the party, inviting their friends.

principles.text: Done well, community drives word of mouth, retention and a sustainable brand, but only after utility.
principles.quote: When done well, community drives WOM, increases retention, and creates a sustainable brand. However, this must come after utility.

principles.text: Define the specific problem and who it's for before trying to build community.
principles.quote: Too many founders reach out to me asking how to build community before they've figured out utility (i.e. the specific problem they're solving and for whom).

principles.text: Focusing on community without clear utility is a trap.
principles.quote: As much as I advocate for community building, focusing on it without clear utility is a trap.

sources.title: The Rise of Maker Communities: where makers connect and the gaps left
sources.originalTitle: The Rise of Maker Communities
sources.summary: Ryan argues that building products has become cheap and easy enough that one person can out-ship a team, which shifts the bottleneck to getting feedback and standing out. He maps maker communities by focus (vertical, role, demographic, general) and spots opportunities in underserved audiences and mobile.

principles.text: As building gets cheap, one person can out-ship a team, so the scarce thing becomes distribution and feedback.
principles.quote: Today a single person can build more than a team of ten in a weekend. We see it every day on Product Hunt.

principles.text: Easier making creates a new problem: getting feedback and breaking out from the noise.
principles.quote: This is a good thing, but it introduces another problem: Difficulty in getting feedback and breaking out from the noise.

principles.text: Growing creator audiences create demand for communities to connect, learn and collaborate with peers.
principles.quote: There seems to be increasing demand to connect, learn, and collaborate with other makers as new spaces emerge.

principles.text: Look for underserved audiences: where one role is saturated with communities, other types of makers lack a home.
principles.quote: There are many underserved audiences. Engineering-focused communities are relatively abundant which makes sense considering the evolution of the internet.

principles.text: Young communities signal a growing desire for community in every niche.
principles.quote: Most communities are young, illustrating a growing desire to build community for every niche.

principles.text: Most maker communities are desktop-first, so mobile may be a bigger opportunity.
principles.quote: Most communities are focused on the web and desktop experience.

sources.title: Why you should build your product in public: feedback, buy-in and excitement
sources.originalTitle: Why you should build your product in public
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover shared unfinished Product Hunt comment-system mockups and got 50+ annotated pieces of feedback within 24 hours. He argues most startups, especially those building a community, gain more than they lose by involving users in the design process. He names three benefits (buy-in, early feedback, excitement) and points to companies like Buffer, Quibb and Assembly as examples.

principles.text: Share work before it's finished; early public feedback arrives fast and in volume.
principles.quote: The design certainly wasn’t perfect. It wasn’t even complete. But I shared them anyway and am glad I did.

principles.text: Most startups, especially community builders, have more to gain than lose from building in public.
principles.quote: the majority of startups, especially those building a community, have more to gain than lose.

principles.text: Acknowledging and using user feedback builds ownership, engagement and loyalty.
principles.quote: People want to be heard and when their feedback is acknowledged, their investment in the product increases.

principles.text: Get fresh-eyed feedback before design is committed to code, and learn which feedback to act on.
principles.quote: Early feedback, ideally before design is committed to code, results in a better product and less waste.

principles.text: Sneak peeks create excitement that turns users into evangelists.
principles.quote: This excitement captures the attention of consumers and creates evangelists for the product.

principles.text: Building in public isn't for everyone, but sharing your story openly helps build community.
principles.quote: While not every startup can or should build in public, I appreciate those that do

sources.title: Generative AI and Moats: why media incumbents are vulnerable and human networks are defensible
sources.originalTitle: Generative AI and Moats
sources.summary: Ryan argues that generative AI will challenge incumbents who built content libraries, since on-demand media can be personalized, niche and unlicensed. He sees the innovator's dilemma at work and says real-human networks are the more durable moat, leaving room for new startups to rethink media.

principles.text: Startups are born from change, which creates vulnerabilities for incumbents that fail to adapt.
principles.quote: Successful startups are born from change. Regulatory updates, cultural movements, and new technologies introduce vulnerabilities for incumbents that fail to adapt.

principles.text: Generative media beats static libraries by adapting in real time to the user and serving the smallest niches.
principles.quote: Unlike traditional static media, generative AI media can adapt in real-time to the user's requests, preferences, and context. It can appeal to the smallest niche.

principles.text: Incumbents struggle to adopt new tech when it cuts against their business model or existing stakeholders.
principles.quote: Of course, incumbents can also leverage this technology. But if it interferes with their business model or existing stakeholders, they may struggle to adapt.

principles.text: Content libraries are a weaker moat when synthetic content is as good and far cheaper; timeless cultural relevance protects some more than others.
principles.quote: The defensibility of content libraries may be at risk when synthetic content is just as good (or better) and available at a fraction of the cost.

principles.text: As media becomes abundant and cheap, bet on moats built around real humans, since people still crave connection and status.
principles.quote: In a future where media is abundant and cheap (and humans are synthetic), I'm increasingly bullish on companies that establish a moat with real humans.

principles.text: Even when incumbents might adapt, the gap gives new startups room to reimagine how media is consumed.
principles.quote: But until then, there's an opportunity for new startups to reimagine (literally) media consumption.

sources.title: Selfish investing: why Ryan Hoover backs startups building products he wants
sources.originalTitle: Selfish investing
sources.summary: Ryan argues the build-for-yourself advice also works for investing: he gets most excited about founders building products he'd personally use. He lays out five themes he wants to back (distributed living, edge health, people investing, new work, weird consumer), each from his own life as the customer.

principles.text: Solving your own problem makes it easier to empathize with the audience and know what to build.
principles.quote: Easier to empathize with the target audience and know what to build when you’re the customer.

principles.text: Founders who speak firsthand about a problem are more convincing to hires and investors.
principles.quote: More convincing to future hires and investors when you can speak firsthand about the problem or opportunity.

principles.text: As an investor, avoid imposing your own view of the future, but get extra excited by products you personally want and can give customer input on.
principles.quote: But I personally get very excited talking to founders that are building products that I want.

principles.text: Venture is limited to a narrow set of founders and its company-level economics can misalign founder and company incentives, creating room for new asset classes.
principles.quote: There’s an opportunity to create a new asset class that aligns people with their long-term goals and capitalist incentives.

principles.text: Fractional work is inefficient because people burn time sourcing clients; platforms should rethink talent matching and the economics of work.
principles.quote: I’m interested in platforms that are rethinking the talent-matching and economic system of work.

principles.text: Back novel consumer products built for emerging behaviors; the weirder and more counter-intuitive, the better, as AI reshapes UGC and interfaces.
principles.quote: I’ve always been drawn to novel consumer products, especially those that build for emerging behaviors. The more weird and counter-intuitive, the better.

sources.title: Why Ryan Hoover invests in small venture funds as an LP
sources.originalTitle: Why I invest in venture funds
sources.summary: Ryan explains why he has backed about 30 venture funds over 8 years: learning, deal flow, supporting fellow investors, and (lastly) returns. He focuses on small pre-seed/seed funds, connected generalists or deep specialists, and investors who take the job seriously.

principles.text: Back small funds (ideally sub-$30M) at pre-seed and seed; they have historically returned more on average.
principles.quote: Small funds, ideally sub-$30M, investing in pre-seed and seed. Small funds have historically delivered better returns on average

principles.text: A small check can return a small fund, while big funds must deploy far more capital to get meaningful ownership.
principles.quote: A $300K check into an early-stage opportunity can be a multiple-fund returner for small funds, whereas larger ($250M+) funds are required to invest far more capital to capture meaningful ownership and outcomes.

principles.text: Large funds often need to lead rounds, competing against multi-stage funds with big teams and scout networks.
principles.quote: These funds often need to lead, beating out a growing number of competing investors, including the behemoth multi-stage funds with massive teams and scout networks.

principles.text: Use fund LP stakes as a source of learning and deal flow, not just returns.
principles.quote: I love reading quarterly LP updates. Investors highlight new investments, explain their perspectives on the market, and share the results of their experiments.

principles.text: Mix connected generalists (deal flow) with deep specialists (diversification into verticals you don't invest in).
principles.quote: Generalist funds are helpful for deal flow as they align with what we typically invest in at Weekend Fund. Specialist funds are helpful for diversification

principles.text: Back investors who treat managing other people's money as a serious responsibility.
principles.quote: Managing other people’s money is a responsibility. I want to back investors who are thoughtful, disciplined, and committed to the craft.

sources.title: Weekend Fund: why Ryan Hoover started a $3M fund for nights-and-weekends founders
sources.originalTitle: Weekend Fund
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover announces Weekend Fund, a $3M angel fund backing founders at the earliest stage. He argues many of the biggest companies began as side projects driven by curiosity, and that the next big thing is probably being built on nights and weekends right now. He also notes Product Hunt itself started as a side project.

principles.text: Big companies often start as nights-and-weekends side projects driven by curiosity, not as formal startups.
principles.quote: Some of the most transformational companies started as a side project driven by curiosity and an eagerness to build something new.

principles.text: Back curious, creative builders early: the next big thing is probably being built on nights and weekends right now.
principles.quote: Right now, the next Facebook is being built on nights and weekends and its these curious, creative founders that I’d like to support.

principles.text: Start with a simple personal goal and build with friends; a side project can grow into a platform when momentum appears.
principles.quote: The goal was simple: I wanted to share and discover interesting new apps and products with friends.

principles.text: Community and friends who help build early are essential to a product's existence.
principles.quote: I worked nights and weekends and friends joined to help build the community (of course, without them Product Hunt wouldn’t exist).

principles.text: What smart people do for fun on weekends predicts what everyone will do at work in a decade.
principles.quote: What the smartest people do on the weekend is what everyone else will do during the week in ten years.

principles.text: Operator angels with full-time jobs can use cheap fund infrastructure to invest without the back-office burden.
principles.quote: Angel Funds is a potentially great option for operator angels, people like me who work full-time at their startup.

sources.title: Second-Time Founder Anxiety: why starting again is harder, and why second-timers still have the edge
sources.originalTitle: Second-Time Founder Anxiety
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover describes the mental toll of founding (a threatened lawsuit, an internet mob, near-bankruptcy) and why founders hesitate to start a second company. He splits the anxiety into three fears (past pain, reputation, "my next thing has to be huge") and argues second-time founders are still better equipped if they start small and act.

principles.text: First-timers benefit from naivete; scars make second-time founders hesitate. Don't let that stop you from trying.
principles.quote: Second-time[1] founders have scars that can introduce hesitation. They know how hard it is, so they make excuses not to pursue ideas or simply bow out of entrepreneurship.

principles.text: Use long-term regret as a test for whether to start an idea.
principles.quote: How would you feel 10 years from now knowing that you didn't try to bring your idea to life?

principles.text: Reputation pressure is mostly imagined; people who care about you care about you, not your startup results.
principles.quote: The truth is, most people don't care about you and the people that truly do, care about you for you, not for your startup success or lack thereof.

principles.text: Don't over-intellectualize into paralysis; solve a specific problem for specific people and start small.
principles.quote: It's OK to start small because even the smallest nudges can lead to an avalanche.

principles.text: Second-time founders have real advantages: experience, network, and credibility. Recognize the edge with humility.
principles.quote: Second-time founders have more experience building, recruiting, raising, selling, and scaling a startup.

principles.text: Building something that solves your own problem makes it fun to start again.
principles.quote: A few months ago I started working on a couple projects that solve my own problems[2]. I'm having so much fun.

sources.title: Easter Egg Marketing: How Snapchat, Apple, Lyft and Google use hidden surprises to spread
sources.originalTitle: Easter Egg Marketing: How Snapchat, Apple, and Google Hook You
sources.summary: Ryan argues that Easter eggs (hidden features or inside jokes) are a powerful, cheap form of marketing. They get people talking, bond users who share the secret, and build a memorable brand. He cites Snapchat's B&W filter, Siri's jokes, Lyft's pink mustaches, and Google's "do a barrel roll".

principles.text: Hidden features and surprises turn users into marketers because people love sharing secrets.
principles.quote: People love knowing secrets but they like to share them even more.

principles.text: Shared secrets create an in-group that bonds users and strengthens community.
principles.quote: Those aware of the Easter egg secret share a common understanding, separating people “in the know” from outsiders. This helps form a bond between holders of the secret and strengthens a community.

principles.text: Delight builds a memorable brand connection through a shared understanding not everyone has.
principles.quote: Easter eggs are fun and produce a “WOW!” effect. This delight forms a memorable connection between the brand and its users through a shared understanding not privy to everyone.

principles.text: Free word-of-mouth from product quirks can outperform a huge ad budget.
principles.quote: The free marketing instigated by these Easter eggs was arguably more impactful than Apple’s multi-million dollar advertising budget.

principles.text: Provoking curiosity beats plastering your brand name; it drives recall in competitive markets.
principles.quote: Instead of plastering its brand name on the side panels of its cars, Lyft used an Easter egg to catch people’s attention and get them talking.
