principles.text: Playful extras with no core value still give the brand personality and get users to spread it.
principles.quote: Although Easter eggs provide no value to the product’s core offering, it creates a personality to the brand and encourages users to engage in marketing the product by forwarding it to friends.

sources.title: Why YourStack failed: five product mistakes and one burnout lesson
sources.originalTitle: Why YourStack failed
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains why YourStack, a product-recommendation spin-off from Product Hunt, failed after a decent launch of 15K signups. The causes were an infrequent use case, too-broad scope, web-first instead of mobile-first, overbuilding before launch, and founder burnout. He still believes in the thesis that trusted recommendations drive product adoption.

principles.text: Check how often the core need occurs. If the internal trigger is infrequent, a daily-use habit never forms.
principles.quote: if the underlying internal trigger (e.g. a desire to discover and/or buy products) is infrequent, you will constantly fight against the natural state of what people want when attempting to design for DAU adoption.

principles.text: Start narrow. A tight focus makes the experience easier to build and the target audience and go-to-market clearer.
principles.quote: The more narrow the focus, the easier it is to build the ideal experience for that use case or interest. It also clarifies your target audience, simplifying the messaging and GTM strategy to reach those people.

principles.text: For wide consumer audiences needing frequent engagement, build mobile-first. Retrofitting mobile later splits focus.
principles.quote: If you’re building for a wide audience of consumers, especially one which demands frequent engagement, mobile should probably be the priority.

principles.text: Launch sooner to test the core interaction model. Extra features delay launch, split engagement and add surface to maintain.
principles.quote: We should have launched YourStack, or a version of it, much sooner to test the core interaction model and assumptions.

principles.text: Expect many iterations to reach product-market fit, especially in consumer social. The first version is never it.
principles.quote: Some founders underestimate the number of iterations required to build something people want, especially in consumer social where the smallest changes can make a massive difference. The first version is never _it_.

principles.text: Authentic recommendations from trusted people are the strongest driver of product adoption, and curation matters more as launching products gets cheaper.
principles.quote: The best way to drive product adoption is through an authentic recommendation from a trusted person.

sources.title: How to come up with side project ideas: eight places to look for inspiration
sources.originalTitle: How to come up with side project ideas
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover lists eight practical ways to find side project ideas, from reflecting on your own day-to-day to exploring emerging platforms, Product Hunt, GitHub and hackathons. He argues side projects make you a better builder and can grow into real businesses, as Product Hunt did.

principles.text: Side projects build skills and can become real businesses.
principles.quote: They can make you a better engineer, designer, marketer, or salesperson. Side projects can even turn into a business (Product Hunt started as a side project).

principles.text: Mine your own daily frustrations: log your day and spot what could be improved.
principles.quote: Often the best ideas come from one’s own experiences. Write a detailed diary of everything you do in a typical day and identify things that could be improved.

principles.text: Ask friends about their pain points to find problems worth solving.
principles.quote: Run through the same exercise above with your friends. Try to find frustrations or pain points that could be eliminated.

principles.text: New platforms create new opportunities, so dig into their APIs and docs early.
principles.quote: As platforms emerge and evolve, new opportunities arise.

principles.text: Take a feature of a favorite product and turn it into a standalone product.
principles.quote: Look at some of your favorite apps, sites, or products. Can you repurpose and improve upon one of its features as a standalone product?

principles.text: Great ideas are rarely forced in a brainstorm; stay exposed to the world and they find you.
principles.quote: It’s difficult to manufacture a truly great idea in a whiteboarding session. Sometimes they’re serendipitous, triggered by stories and changes in the world.

sources.title: Non-obvious problems: why founders should chase problems the market hasn't priced in
sources.originalTitle: Non-obvious problems
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover adapts the venture "right and non-consensus" framework to founders: obvious problems with obvious solutions rarely win, while non-obvious problems offer less competition and a shot at owning a new category. He uses Calendly and Deel as examples and lists questions for finding non-obvious problems.

principles.text: Obvious problem plus obvious solution is unlikely to succeed: past failed attempts and crowded competitors make it hard to break through.
principles.quote: If you pursue an obvious problem with an obvious solution, you're unlikely to succeed. Why? There's likely a graveyard of similar attempts before you that didn't work for legitimate reasons.

principles.text: An obvious problem can work with a non-obvious solution, enabled by new tech, cultural shifts, or an earned insight, but expect fast-followers.
principles.quote: The non-obvious solution might be possible only now due to technology or cultural shifts.

principles.text: Non-obvious problems mean far less competition, a chance to lead a new category, and customers who are less inundated with pitches.
principles.quote: you'll be met with far less competition and the potential to establish yourself as the leader of a new category. Your target customer will be less inundated with potential solutions, likely more receptive.

principles.text: Non-obvious problems are usually driven by a change in the world: new, growing in market size, or becoming more painful.
principles.quote: Non-obvious problems are often driven by a change in the world. It might be a new problem, a problem that is affecting a growing market, or a problem that is becoming more painful.

principles.text: Markets often dismiss early non-obvious problems as niche (Deel's remote payroll in 2018), only for them to explode later.
principles.quote: In 2018 the company was focused on remote payroll for globally distributed teams. This wasn't viewed as an obvious problem at the time, discounted as too "niche".

principles.text: Find non-obvious problems through your own unique experience: hacked-together fixes, worsening problems, recurring complaints, and a strong view of the future.
principles.quote: Have you hacked together a solution to a problem that few people have identified?

sources.title: The Rise of "No Code": why makers no longer need to be engineers
sources.originalTitle: The Rise of No Code
sources.summary: Ryan argues that GUI-based "no code" tools are cutting the time, cost and expertise needed to build software, much as cloud hosting replaced racking servers. He expects more makers, more MVPs built without code, and growing demand for maker communities and monetization tools.

principles.text: No code tools sharply cut the cost and time to build software; expect another ~10x drop.
principles.quote: The time and cost to build software products will drop by another 10x. This is part of our thesis at @ProductHunt.

principles.text: Even teams with engineers should pick no code when it is faster to build and easier to maintain.
principles.quote: Of course the company has an engineering team and could build anything they imagine, but he opted to use “no code” tools because it was faster to build and easier to maintain.

principles.text: Hard does not mean better; as tools mature, doing it the old way becomes foolish.
principles.quote: We often perceive things that are hard to do as better. Sometimes that’s true. But as these “no code” tools advance, it will be silly to do it the old way.

principles.text: Abstracting infrastructure is the precedent: experts use hosted services rather than rack their own servers.
principles.quote: Even the most experienced, talented dev ops engineers use their services to get started and scale. It would be foolish for them to spend the time racking their own servers.

principles.text: Lower barriers to making bring a wider, more diverse set of creators and ideas.
principles.quote: You no longer need to become a programmer to build things on the internet, empowering a new wave of makers from different backgrounds and perspectives.

principles.text: More makers means more demand for community, plus tools to monetize, find collaborators and get the word out.
principles.quote: Maker communities will become increasingly popular[3] as everyone becomes a maker. So will tools to help makers monetize, find side project buddies, and get the word out.

sources.title: 5 Years of Product Hunt: Ryan Hoover's lessons on building a startup
sources.originalTitle: 5 Years of Product Hunt
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover reflects on five years of building Product Hunt, sharing the mistakes and learnings from running a venture-backed company. Topics include org structure, repeating your mission, hiring, distributed teams, avoiding pointless redesigns, and planning for fundraising and acquisition early.

principles.text: Some structure and clear ownership beats a fully flat org; flatness can backfire.
principles.quote: For years Product Hunt had a very flat structure, driven by my desire to encourage autonomy and a culture of mutual respect across the org. But this lack of structure and clear areas of ownership resulted in the opposite effect.

principles.text: Over-communicate mission and strategy; if teammates ask what and why, it's the founder's failure.
principles.quote: I did a poor job of communicating our mission and strategy clearly and frequently to my teammates that are often heads down on a very specific part of the business.

principles.text: A founder's words carry outsized weight, so choose them carefully.
principles.quote: The ideas a founder promotes or shoots down can dramatically shift the team’s focus and motivation, for better or worse.

principles.text: Hiring the wrong people can sink a startup; fit depends on product, culture and stage.
principles.quote: Sometimes it’s simply not the right fit for the product, culture, or stage of the company at that time.

principles.text: Distributed teams unlock global talent, but may not work for everyone or at large scale.
principles.quote: This has enabled us to hire amazing talent from anywhere in the world, not just the <1% that live in or can relocate to San Francisco.

principles.text: Skip cosmetic redesigns unless they change user behavior or metrics.
principles.quote: Don’t let your ego get in the way of prioritizing what’s right for the business and your users.

sources.title: Why sourcing and picking edges vanish for investors and winning allocations is what matters
sources.originalTitle: All that matters is winning
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover argues that the traditional VC edges of sourcing and picking startups are eroding because public signaling, discovery tools and AI make every deal visible and evaluable by everyone. What remains is winning the allocation, which depends on helping founders and earning access.

principles.text: Sourcing and picking edges are eroding; winning the allocation is what matters most.
principles.quote: In other words, there’s no edge in sourcing and picking in the near future. All that matters is winning.

principles.text: Everyone will see every deal as founders signal publicly and tools surface them.
principles.quote: It’s obvious when a founder is preparing to raise. They launch on Product Hunt. They get loud on X

principles.text: AI will evaluate deals and founders more thoroughly than humans can.
principles.quote: It will comb through data rooms more thoroughly than any human could, instantly evaluating comps, the market, and the team’s background.

principles.text: Spend less time hunting and analyzing, more time helping founders; that is the input to winning the next deal.
principles.quote: They can spend more time helping founders\[1\], the core input into their ability to win the next deal.

principles.text: Proprietary, non-public data is the exception where sourcing and picking can still produce alpha.
principles.quote: Investors that have truly proprietary, non-public data may still have alpha in sourcing and picking.

principles.text: Reputation is earned by helping founders; brand is shaped by perception.
principles.quote: Reputation is what you earn by helping founders, but brand is informed by perception, for better or worse.

sources.title: Vibecoding is self-expression: why consumer utilities are exposed and what stays defensible
sources.originalTitle: Vibecoding is self-expression
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover argues that vibecoding turns software creation into entertainment and self-expression, which threatens the durability of many consumer utilities. When features are easy to clone, defensibility shifts to social graphs, distribution, licensing, data moats and hardware, and the strongest products combine several.

principles.text: For consumer software, value shifts from output to the act of making it; creation itself becomes the product.
principles.quote: Software stops being purely a _time-saving device_ and starts becoming a _time-spending activity_. The value isn’t only in the output. It’s in the act of making it.

principles.text: Consumer utilities are more exposed to vibecoding than B2B, which is protected by trust, security and inertia.
principles.quote: In B2B, software selection is constrained by trust, security, integration complexity, and organizational inertia. Consumer is different.

principles.text: A product's real value can sit in its network rather than its simple core function; social graphs stay defensible.
principles.quote: At its core, LinkedIn is a simple online resume to showcase where you’ve worked but the real value is in the network

principles.text: Distribution outlasts code: a product buildable in a weekend can still win on its flywheel.
principles.quote: The core product—a daily leaderboard of product launches—could be vibecoded in a weekend but the value isn’t in the code.

principles.text: Licensing, regulation, proprietary data and hardware remain hard to replicate when software gets easy to build.
principles.quote: Spotify succeeded because it was able to secure licenses with major labels, aggregating the world’s music into a single destination. Replicating this is incredibly difficult and time-consuming.

principles.text: The most durable products stack multiple moats rather than relying on just one.
principles.quote: The most durable products will incorporate more than just one of the above.

sources.title: Blogging is the New Resume: why writing beats a resume for non-technical roles
sources.originalTitle: Blogging is the New Resume
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover argues that resumes poorly communicate ability, and that blogging does what GitHub does for developers: it shows how you think. He shares how a year of writing built a network that produced job offers and seeded the Product Hunt launch, then lists the caveats of blogging.

principles.text: Show your thinking publicly instead of telling it on a resume; blogging reveals thought process and culture fit.
principles.quote: Blogging is an effective way to illustrate expertise, personality, and most importantly, thought process.

principles.text: Writing builds a network that creates opportunities when you need them, including jobs and founder intros.
principles.quote: When I announced my departure without a plan, the network I grew from blogging, reached out with support.

principles.text: Seed a new product's community with relationships earned through your writing.
principles.quote: We seeded the community largely with relationships formed through my writing, inviting several dozen well-respected startup founders, investors, and product people to participate.

principles.text: Blogging only works if you enjoy it; intrinsic motivation is what sustains it.
principles.quote: If you’re not intrinsically motivated to do so, you’ll quit.

principles.text: Treat blogging as a long-term investment: accept that early posts won't go viral and that quantity leads to quality.
principles.quote: First, you must accept that most people don’t care what you think and that quantity leads to quality.

principles.text: Write about genuine passions, not trending topics, and don't make every post self-promotion.
principles.quote: You should write about growth hacking if you’re genuinely passionate about it.

sources.title: Do "Shitty" Work: prioritize what's needed over what's fun
sources.originalTitle: Do Shitty Work
sources.summary: Ryan argues founders gravitate toward their own craft (coding, wireframing) because it feels like progress, while neglecting unglamorous but critical work like talking to customers and acquiring users. He shares his PlayHaven wireframing mistake and a simple fix: ask "why" about every to-do item.

principles.text: Startups need attention in every area, not just your craft; someone must figure out user acquisition.
principles.quote: successful startups require attention in all areas. You may not have a marketing title but someone has to figure out how to acquire users.

principles.text: Founders default to work they like instead of work they should do, because their craft feels comforting.
principles.quote: If we’re not careful, we prioritize things we _like_ to do over the things we _should_ do.

principles.text: Validate market need and talk to customers and engineers before polishing designs for features.
principles.quote: we should have validated the market need and business feasibility rather than waste time pixel shifting for a product no one wanted.

principles.text: Sketch and use paper prototypes first to bring ideas to life in less time.
principles.quote: I should have [sketched](http://ryanhoover.me/post/48834597557/stop-using-wireframe-tools) first and used paper prototypes to bring my ideas to life in less time.

principles.text: Building output (code, wireframes) gives fake progress; marketing and sales have delayed, unpredictable rewards so people avoid them.
principles.quote: People, on the other hand, are often unpredictable and non-responsive.

principles.text: Hold yourself accountable by asking why about every item on your daily to-do list.
principles.quote: The best way to avoid the fake progress trap is to hold yourself accountable. Each morning as you review your morning to-do list, [ask yourself why]

sources.title: Knowing when to move on: why Ryan Hoover left a good job at PlayHaven
sources.originalTitle: Knowing When It's Time to Move On
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains why he left a well-paid, growing startup role after nearly three years. His top priority is learning, and he'd lost passion for the market. He closes with three questions he uses to evaluate his next opportunity.

principles.text: Make learning your number one priority when deciding whether to stay or go.
principles.quote: my #1 priority is to learn. I’ve grown a _ton_ in the past three years, especially during times of [discomfort](http://ryanhoover.me/post/42414716750/fear-is-healthy) when I am challenged the most.

principles.text: If you don't look back at your past self with embarrassment, you've stopped growing.
principles.quote: When you look back at yourself six months from today and don’t feel embarrassed by your naiveté, there’s a problem. That means you’re not learning, growing.

principles.text: Lost passion for the market is a valid reason to leave, even when pay, growth and team are great.
principles.quote: But if I am to be honest with myself, I’ve lost passion for the market and industry we’re in.

principles.text: Builders who are their own user have an advantage: they understand the problem and persevere longer.
principles.quote: People that build products for themselves have a tremendous advantage because they _are_ their own user.

principles.text: A role narrowing from generalist to specialist can signal it's time to move on.
principles.quote: my role has become more specialized from my generalist roots.

principles.text: Evaluate opportunities with three questions: want, passion, and growth.
principles.quote: Is this really what I want to do? Am I (strongly) passionate about the product, market, and vision? Will I be challenged, learn, and grow to my full potential?

sources.title: How Ryan Hoover launched Product Hunt: build an audience first, find a hole and fill it
sources.originalTitle: Ryan Hoover Talks All Things Product Hunt, Life, & Entrepreneurship
sources.summary: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt grew from a simple email list into a community, crediting years of blogging and relationships for the initial 300 subscribers. He covers early growth via press and word of mouth, the hardest parts of running a company (firing, momentum), and his advice to build an audience before you launch.

principles.text: Spot a problem you personally have or observe, then build the thing you want to exist.
principles.quote: My dad’s always said, “Find a hole and fill it.”

principles.text: Build an audience before launching; distribution is the hardest part of any product.
principles.quote: The hardest thing is distribution for any kind of product, and even just getting beta users can be really difficult, but if you have an audience of people who care about what you’re doing, you now immediately have access to people to support you and what you’re building.

principles.text: Years of writing and relationships gave Product Hunt its first 300 subscribers; without some following it wouldn't have worked.
principles.quote: without the prior years of blogging and building relationships with other people, Product Hunt wouldn’t have worked if I didn’t have at least some sort of following.

principles.text: Press only works as acquisition when the outlet's readers match your target audience; otherwise it's vanity.
principles.quote: For most companies, press doesn’t reach their actual target audience and it can be a more vanity metric than a growth strategy.

principles.text: Early growth came from press plus sharing and word of mouth from users and makers sharing their product pages.
principles.quote: Those two vehicles were really how Product Hunt grew in the first year.

principles.text: Prioritize ruthlessly: write down three must-do things each week so lesser tasks don't consume the week.
principles.quote: in the beginning of every week I write down, essentially three things that need to get done that week. If I get nothing else done but these three things, then it’s still a win.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover covers how to approach a launch on Product Hunt, why to stay narrow and write like a human, and what he would change (monetize sooner, stay vertical, delegate). He also shares how he generates startup ideas, why consumer is hard, and why momentum matters.

chunks.heading: Launching: decide the goal first, then write like a human
chunks.text:
- Ryan's default answer on launching is "it depends." He starts by asking the same question he asks about fundraising: what is the goal?
- Many founders default to customer acquisition, but launching can serve other goals:
  - Recruiting: sharing the story gets people excited about the company, which can help land engineers and designers.
  - Fundraising: more public attention creates momentum and heat around a deal.
  - Feedback from users, and serendipitous partnerships.
  - SEO: positive articles and a product launch page help.
  - Team morale: a launch lets the team celebrate what it built, for example sharing a TechCrunch article with a parent.
- He warns against launching only to chase likes, tweets and votes, but sees morale as an overlooked benefit.
- He has seen tens of thousands of launches on Product Hunt.

chunks.heading: Launch copy and Product Hunt page tactics
chunks.text:
- Founders tend to "write like a PR person and not like a human." Buzzwords and vague language don't click.
- Tagline test: write how your customers describe the product to other people, or how you'd describe it to friends when hanging out.
- Keep the maker introduction short. Most browsers are skimming many ideas looking for something that sparks curiosity, and they won't read an essay.
- The gallery is often the first thing people see. Some of the best launches use it like a slideshow that tells a story, such as a before/after with the product or the evolution of what it can do. Keep it clean and visually interesting.
- Product Hunt has links to guides, FAQs and a post-launch checklist.
- Before the launch, understand who you're building for and how to communicate the value prop, and know where the product fits in the user's mind.
- Results vary widely. B2B products probably do better there than B2C, boring-seeming products that tap into a real need can reach #1, and silly apps do too. Success is partly driven by the zeitgeist of what the early-adopter tech community finds interesting.

chunks.heading: Whether and how to raise money
chunks.text:
- Ryan challenges founders on why they need to raise. Tech culture treats raising as the default first step after an idea, but it's a huge decision and the answer should be clear.
- Product Hunt began as a side project and newsletter. About four to five months passed before incorporating, during which he considered whether to raise, whether he wanted to work on it for years, and whether it was venture-backable. Investors were courting him at the time (late 2013 to early 2014).
- He raised because he needed to hire and had no personal capital. An open-source build was the alternative, but he doesn't think a company should innovate on too many things, including how it builds a product and team.
- Today he thinks he could fund about a year of a very small team himself, so he might not raise venture capital. Product Hunt had no direct competitors that forced a war chest, unlike an Uber and Lyft situation.
- Raise from people aligned with you. Series A, B and C bring different expectations than pre-seed or seed, and founders can't easily quit: "you can't get off."
- Rule of thumb on starting: do you see yourself working on this for a decade? It probably won't last that long, but it's a litmus test of whether you care.
- Call early projects "experiments." The goal is to learn whether people want the thing, not "success." This is partly why it's named Weekend Fund.
- For his next build, he'd like to own 100% for now: "you can always raise venture later, it's a one-way door."

chunks.heading: Regrets building Product Hunt
chunks.text:
- Expanding horizontally was a mistake. Product Hunt tried podcasts, video games and books. He severely underestimated two things: the product experience for discovering games or fashion differs from tech products, and translating a community into other communities is very hard (Reddit is one of the few that did it). He says they should have focused vertically on the tech community.
- Monetize sooner. They raised a seed and a Series A but didn't try to make money until after AngelList acquired them. Once they started generating revenue, they reached cash-flow break-even in about 12 months. Had they started in 2014, they could have been break-even around 2015 or 2016, with flexibility and ownership of their destiny. He says he should have put roughly 10% of focus on revenue.
- Delegate more. Until shortly before leaving he was editing the newsletter every morning around 5 to 5:30 a.m. The team was great; the issue was his own trust. Caring about details helps, but he can't scale himself and isn't the best person at everything.

chunks.heading: Finding consumer startup ideas
chunks.text:
- Consumer is hard for several reasons:
  - Monetization is harder than B2B, and is often advertising-driven, which requires massive scale first.
  - You compete for attention with everything, such as Netflix, and against incumbents' built-in habits.
  - Eventually you need an internal trigger in the user's mind, though you start with external triggers.
  - Problems are fuzzier. Twitter's use comes down to innate desires like staying informed or feeling less lonely, whereas DocuSign solves a clear problem (signing legal docs online).
- It's very hard, maybe impossible, to build a consumer company without a unique insight.
- Idea sources he uses:
  - A "problem journal": write down annoyances without trying to solve them (for example, no laundry in many San Francisco units).
  - Immerse in niche or long-tail communities (subreddits, a robotics hobbyist community) and watch for repeated problem statements.
  - Observe consumer behavior shifts. In 2017, Weekend Fund had distributed work as a theme. After COVID, Airbnb reshaped its home page toward exploring places at different times of year.
  - Observe technology shifts: what can be built today that couldn't be yesterday (mobile in the early 2010s, web3, AI).
- Because more people build, the market for problem discovery is more efficient, so you need a stronger "why now" and a reason it doesn't exist already.

chunks.heading: Start narrow
chunks.text:
- The narrower the audience, the easier it is to build a great solution, with tighter product experience, messaging and homepage value prop aimed at exactly those people.
- He cautions this isn't universal, but if the goal is a massive company, don't worry too much about the niche being too small. Expansion opportunities appear over time.
- Example: Airbnb started with couches and extra rooms, which most people wouldn't do, and expanded to housing.

chunks.heading: Angel investing and running a fund
chunks.text:
- A product management background helps in early-stage investing: it gives perspective on ideas and, more importantly, on how the founder thinks and reached their product insights.
- Weekend Fund has invested in over 110 companies. The third fund is $21 million and about 30 to 35% deployed. He prefers staying small so he can write smaller checks, fit into competitive deals and be collaborative, and may keep the next fund around this size.
- Operational "hygiene":
  - Always respond to a founder after a meeting, with context, not just "pass".
  - Always follow up with the person who made the introduction to close the loop.
- Biggest surprise: companies he mentally wrote off (product not working after many months) later pivoted or got a major partnership or M&A event. His lesson: "never count a portfolio company out until it's over."
- He evaluates holistically (team, market, product), judging the team indirectly through the product thinking and traction. He makes pure founder bets only on people he knows well, for example a talented designer-engineer who may launch ten apps before the eleventh succeeds.
- Ways to get into investing:
  - Angel investing: maximum flexibility but needs disposable income you can lose, and takes about 10 years to pay off.
  - Scout programs: easier to start, but less autonomy.
  - SPVs: deal-by-deal carry and you can bring in strategic people, but it's a lot of work to fundraise for each deal.
  - Raising a fund (his 2017 choice): the most work and responsibility, but the most flexibility to write many checks without much personal capital.
  - No capital: write memos on companies you'd back (his colleague Vetica did this before joining) to build a track record.

chunks.heading: Momentum and founder mindset
chunks.text:
- Momentum matters hugely in early-stage startups and is reflexive: high momentum creates more of it, and slow shipping drags others' motivation down.
- Being a CEO means wearing a confident "mask" for the team without subjecting them to all of your anxiety. He values authenticity but can't share everything.
- When founders DM him for free advice, many are vulnerable, such as having three months of runway left. He answers by DM, then tweets anonymized Q&As about every three or four days as "micro blog posts" that refine his own thinking.
- He deprioritizes dark mode before product-market fit: building small things before the product is useful is a red flag, with the exception of audiences like developers who may need it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt grew from a tiny email list into a launch platform through a maker-driven flywheel, Twitter-graph replication and borrowed UX. He also covers why communities differ from audiences, why human psychology outlasts technology shifts, and how he runs a small, collaborative, generalist fund.

chunks.heading: Why Ryan helps founders and how he does it
chunks.text:
- Ryan says helping founders "gives me purpose" and feels good, especially because founders are told no constantly and fundraising is hard for most.
- He has a bias toward supporting very young or inexperienced builders who lack support. Example: a 10-year-old DMed him before a Product Hunt launch. Ryan first suspected an adult posing as a kid, then confirmed it via a video.
- He argues even a single tweet or like can be meaningful: it nudges people past the fear of "what if people don't like it?". The default outcome of posting is that nobody cares, but the upside is nearly unbounded.
- When advising portfolio founders, he shares experience, frameworks and ways of thinking rather than answers, since founders have far more data on their own company.
- He only advises where he has expertise (product, community building, marketing). For data science or enterprise sales questions, he connects founders to the fund's LPs. Weekend Fund raised from over 350 LPs, mostly operators and founders.
- He increasingly prefers building software that scales help beyond his own time, since software "can exist while you sleep."
- A pivotal nudge in his own life: a college friend (Luan) told him to run for president of the investment club, which made him realize he could lead.

chunks.heading: How Product Hunt started and was built
chunks.text:
- 2013: he left a job of about three years (the company grew from 6 to ~100 people) by going part-time at half salary and 20 hours a week to tinker.
- He applied to Medium, MessageMe and Bibo, and was rejected or didn't pursue them. He then built Product Hunt as a side project because he wanted a list of cool new apps (mobile was taking off).
- Version one was an email list on a tool called Linky Inc., where friends collaboratively submitted links that were sent out as a daily email. It took 20-30 minutes to set up and was shared on Twitter.
- It had fewer than 1,000 subscribers, but "nudges of confidence" came from organic growth and random people saying they read it every morning.
- He then pinged Nathan Bashaw (a product designer/engineer hybrid he'd worked with on Startup Edition). Over a Thanksgiving week they built the website MVP.
- The site replicated the email as a daily leaderboard, adding comments and upvotes as the curation mechanism.

chunks.heading: Product design principle: reuse familiar patterns
chunks.text:
- Ryan borrowed from Reddit and avoided inventing new language: "upvotes" were already understood by people in tech, so they didn't invent a new verb.
- He warns people sometimes get "too cute" with new terminology or UX, which can hurt understanding.
- Naming example: they chose "makers" rather than "founders" so anyone involved in a product (CEO or customer support) is celebrated. It is deliberately flat, with no hierarchy of founders and VPs.

chunks.heading: The Product Hunt growth flywheel and tactics
chunks.text:
- Flywheel: a maker launches and shares with their audience, some of those people sign up, some are makers too, so they launch and share with their own audience. More people engage, which drives more engagement back to the site.
- He thinks about social product design as building flywheels, then asking what speeds the spin or raises conversion.
- Twitter-only sign-in at the start let them replicate the Twitter graph. When someone you follow launched, you got an email. This was one of their highest open and click-through emails, since people genuinely care what people they know are building.
- Outreach to top launchers: they contacted the top 10 by upvotes each day and asked them to write about their launch experience, promising cross-promotion on the newsletter and social.
- Many wrote posts (often 1-3 hours of work) on their own blogs or Medium. This gave Product Hunt authentic content not hosted on its own blog, plus backlinks that improved SEO. Hundreds of people wrote these posts.
- Ryan describes it as "giving them permission to promote themselves to promote us," a win-win.
- Scale: Ryan believes over 250,000 makers launch per year (rough napkin math, possibly off by 2x). Early skeptics said there weren't enough products to launch daily; he disagreed.
- Defensibility: Product Hunt's flywheel, brand and network mean clones haven't worked, and it would keep spinning even if no features were added. He argues products with a people or network component are far more defensible than purely software-driven ones.

chunks.heading: Building communities
chunks.text:
- Audience vs community: "There's a big difference between an audience and a community." Twitter followers are usually an audience. A community means members connect with and help each other.
- The leader is like a good party host who sets the environment, rather than the one talking to everyone.
- Benefits: more word of mouth, higher engagement and retention, and more enterprise value, all else equal (his thought experiment: Figma invested heavily in community and events versus a comparable rival).
- Not every SaaS company needs one, and nobody wakes up wanting to join a community, so it needs utility.
- How to start: find the member's motivation. On Product Hunt, people come to get users, feedback and status. That hook pulls them into higher engagement and events.
- Hundreds of Product Hunt community events were largely community-led. Ryan attended only about four or five. Early ones had lines wrapping two blocks.
- Observed shift: communities have moved toward small private group chats. He is in a ~30-40 person health group and another group of LPs. He cites Greg Eisenberg's Islands as a company built on that thesis.

chunks.heading: Product building in the age of AI
chunks.text:
- Human psychology stays constant while technology changes. He worked with Nir Eyal on Hooked and has long studied what makes products compelling. Status, human connection and status within a community will still matter.
- AI collapses idea-to-software: far fewer people are needed, and non-engineers (marketers, PMs, designers, accountants) can build their own ideas, removing translation loss. Today it suits MVPs and testing more than production, but he expects it to improve.
- Example workflow: a PM spends an afternoon building a working prototype instead of a clumsy Figma clickthrough.
- He mentions personalized, remixable software and notes Weekend Fund invested in Adaptive in that category, though he isn't sure where he stands on the thesis.
- He compares AI today to mobile in 2011-2013: a new mature-enough platform with lots of opportunity (he cites subscriptions in app stores as an unlock). "We're still in the fog of war."
- Cost advice for founders: bet on where the technology is heading. Example: Rosebud (journaling app) charged around $5 a month while power users cost more via API calls; the bet was that costs would keep falling.
- Practice: retry old AI tasks periodically. A year ago OpenAI deep research missed companies in his diligence; he expects it to become far better.
- Rule of thumb: people overpredict one year and underpredict ten.
- Being positioned for what AI won't change, such as in-person events, is a barbell strategy.

chunks.heading: Starting Weekend Fund and his investing approach
chunks.text:
- After Angelist acquired Product Hunt (end of 2016), he started Weekend Fund in mid-2017 while still running Product Hunt. He aimed to raise $1M, raised $3M (3x oversubscribed) and deployed it over two years into 40-something companies.
- He took no management fees at the time (on $3M fees are a rounding error) and prefers that money go into companies.
- Product Hunt rule: if you hold a stake in a company, you cannot hunt it.
- The first fund's results: one position (Deel) is roughly a 10x fund returner on paper, and he sold about 15% of that position around 24 months earlier to return the whole fund to LPs. In hindsight he'd have made more by holding, but he valued getting LPs distributions and reaching carry.
- Fund size: he keeps it small on purpose. Larger funds mean leading deals, sharp elbows, more flying and schmoozing; he dislikes transactional conversations and rejecting founders.
- His view: a first-round founder is better served with a cap table of 20-40 investors (angels and small funds) than one lead investor taking a majority of the round, and then putting them to work. Unless the lead is exceptional in an area the founder desperately needs and trusted, he would not take a majority lead check himself.
- He stays generalist because trends change, and asks what a thematic fund does when its theme falls out of favor. He oscillates on valuation sensitivity (passing at a $30M post pre-launch company that later became multi-billion) and on whether to make more, wider bets in a fast, noisy market.
- Leverage via products: Rolodexer (searches his ~300k Twitter followers, half perhaps fake) helps portfolio founders find intros and helps diligence, e.g. finding accountants who follow him. He argues CRM should be "who knows you, not who do you know." He values tools that "barely work" but are extremely valuable.
- Sourcing: he asks founders "what do you see that other people don't?" He would raise venture only with a secret or traction. He cautions founders against raising when they lack either, since they may regret it after a year or two.

chunks.heading: Investing in consumer health and other categories
chunks.text:
- About 80% of Weekend Fund's investments are B2B or B2B-to-C, since that has been a clearer path to revenue.
- He is excited about consumer health: GLP-1s opened people's eyes to non-traditional health approaches, people are acclimating to self-injection, and AI can interpret blood work (he uses Function Health). Health is huge ("if you're not healthy nothing else matters") and has a very high share of wallet.
- Examples he cites: Mindbloom (at-home ketamine; injectables preferred over lozenges by many users), and TrueMed (use HSA/FSA funds for products like Peloton and AG1).
- Personal angle: peptides (BPC-157, melanotan) after knee issues. He admits he is not a scientist and is partly investing in what he finds fun and could be a customer of.
- He is open to unglamorous categories such as CPG: valuations are more reasonable, and incumbent competitors may be poorly incentivized. He cites a friend's $1M post CPG investment that became his best.

chunks.heading: Status in Silicon Valley, LP investing and founder realities
chunks.text:
- Status has shifted: raising money was once a primary signal; today revenue and shipping matter more, along with credentials. Twitter has become the launchpad (algorithmic reach, video demos, tech town-hall mindshare), replacing press such as TechCrunch.
- Product Hunt's original premise: press can't promote every company, so a community-led launchpad was needed.
- On status-seeking: avoid inauthentic routes or chasing fads. They may work short term, but "people are going to see through it" and the trend may fade.
- LP investing: he has invested in about 30 funds, starting organically (e.g. Andreas Klinger's early fund) to support friends. Checks are small (around $10K), and the motivation is partly fun, partly updates and some deal flow.
- How LPs help GPs: number one is simply honoring capital calls (one LP refused a small call; the commitment was reduced). Beyond that, introductions to other LPs are the most valuable help, since LPs are hidden and fundraising is hard.
- Writing: he published over 100 posts early on and still uses it to test whether he understands an idea. "If I can't write about it... maybe I don't understand it enough."
- Founder hardship: once you raise, you can't give money back, you must project confidence to the team, and can't be fully honest with the board or team. He cried inside while smiling during hard Product Hunt days.
- Advice: lean on close friends, and remember the worst case is usually not that bad since most founders can get a job.
- Reward: a portfolio company acquisition returned cash to LPs; emailing LPs "here's money back" is the best feeling.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains how a non-technical solo founder validated Product Hunt with a 20-minute email list, grew it from an audience built over years plus manual maker outreach, and later added monetization via Ship. He also covers distributed teams, giving up work as a founder, and engaging users directly.

chunks.heading: Starting without engineering: validate with non-code tools first
chunks.text:
- Ryan applied to YC as a non-technical solo founder, which he assumed YC disliked. His answer was traction: Product Hunt was growing about 50% month over month in top-line user visits, consistently for the first 2-4 months.
- His view: "if you can demonstrate data like that it's hard to argue." Proof that people use the product is the ultimate proof, whether or not you can code.
- Product Hunt began as an email list that took about 20 minutes to set up and reached a few hundred subscribers initially. Not being an engineer forced him to avoid spending weeks building something people might not want.
- Email suits an audience that uses it daily, and it is easy to iterate on. Each day's send can change the copy or the format, whereas code is much harder to change.
- Ryan wrote an early Hacker News article, "email first startups", noting that AngelList's MVP was also an email digest.
- Non-code stack suggestion: Typeform plus Stripe lets you collect money without coding, and getting people to pay is "the ultimate test."
- He says even technical founders should often start with non-technical tools so something is out there sooner.

chunks.heading: Ship: tool for building demand and talking to users before launch
chunks.text:
- Ship is a toolkit for makers and startups. It announces a new product, collects emails and gets feedback from those users.
- Product Hunt ran this workflow by hand for years using MailChimp and Typeform, then productized it after makers kept asking how to get initial users and feedback before launch.
- Makers use it to capture interest in upcoming apps and to seed beta users for feedback.
- Ryan's belief: the more you communicate with your audience, make them feel involved and get their feedback, the higher the chance you build something people want.
- Product Hunt had never charged for anything except job postings long ago, which it dropped to focus on the community. Ship was the first direct charge.
- A Slack bot notifies the team of each payment, including a $249/month subscription on launch day.
- Q4 strategy: build things people like enough to pay for. A second planned stream is connecting companies with talent, using Product Hunt's engineers, designers and marketers and AngelList's talent platform, without heavy-handed pop-ups.

chunks.heading: Launching on Product Hunt: build an audience and engage it before launch
chunks.text:
- Ryan says upvote counts don't predict success. Launching is one moment, while startups are multi-year journeys, and many succeed only in year five to seven.
- Product Hunt doesn't cover everyone either. A product for an audience that doesn't use it shouldn't be judged on upvotes.
- Common mistake: building a product you think the world will love without getting community feedback or building an audience first.
- He cites Casey Winters as an example. Before building, he built an audience, so whatever he ships gets at least some attention.
- His tips: build an audience of the people you're targeting, engage them and get early feedback, and use Ship to do both.
- Without his first few hundred sign-ups, built from years of audience-building, Ryan doesn't think Product Hunt would exist today.
- Customer service is an engagement opportunity: "people care enough to talk to you." He runs TweetDeck with a column for every Product Hunt mention and replies to issues.

chunks.heading: Growing the early community
chunks.text:
- First few hundred users: people who had followed his writing for years. He wrote about products and behavior, wrote with Nir Eyal on *Hooked*, and had relationships with founders and investors who were comfortable joining.
- Press was a strong early growth driver. He wrote a Fast Company guest piece on how they got their first 2,000 users, aimed at getting another thousand.
- Maker outreach: when someone's product was posted, Ryan searched Twitter each morning for their handle and invited them to answer questions. About 80% said yes. He spent the first hour of each day on this, which led to several thousand early users.
- Productized it: the community tags makers, and a bot notifies them they were added to a product with a link. Makers get upset if they are never notified.
- Audience is international from early on (no 80% US skew), tracking startup hubs such as Paris and Berlin.
- Product Hunt reflects trends: anonymous social apps around Secret, then blockchain/crypto and AI.

chunks.heading: Category expansion and staying focused
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt added games, books and podcasts, and Ryan admits mistakes in that execution.
- Podcasts were quietly shut down: discovering podcasts differs from discovering apps, and new episodes appear weekly or faster, which didn't fit the existing community dynamics.
- Conclusion: "podcast is not our business." Product Hunt focuses on product discovery.
- He still thinks a community place to discover and discuss podcasts will exist, and names Breaker (YC) as executing on it.
- Why not a syndicate or fund for top products: it would shift priorities toward building an investor platform, a different product from product discovery for the world. They hold lightweight founder and investor dinners and meetups with AngelList instead.

chunks.heading: YC lessons and interview advice
chunks.text:
- YC's main value for him was accountability: weekly group office hours where partners (Kevin Hale and Kat Manalac) asked "did you do that thing we talked about last week?" He calls this uncomfortable but the best way to get off the ground.
- Interview approach: he sold the vision, a place to discover the products being built. He projected confidence, and expected interruptions. He prepared to move on when cut off and tried to be succinct.
- YC instilled a data-driven, talk-to-your-customers culture that he thinks Product Hunt already had.
- Process keeps changing as the team grows: Product Hunt raised a Series A right after YC and hired, and he expects to revise process again each quarter based on what went poorly.

chunks.heading: Building a remote team and managing as a founder
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt had 17 people across eight or nine time zones, about two-thirds outside SF. The first hire, Ricardo, was in Italy and paid out of pocket. Being distributed began as necessity, not strategy.
- Advantages: hire anyone in the world, lower cost than SF, avoid competing with Google/Facebook pay and perks for seed-stage hires, and a global product perspective (over half the product and community is outside the US).
- Challenges: communication and limited overlap, sometimes about four hours of shared time. He calls them workable. Tools: Slack and Zoom.
- Early PM mistake: he rewrote a UX designer's work over a weekend to save time, which caused frustration, and he's not a UX designer.
- Lesson: as a team grows, founders must give up work, hire the right people and give them autonomy. It feels less productive short-term but is better long-term.

chunks.heading: Weekend Fund and early-stage investing
chunks.text:
- Raised a $3M fund via AngelList's Angel Funds, a "VC in a box": they handle legal setup, banks and LP communication for about $12,000 plus a share of carry, versus roughly $100,000 normally.
- Checks: $50,000 to $200,000 in early-stage companies.
- Thesis is intentionally open, favoring companies where he can be helpful, such as community-based products. Interested areas: remote and distributed team tools and voice.
- Early investments leaned community-focused. The name "Weekend Fund" nods to Product Hunt starting as a side project and to humble weekend projects growing big.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover recounts how Product Hunt grew from an email list into a YC company, why he raised money, and what he'd change (monetize earlier, avoid expanding to other verticals too fast). He also shares his view on what makes launches work.

chunks.heading: Starting Product Hunt as a side project and deciding to raise money
chunks.text:
- Ryan started Product Hunt as an email list while between startups. It got traction, became a website modeled on Reddit and Hacker News, and was still an unincorporated side project about four months in. He woke up excited about it and thought about it constantly, but did not know what it should become.
- Nicholas from Algolia (previous YC batch) DMed him that many YC founders were launching on Product Hunt and that Gary Tan wanted to meet.
- Ryan's open question for Gary was whether he wanted VC funding at all, and whether doing YC put him on that path. He had little savings and is not an engineer, so he needed money to pay people to build the roadmap.
- Gary's advice: "when you strike lightning in a bottle that doesn't happen very often." Ryan says very few times in life do you build something showing real traction, and that advice stuck. Gary never pressured him either way.
- Ryan weighed bootstrapping (pocketing something like $20,000 a month at 100% ownership) against raising, and cites bootstrapped examples like Wirecutter and Techmeme.

chunks.heading: The manual growth flywheel before the YC interview
chunks.text:
- Growth going into the YC interview was roughly 50% month over month over a few months, from a small base.
- The tactic was manual: Ryan emailed and tweeted at makers and founders. When he messaged them, they joined the conversation and shared it, which drove more traffic. Ryan says this flywheel still exists today.
- After discovering it, he did it as often and as fast as he could before the interview so he could honestly cite the growth numbers. Real metrics gave him confidence without needing to "pump his chest."

chunks.heading: Raising money: seed and a preemptive Series A
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt raised about $1M before demo day, targeting about $400k. Investors included GV, Greylock and SV Angel (first check), plus strategics.
- Strategy: because the product served the tech community, having notable tech people involved was beneficial. Ryan admits they probably gave up more equity than needed.
- Mark Andreessen's firm reached out mid-batch, then again weeks later before demo day, and ended up doing a preemptive Series A. Ryan says they were very early for that kind of round.
- His reasoning: metrics were great and the opportunity massive, so it was better to raise more capital now with a great firm than risk raising in six months with a weaker firm and weaker numbers. The money funded several years of hiring and building.

chunks.heading: Mistakes: revenue, premature vertical expansion, and redesigns
chunks.text:
- **Revenue:** Ryan says they should have focused on revenue earlier. Before funding he paid the Heroku bill (a couple thousand dollars a month at one point) from his own credit card and added job ads, which made about $4,000 a month (transcript says "$44,000", which is ambiguous). He notes the community could easily have supported more. The tradeoff: consumer startups that make money get judged by VCs on that revenue.
- Product Hunt made covering costs the number one goal last year, which took a lot of experimentation, and became profitable.
- **Expanding verticals too fast:** The demo day vision was to replicate the community across categories (gaming, music, books, podcasts). Ryan was "a little bit naive" thinking communities could be replicated quickly. They launched gaming, then books, then podcasts, but the community stayed tech-focused and the side communities saw little engagement and never became standalone.
- Game discovery works differently than tech discovery (more visual, video, different focus). Ryan thinks a separate domain and experience would have been needed. He thinks someone should still build it.
- He rejected a "Product Hunt fund" suggested by investors, believing it would have changed the business into something like AngelList.
- **Redesigns:** He prioritized redesign work partly because he wanted it himself. Redesigns are often a trap: users care about the content and conversation, not whether the upvote button looks shinier. Communities also resist change; some changes were reverted, others users got used to.
- Treat funding as if you don't have infinite runway.

chunks.heading: Product Hunt's current strategy: go deep, three KPIs, and what is next
chunks.text:
- Ryan's strategy shifted from going wide to going deep on technology, his "bread and butter," about three years before this talk.
- Three KPIs last year: revenue (number one, to build a scalable model covering expenses; they hit profitability), user growth, and community contributions (upvotes, comments, as a health measure).
- This year the priority flips to user growth, with revenue no longer number one.
- Themes: help people find the best products for a need (e.g. best analytics tool for a given budget), building a "product graph." Product Hunt has been about new products, but more people want the best product for a specific job.
- Social and maker side: virtual co-working for side-project builders, freelancers and remote workers who want to meet others, get help across skill sets, and escape loneliness. Most people lack a large following, and friends give overly positive feedback, so there is a need for a support network.
- Build process: usually one engineer starts a project, working with a designer. This lets them run many projects at once.
- Ryan sees maker communities (Product Hunt, Indie Hackers, Dribbble, Stack Overflow, Lpath) as a growing ecosystem, since more products will be built as it gets easier.

chunks.heading: Launch advice and what makes launches stick
chunks.text:
- Launch basics: make the imagery clear, make the tagline clear, bounce it off people who don't know you, and "speak like a human not like a marketer."
- Feedback loops matter: building something and getting no use or feedback is hard. Product Hunt gives makers feedback; one maker of the year learned to code, launched on Product Hunt, and went on to ship many products.
- Meerkat example: a clear tagline ("broadcast live video to your Twitter followers"), a design leveraging the Twitter graph, and it blew up. But live video had poor retention (hard to create, must be watched live).
- Founders noticed people hacking it to hang out with friends, which inspired Houseparty. Ryan's takeaway: a launch spike is not a business, and the team had to be honest with themselves and change rather than persist.
- Ryan advises starting by thinking "side project" or experiment rather than market: ask what you would want to build or use. Product Hunt was "me in many ways," which is why it worked. He named his fund Weekend Fund because much can be built on a weekend.
- Ryan values progress: he has invested in companies after following them for just two or three weeks based on what they ship and how they interact with users.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt began as a half-hour email list, grew through a five-day site build and a hand-picked beta, and then joined Y Combinator. He shares launch lessons: build an audience before the product, use plain language, launch continuously, and share openly instead of hiding your idea.

chunks.heading: Launch as a continuous process, not a one-time event
chunks.text:
- Ryan says launching is never a single moment: "you're always launching."
- Product Hunt launched an email list, then a beta, then the website, then many features.
- Because of that, he stays in constant contact with users. Product Hunt runs feature flags and beta users, and tests both qualitatively and quantitatively.
- Example: one weekend he planned an MVP of a new idea using only a Typeform survey and a Quip document, with no software, to see whether people would use it.
- He applies the same logic to any creative work (photo series, paintings, mini-documentaries): everything you make is a chance to get feedback and earn some respect.
- Going into a bunker and coming out with a "tada" is, in his words, fiction.

chunks.heading: Build an audience before you build the product
chunks.text:
- Ryan says the overlooked part of launching is building an audience or community in your space before the product exists.
- Product Hunt would not exist without his earlier writing, which gave him people who loved tech.
- He wrote about 150 essays in 2013, some very short, on technology, user psychology and marketing. Over about two years that produced a small following on Twitter and a personal email list.
- That gave him an audience to post the launch to, and a community of tech people.
- You don't need thousands of people on day one. You need about 100 who love what you're building.
- This is not transactional self-promotion. Create something of value for a community: a podcast, a video show, writing or meetups.
- That audience becomes your first feedback, first users, first customers and possibly hires. Andreas, Product Hunt's CTO, was an early prototype user.
- Old model: build in the basement, ship, and hope people find it. His view: "if no one finds out about it doesn't matter." Distribution and discovery are now the hard part because building is easier and more people are building.

chunks.heading: How Product Hunt went from idea to company
chunks.text:
- Ryan quit his product job gradually. He gave two months' notice, then went part-time at roughly half salary (20 hours a week) while exploring ideas. He says early on you need time and space more than money.
- It started as an email list, set up in about half an hour or less. He sent daily new products to people following him on Twitter.
- After 2 to 4 weeks, people kept signing up and replying that they liked it.
- Around Thanksgiving, four years before this interview, he and Nathan Bashaw (who built it, as Ryan is not an engineer) made the website in about 5 days. It was a simple Ruby on Rails app with posts and a comment feed.
- Beta ran about 5 to 10 days with roughly 100 people. He emailed each one individually and involved them in the process, then launched in December.
- It kept growing for 3 to 4 months as a side project, not even incorporated.
- The next decision was whether to raise money, build a team, or stay a side project monetized with job postings. He talked to Gary Tan, Kevin Hale, Kat and Alexis Ohanian before applying to Y Combinator, mainly for feedback, since he could not undo raising money.
- Several YC companies already used Product Hunt, so it circulated there. He applied, interviewed and got in.

chunks.heading: Why mentorship and Twitter relationships work
chunks.text:
- Ryan has no formal mentors, and thinks "can you be my mentor?" emails from strangers are a hard ask. His approach: identify who you can learn from and create value for them, or keep it casual.
- He met Nir Eyal by emailing him after admiring his writing for 3 to 4 years, which led to him helping write Nir's book.
- Twitter is the main tool for building relationships, because it is passive and light touch:
  - Follow people and engage over about 12 months, adding value to conversations.
  - Then reach out ("it's me from Twitter") so the ice is already broken.
  - When he read tech blogs, he always tagged the author. It cost 5 to 10 seconds, gave them credit, and built recognition and relationships over years.
- Early advisors included Josh Elman (Greylock) and lawyer Josh Cook.
- He now mentors in return, since people helped him at that stage.

chunks.heading: Does location matter?
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt would not exist if Ryan weren't in San Francisco. The serendipity of the city led to connections such as Josh Elman and future investors.
- He says there is no single right way to build a startup. Identify your biggest current challenge and solve for it:
  - Hiring: distributed teams work (Product Hunt had people in about nine time zones). Local teams need a talent hub, which Eugene, Oregon is not.
  - Fundraising: it is easier in San Francisco, though you can travel.
  - Media: Los Angeles has advantages. Finance: New York.
- Over half of Product Hunt's makers are outside the US, so it is global.
- He prefers digital communication for reach, since one post or tweet reaches thousands, then doubles down on in-person time with the people he most wants to know. He avoids most conferences as costly in time and less intimate.
- He also cites founder-market fit (Chris Dixon's idea): whether you are the right person to build for that market.

chunks.heading: Common launch mistakes and what good looks like
chunks.text:
- **Most common mistake: marketing-speak.** Founders lose touch with the real value proposition, use buzzwords, and describe what the product might be in five years instead of what it does today. The result is disingenuous and confusing.
- **Fix:** use simple, clear language, and get people who don't know you to review the landing page, onboarding and copy.
- **The two-second test:** visitors judge "is this for me?" and "does this look useful or interesting?" If you miss either, they won't sign up.
- **Good example: Superhuman**, the email client from Rahul Vohra (founder of Rapportive):
  - It onboards users manually, one by one, in a long private beta.
  - A 20 to 30 question survey asks how much users care about speed, snippets, read replies and so on.
  - It makes sure the early product serves the needs of its audience (for example, someone who must have labels).
  - It positions around speed and saving time ("give you superpowers"), not "a better email client."
- **Underlying needs people buy for:** saving time, saving money, solving loneliness (a reason people use Facebook and Twitter), or just having fun.
- **Examples:** Instacart implies saving time without saying so. CryptoKitties has a fun, collectible value prop plus an implied crypto and blockchain angle.

chunks.heading: Share openly; don't hide your idea
chunks.text:
- Ryan says being secretive about an idea is not your real risk: "you have a lot more problems other than someone's stealing your idea."
- Many people have asked him to sign an NDA before giving feedback. He thinks people are too busy to care.
- The odds that someone steals your idea and out-executes you are "somewhere around zero."
- Sharing and getting feedback is more advantageous than secrecy.
- For creative people nervous about publishing: haters usually mean people are paying attention, and the worst case is that nobody notices.
- His brother posted dozens or hundreds of videos on YouTube, Facebook and Instagram, built a portfolio, and recently got a videography job.
- Exception: a small number of companies should be stealth, but the majority should not.

chunks.heading: Trends he was watching (December 2017)
chunks.text:
- **Voice:** about 11 million Alexa devices in US homes by mid-2017 (he was unsure of the exact figure), plus Google Home. He cites a claim that half of teenagers' searches are by voice. The opportunity is to build for a future where voice replaces some tap-based computing, such as a voice social network or voice platform tools.
- **Avatars:** face filters and emoji show avatar communication. He thinks it can give a veil of privacy that reduces social-network hate without losing emotional expression. He called the thinking "raw."
- **Blockchain and crypto:** he compares it to TCP/IP, which no one knew would enable Twitter. He said it was full of hype and questionable ICOs but also real innovation.
- **Backlash against Silicon Valley:** problems like harassment, distrust of venture capital, "raise money" culture treated as success, and automation displacing jobs. He is an optimist who thinks tech should push forward responsibly.
- **Timing caveat:** trends like VR were predicted years early, so timing is the hard part.

chunks.heading: What's next, and what drives him
chunks.text:
- **Monetization:** Product Hunt started collecting money about two months before the interview, with hundreds of makers and companies paying monthly. The business goal for the next year was to break even.
- **Mainstream discovery:** use the curated database and community so people can browse for gifts (smart home gadgets for mom) or the best Android photography apps, since more people have that problem than want to discover what's new in tech.
- **Investing:** a small fund raised about 6 or 7 months earlier, investing in early-stage companies. He likes it as an excuse to learn new industries, such as shipping.
- **Motivation:** the satisfaction of helping people. A 21-year-old founder asked why Ryan was helping him; the answer was that people helped Ryan at that stage. He wants a legacy of helping people build valuable products and companies.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt started as a simple email list and a Reddit-style MVP built over a long weekend. He argues distribution is now the hardest part of building a startup, so audience and community matter most. He also covers habit-forming product design (the Hooked model), what he looks for as an early-stage investor, and why people from gaming make strong product builders.

chunks.heading: Ryan's route into tech: entrepreneurial childhood, games, and product management
chunks.text:
- Ryan grew up in Oregon with an entrepreneur father. At 11-12 he ran gumball machines at his dad's video game store, collecting quarters and reinvesting them in candy.
- He disliked hourly jobs: "you could do really well or really poorly and you [get] paid the same amount." Getting paid for output rather than time appealed to him.
- Side hustles: buying and selling on eBay in high school and college, and modding Xboxes. He tried a joke-site idea after a friend reportedly made $100,000 at 14 and made $70.
- He studied business with a computer information tech minor, then took an internship at a video game company. That led to marketing and then product management, a role he says he hadn't heard of before becoming one.
- In 2010 he moved to San Francisco and joined a mobile gaming tools company (Play Haven) at about employee number 10. It grew to roughly 100 people over about three and a half years. He left when he felt he "wasn't learning as much."
- His rule for early careers: "if you're not learning, you need to figure something out" and do something different.
- He says he never had a clear game plan, and Product Hunt wasn't intended to be a company at first.

chunks.heading: What a product manager does
chunks.text:
- A PM works with internal and external stakeholders (customers, engineering, design) to decide what gets built, and recommends options aligned with company strategy.
- The work can include wireframes and scoping projects. Smart people generate endless feature ideas, so a good PM narrows to the core necessities, ships, then learns and iterates.
- Ryan loves product because "the product is the thing" delivered to customers.
- He thinks PMs should explore what others are creating: "I would just play with products... not to use them... just because I was curious." He saw this as a way to learn.

chunks.heading: How Product Hunt started and the MVP approach
chunks.text:
- It began as an email list in late 2013: Ryan and a couple dozen friends sharing cool new products daily.
- It got traction quickly. He saw a gap: no simple daily list of what's new and cool, and no place for the global tech community to discuss new products.
- He and Nathan Basha built a simple website over about five days during Thanksgiving break, scoping an MVP by asking what was the minimum to bring to market.
- They modeled the UI and UX on Reddit, with comments, discussion and upvotes as the curation mechanism. Ryan's reasoning: "you don't need to reinvent the wheel" in every part of a product; the innovation was in "the content [and] the community."
- It stayed an unincorporated side project for about five or six months. After conversations with Garry Tan and other YC partners they went through Y Combinator and raised a round.
- A Series A from Andreessen Horowitz followed in early 2014, within roughly the first nine months.
- AngelList acquired Product Hunt at the end of 2016. It kept its own codebase, brand and mission inside AngelList's mission of supporting entrepreneurs and startups.
- Naval was a seed investor. Ryan later started a fund (Weekend Fund), led Product Hunt as CEO, then stepped down with Josh Buckley taking over.

chunks.heading: Why game builders make good product people
chunks.text:
- He has a bias toward people who worked in games, calling them "some of the smartest people."
- Games demand deep understanding of human psychology and behavior, since the job is creating fun, which is hard.
- He cites Super Mario World's onboarding: players are taught new skills almost invisibly as they progress.
- Games were early adopters of data-driven optimization over roughly the last 10 years; reading and interpreting that data is a real superpower elsewhere.
- Games often sit on the frontier of new tech (VR, AR, AI).
- Games also taught him about virtual economies, which he sees now being applied to crypto and community tokens.
- Competitive play (Starcraft, soccer) taught strategy, collaboration and pushing through difficulty.

chunks.heading: Engagement, habits and the Hook model
chunks.text:
- Ryan avoids the word "addiction." He worked with Nir Eyal on the book Hooked and frames the goal as building engaging, habit-forming products that are net positive.
- His litmus test: do you use it yourself and believe it helps? A crack dealer who doesn't use his own product fails this test.
- Example: Strava is designed for engagement, and that engagement makes users healthier.
- He is skeptical of The Social Dilemma, saying it ignores user agency and the value products like Facebook create, and he favors equipping users with understanding and tools (Nir's book Indistractable) over blaming products.
- The Hook model has four steps: Trigger, Action, Variable reward, Investment. Using early Twitter over SMS:
  - Trigger: a tweet arrives as an SMS notification.
  - Action: you open it. The lower the friction, the better.
  - Variable reward: you don't know what you'll get, like a slot machine.
  - Investment: you contribute back (for example, replying to a friend), which triggers the other person and pulls you back in.
- Early on, products need external triggers. Over time the product should rely on internal triggers, the user's own thoughts. Ryan has only Twitter DM notifications on, yet checks Twitter dozens of times a day.
- Products have several loops. Twitter DMs have their own, and Product Hunt has its homepage loop and a separate collections loop.
- For designing a loop, start with the user's goal and what behavior they're already trying to hack around.
- He sees Twitter's value as the best place to see what's happening right now, plus community and learning.

chunks.heading: Distribution, audience and community
chunks.text:
- Ryan says the hardest part of a startup is increasingly not building but "can they get users and can they get attention." As competition rises, distribution matters more.
- He wrote about "audience-first" startups: people who build an audience before they have a product. Example: Casey Neistat spent years vlogging, so his later product, Beam, had guaranteed distribution from day one. Beam ultimately didn't take off.
- Audience is one-to-many. Community is many-to-many and more powerful and scalable. He blogged enough to launch Product Hunt with users from day one, and now the community creates the content, so he can go on vacation and it keeps running.
- Writing helps you learn because you must understand something to write about it. It builds relatability and authority, and trust can convert into product users.
- An audience is evergreen: if one product fails, the same audience carries to the next.

chunks.heading: Investing criteria and trends at Weekend Fund
chunks.text:
- There is no formula. They invest very early, sometimes pre-product, and look for teams capitalizing on a consumer behavior shift or a technology shift.
  - Behavior shift: what does the world want now that it didn't before? Example: remote work, which also changes education and travel.
  - Technology shift: what's possible now that wasn't yesterday, such as audio/voice or crypto.
  - Then why this team, with what unique insight or experience.
- Areas of interest: crypto (social and community tokens, with Trevor's FWB tokenized Discord as an example), the creator economy, audio and voice (about half of US homes have a smart speaker; earbuds reduce friction), and distributed and remote work (a thesis since Weekend Fund began in 2017).
- On hiring, he says resumes (school, past company) are insufficient proxies. Better: look at what people have built (code for engineers) and use references, which are powerful but hard to get honestly. His head of engineer at Product Hunt, in Sofia, Bulgaria, is one of the best he's worked with, and Ryan doesn't know where he went to school.
- On India: he cited 12 new unicorns in India in 2021 versus 9 in 2020 and 8 in 2019 (he flagged the figures as unverified). Weekend Fund had invested in six or seven Indian companies.
- He said roughly 50 of about 300 companies in a recent YC batch were from India.
- As companies scale, alumni spin off new startups, a flywheel like Silicon Valley's earlier. The old worry about follow-on funding is, in his view, largely gone.
- His critique of Indian products: design execution often lags, which creates an opening for startups that make design a strength. He noted France as a design strength and said each ecosystem has its own strengths and weaknesses.
- He is a strong optimist on tech and entrepreneurship, and encourages people to build even if the first version is poor: "go build."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt started as a simple newsletter and let user behavior drive the roadmap, why community products should start with a small passionate kernel, and how he now evaluates startups by asking what has changed. He also shares advice for aspiring investors and experiments in community-driven investing.
