chunks.heading: Why Ryan started Product Hunt as a newsletter, not a grand plan
chunks.text:
- Ryan did not set out to build a company. He liked finding new products and wondered why people had to "hunt for the link inside the TechCrunch articles" instead of having a simple daily list of what launched.
- He browsed the App Store in different countries and AngelList's new companies just to see what people were building.
- The first step was a newsletter, because it was easy to start. It proved that other people, not just him, wanted this content.
- A website with comments and curation followed, since the newsletter had no place for discussion or curation at scale.
- For the first 12-18 months, the roadmap "just fell out" of what people were doing and the feedback received. It was close to obvious.
- The first site worked like Reddit: posts, comments, upvotes. He chose to "not reinvent the wheel" and keep it simple.

chunks.heading: Over-engineering and being "too clever" with product systems
chunks.text:
- Ryan thinks in systems and flywheels, but warns that people like him (designers, product thinkers) can become paralyzed and over-engineer.
- He made this mistake inside Product Hunt: he built new products that were "way too complicated" because he thought he was "so clever", adding every feature idea. V1 took far longer than needed.
- His rule: at the end of the day you have to prove out the core dynamic and core value prop early.
- Systems thinking is still valuable to dissect and understand. In his experience it works better emerging organically than being designed from day zero.
- He describes early-stage consumer social building as intuition-led and organic.

chunks.heading: How the Product Hunt roadmap grew into engagement loops
chunks.text:
Ryan's example of a feature that unlocked a system:
1. Makers kept showing up in comments saying "I made this thing, ask me questions."
2. Product Hunt productized it by clearly labeling who made the product.
3. That let community members follow makers and see what friends or people they follow launched.
4. This unlocked email notifications when someone you follow launches, which had very high open and engagement rates.
5. Profiles followed, letting makers show off what they have built. Indie makers and young entrepreneurs were especially proud of this.

His point: a small, seemingly trivial feature (identifying makers) unlocked a whole engagement loop, and it came from watching user behavior.

chunks.heading: Starting with a tight-knit community and doing things that don't scale
chunks.text:
- Before Product Hunt, Ryan hosted brunches and small meetups with founders to build relationships and learn.
- After reaching some product-market fit, meeting in person felt obvious: the community had been talking about tech online, so why not meet up.
- Community members then asked to run their own meetups (e.g. Bangalore, Berlin). There have been maybe over a thousand community-hosted meetups worldwide. Product Hunt supports them and members run them.
- This acts as an IRL version of what happens on Product Hunt: people want to connect and geek out on technology.
- He ties it to "do things that don't scale": for social and community products, "you don't need everybody on there. You actually probably don't want everybody on there." Start with a tight-knit group excited about what you built, and "that kernel can grow into something much bigger."

chunks.heading: Finding contrarian insights and a weird niche for consumer products
chunks.text:
- Ask "what's changed?" Is there a regulatory shift, a consumer behavior shift, or a technology shift that enables the new thing? He uses this lens as an investor and when talking with founders.
- Snapchat example: kids on Facebook did not want parents and teachers seeing their posts, and cancel culture was emerging, so ephemerality ran counter to older generations who want to save everything.
- To build something huge, the initial insight has to be contrarian: "no one really agrees with you at the time and then everyone agrees with you later." If everyone agreed, someone would already have built it.
- After product-market fit, customers lead you into next steps that feel obvious, so the roadmap gets informed by them.
- Generational shifts matter in consumer: people who grew up with smartphones have different expectations and ways of speaking than users of today's giants.
- Pick a niche and serve it very well. Snapchat began as a product for Los Angeles high school students and was the best product in the world for them for a period, then expanded to hundreds of millions of daily users.
- He cites Nikita Bier's TBH as playing to a natural human instinct (high schoolers gossiping). One small insight about a human desire can be a powerful building insight, and one small insight can change a maker's life.

chunks.heading: Podcasting: Product Hunt podcast and why growth is the hard part
chunks.text:
- The Product Hunt podcast brought on one or two guests (investors, founders, people in tech) to talk about products they love, what's on their home screen, and what they were excited about.
- He stopped doing it because it was not the highest-ROI use of time.
- They "never really cracked the growth thing": the most engaged Product Hunt users listened, but it never reached hundreds of thousands or millions.
- He sees podcast growth as the hardest part, like Twitter but harder: both take years to build a sizable audience, and podcasts lack built-in social dynamics and feedback loops.
- He has considered a new podcast but is hesitant to commit right now.

chunks.heading: Ryan's investing approach and the Operator LPs experiment
chunks.text:
- Ryan invests full-time, early stage (pre-seed and seed) across weird consumer, web3 and "boring SaaS". The through-line is what has changed: a consumer behavior shift or a technology shift.
- Private-market startups are not 100% efficient but are getting more efficient as more people build, so he stresses the "why now" question.
- He splits the fund's work in two: business as usual (meeting founders, evaluating, due diligence, supporting founders) and ongoing experiments.
- He believes investing is increasingly customer-, community- and network-driven. The fund raised from 370 LPs in its latest fund, including many operators: designers, data scientists, engineers, salespeople.
- Operator LPs experiment:
  - A "GP demo day" connecting operator LPs (people who might write $10K-$100K checks into funds) with mostly small funds (sub-$20M).
  - They do not charge or take economics. The goal is to build a stronger network with LPs and GPs and to push the industry toward more collaborative, community investing.
  - Two demo days so far, three GPs each: the first generated about $1.1 million in interest, the second about $1.5 million.
  - Next step is a V2 that expands to more GPs and LPs and reduces fundraising friction.

chunks.heading: Advice for breaking into investing
chunks.text:
- Write "fantasy memos". His partner Vedika, then a product manager, wrote memos on companies (such as Retool) as if proposing an investment, without sharing them publicly. Anyone can do this with no money or connections.
- It refines your thinking and creates a paper trail. When he interviewed her, she sent him the memos and he could see her work and how she thinks. His view: "if you don't want to do that, then maybe you shouldn't be investing."
- Become the XYZ person (e.g. "the community person" or "the product person"). Develop a niche and people start coming to you, becoming a center of gravity for your vertical.
- Caveat on picking a niche: choose something you have extremely high conviction in, that is authentic and sustainable. If you brand yourself around a hot trend like chatbots and it cools, you start behind the starting line and must rebrand. He notes his own firm does not follow the one-niche advice: "do as I say, not as I do."
- Creating language is a powerful signal. He points to Andreessen Horowitz and Chris Dixon coining terms (e.g. "skeuomorphism" applied to web3 social) that move thought and an industry forward. It must not feel cheesy or forced, and it must be valuable and not selfish.
- Founders should weigh check size against helpfulness. He endorses Pipe's Harry Hurst's "check size to helpfulness ratio": a $10K angel can be more helpful than a $5M lead who takes far more equity. This is why he supports small funds and angels, and he asks how founders can bring on many helpful people without taking the entire round.

chunks.heading: Ideas Ryan floated: an influencer-sports league and "Weekend Cafe"
chunks.text:
**Influencer sports events (Ryan's view as audience member)**
- He attended a TikTok vs YouTube influencer boxing event, where the energy was "insane" and it was more interesting than a professional match, because influencers are entertainers who know how to work a crowd.
- His open question was whether it would get stale as a recurring league versus a one-off. He likened it to reality TV, which made regular people feel relatable and famous.
- He noted pay-per-view software exists, and the math can add up (he cited 50,000-100,000 buyers at $30-$50), though he was unsure it is venture-scalable. Someone could start small locally by reaching out to a few influencers and prove out the model.
- The concept could apply to other communities, like tech founders and investors.

**Weekend Cafe (Ryan's own idea)**
- An intimate co-working space with good music, a comfortable temperature, and first- or second-degree connections. He finds WeWork valuable but cold and not his vibe.
- The idea includes a bunch of phone booths for calls as more people work remotely.
- Possible business-model twist: 100 membership slots as utility or membership NFTs. Members can resell on a secondary market and the operator takes about 10% of secondary transactions, giving better price discovery (e.g. a $100 membership becoming $10,000).
- He had thought about it for years without acting because he is "scared of commitments."
- His concern with token-gated clubs generally: how to avoid wealthy buyers diluting the curation. Soho House was cool when curated toward artists and designers and became more corporate and finance-heavy. (He raised this as a pushback on others' versions of the idea, applying it to this one too.)

chunks.heading: Remote work, Miami, and where founders actually are
chunks.text:
- Ryan grew up in Oregon, then lived in San Francisco for 10 years, LA for two, and Miami for a year at that point. He is glad he moved.
- He has always worked remotely or distributed, so Miami is one of many places he spends time (New York, LA, Tulum in coming weeks).
- Pros: no West Coast morning rush, nightlife, warm weather. Cons: summer hurricanes and heavy rain.
- His observation: more investors than founders seem to be in Miami, and he does not see a substantial number of tech founders there, though he meets founders over video anyway.
- He sees a missing shelling point for founders to meet and co-work, and is open to small events of 10-20 builders rather than large ones.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains his generalist angel thesis (early rounds, platform and behavior shifts like voice), how community can add defensibility to a product, and how Product Hunt finally made money with a single promoted slot. He also covers valuation discipline, portfolio size and building remote teams.

chunks.heading: Ryan's investing thesis for the Weekend Fund
chunks.text:
- The Weekend Fund is a $3M fund, about two years old at this taping, with 37 investments made. Checks run $50k-$100k, with a median of $75k.
- It invests in the first round of funding, sometimes before a product exists. Ryan buys roughly 1% at a pre-money of about $6.5M.
- He calls himself a generalist, but he focuses on product, marketing and community, where he thinks he adds help.
- His core thesis is backing "people who are building for platform shifts and consumer behavior shifts": someone building something nascent today for a future they can articulate.
- He is not strict about the thesis. Some investments don't fit it.
- Voice and audio is a category he is excited about.
  - About 70 million US homes have a smart speaker, roughly a quarter of the US population. Amazon bundles Echo Dots for $20-30.
  - He compares it to early mobile, which had no app store and no consumer understanding of how to use the device. People are still working out what to use voice for.

chunks.heading: Investing in community-driven companies
chunks.text:
- Ryan says community is trendy and not every business should have one. A community can add defensibility and strength on top of a core product.
- Voiceflow is a no-code tool for building voice apps, which he describes as "Squarespace for voice or Wix for voice." He built a joke app in about ten minutes.
  - The CEO runs a Facebook group, where he posts authentic vlogs. He thanks members for suggestions and for submitting apps to the marketplace.
  - Members show off what they are building, which gives a new, underserved group of voice-app builders a place to gather.
- Girlboss (Sophia Amoruso) is another community bet.
  - Ryan says Sophia is a natural community builder, and that is the "X factor" that got him to participate.
  - Girlboss runs community-driven live events. They have discussed a possible LinkedIn for women.
  - Her draw is authenticity and personal style. He says "her superpower is people want to hang out with her."
- Breaker is a podcast app, an investment from YC 2017.
  - Product Hunt once ran podcast discovery, with the This Week in Startups and Kara Swisher shows among the few podcasts posted. It failed for several reasons.
  - The need stuck with him: podcasts lack discovery and community. They share traits with apps, since both need users, feedback and listeners.
  - Ryan was drawn to the market need and to how Breaker supports creators.

chunks.heading: Where his community instincts come from
chunks.text:
- Ryan traces it to gaming. Starcraft led him to Blizzard's Battle.net, clans and meeting people under pseudonyms. That led to IRC.
- He describes the IRC "warez" scene as a reputation economy.
  - Access came through friends. You earned your keep by uploading movies and games for credits and a leaderboard rank.
  - People worked together mostly for status inside the group, not money.
- He also says much of what he knows came from doing things and following his interests.

chunks.heading: Monetizing Product Hunt
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt only started prioritizing revenue in early 2018. Ryan says revenue was not the priority before, and in hindsight it perhaps should have been.
- In 2018 the goal was profitability. At the time of this taping the team was making more than it spent, and the model worked every month.
- Revenue comes from product promotion, job promotion, event promotion and a few other products.
  - Founder Kit is a bundle of deals on tools and services.
  - The simplest and best performer is the promoted post: one slot, fourth down on the homepage, sold to one company at a flat fee.
  - The price is roughly $4,000-$6,000 per day.
- To avoid community backlash about pay-to-play, the promoted product must have been posted to Product Hunt before. You can't launch a new product and pay for the slot.
  - So whatever is promoted has already been validated by the community.
  - Ryan frames it as selling the brand and unique real estate in front of early adopters, investors and reporters.
- He estimates introducing it sooner would have covered a third to a half of the burn.
- Ryan says he has no regrets, and that advice always depends on the founder's context. A community like Girlboss differs from Product Hunt.

chunks.heading: Why he stayed independent and how the fund works
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt was acquired by AngelList. Ryan says he has "unfinished business" there.
  - He has teammates of over four years who are taking on more responsibility, which frees his time for strategy and for investing.
  - He turned down offers to join other firms. He wants to build his own brand and the Weekend Fund long term, though he might join a firm someday.
- Fund economics: he takes carry only and no management fee on Fund I. AngelList takes part, and he says the setup cost is a small percentage of the fund.
  - He doesn't expect to see carry until about year six.
- For the next fund he plans a management fee of roughly 2% per year, part of which goes to AngelList. On a $10M fund, he says, his share could be around $100k a year.
  - That would cover a chief of staff's cash pay and a small working budget.
- He hired a part-time chief of staff on carry.
  - Duties are evaluating investments, market research, diligence and sourcing.
  - The job listing drew Twitter backlash for sounding like unpaid labor. Ryan says his wording was poor.
  - He now offers options: more carry and less cash, or less carry and more cash. He wants the hire to feel well compensated.

chunks.heading: How he evaluates deals
chunks.text:
- Founder-market fit: he doesn't mean the founder came from that industry. He means the person has "some unique quality that's competitive in the market to solve this problem," such as extreme passion or domain expertise.
- A great founder has a strong perspective on the future and knows what they are building toward, without needing every answer. Greatness depends on context and what they are building.
- Authenticity matters to him. As an example, he notes KC (Casey Neistat) drove more traffic on a Product Hunt live chat than Snoop Dogg.
- Valuation matters because he is not leading rounds. He has passed on exceptional founders at $35M pre-launch valuations.
  - At a $50k check, a $35M pre-launch company needs a $3-4B exit to move the fund.
  - He compares putting the check in three companies instead of one. A $12M-15M cap beats the $5M-6M average only if the company is exceptional.
- On portfolio size, he believes odds improve with scale. At five companies you probably won't hit a unicorn.
  - Around 30-40 companies is where outcomes start to distribute, so he planned about 40 for Fund I.
  - You can only lose 1x on a check but can win 100x or more.
- He asks for pro rata in nearly every deal. For follow-ons he uses AngelList SPVs to raise allocations from his LPs, since a $3M fund can't write million-dollar checks.
- Process:
  - He receives hundreds of emails a month.
  - He estimates about ten meetings per investment, which he calls a low guess.
  - He takes meetings over Zoom or Hangouts, which he says is about 95% as effective as in person and gives him access to companies worldwide.
  - His portfolio is roughly 30-35% San Francisco-based, with the rest spread from Canada to London to New Orleans.
- On TAM, mature markets suit TAM math. For nascent categories like voice, it's "fuzzy math." You can't quantify what mobile would enable, so you ask whether enough people will pay.

chunks.heading: Where founders should build
chunks.text:
- Ryan moved to San Francisco in 2010, and Product Hunt wouldn't exist if he hadn't. Being there let him build relationships and absorb ideas he can't fully articulate.
- Location depends on what you're building. If it's for the tech world, be in the Bay Area. A media or music company might belong in LA.
- Teams can be remote. Product Hunt's team is spread around the world, and he'd build remotely if starting another company.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover talks about how Product Hunt began as a simple newsletter, how he seeded its community, and how he now invests at Weekend Fund. He covers what he looks for in founders (insights, team fit for the risk), how he sets terms, and his cautious but open view of consumer social.

chunks.heading: Product is a solution to a real need, and positioning matters as much as the build
chunks.text:
- Ryan grounds product thinking in his dad's phrase: "find a need and fill it." At its core a product solves a real problem for a very specific customer or user.
- Building the best product is not enough. If nobody knows about it, or it doesn't resonate, it goes nowhere.
- He wants a holistic view: how the product positions in the user's mind, what people do today to solve the problem, and how you insert yourself into that decision or workflow. This needs marketing and writing perspective, not just building skill.
- Products often stay close to their MVP. Twitter's core is still text broadcasting with a follower model, and more features don't automatically make a product better. Some products (he cites Airtable) really do need years of depth, so he avoids absolutes.

chunks.heading: How Product Hunt started and grew from a newsletter to a funded company
chunks.text:
- It began as a newsletter of products Ryan and friends found. He was scratching his own itch: he wanted one daily list of cool new things. He was not thinking about makers or founders, and admits he never thought of it as a distribution channel for them.
- The newsletter lasted only about a month to six weeks. Ryan and Nathan Bashaw then built the site over Thanksgiving break in roughly five days, from mock-ups to an MVP.
- The site MVP was a daily list of posts with upvotes and comments. It later added product pages, mentions, a follower graph and galleries, but the core loop stayed the same.
- It evolved into a launch pad because makers and founders showed strong demand for getting new products out.
- Ryan worked on it on the side for about four to five months before going all in. The site had been live three to four months before he raised money.
- The first round was a $5M cap with strong traction. He says that would be roughly a $20-25M cap today. Early growth was very high and consistent for about six months, and he recalls something like 50% week over week or month over month (he's unsure which).
- He was not trying to build a startup at first. He just liked building and community, and the idea was thrown on the internet to see what happened.

chunks.heading: Raising the first round: traction plus a vision that could expand
chunks.text:
- Investors understood Product Hunt easily because they were effectively the customer, since it served the tech community.
- Some doubted there would be enough products launching every day. Ryan believed there were plenty and that the supply would grow.
- He communicated two things: the short term (here's what it is today and the traction) and the long term (here's what it could become). The pitch was starting with tech, then expanding to music, movies, fashion, beauty, games and more, in the way Pinterest expanded across user-generated content categories.
- He says the pitch later changed from the original vision, and that adapting to the market is fine.
- He didn't want to take money until he was convinced it was the right path, even with lots of investor interest.

chunks.heading: Seeding a community: design it like a good house party
chunks.text:
- Ryan says community design matters enormously: the same product with two different communities can have very different outcomes.
- His metaphor: a house party where you know nobody feels unwelcoming, while a party where a friend introduces you to people you respect feels like "here are my people."
- He replicated that early on by inviting designers, founders and early adopters, many with small to medium Twitter followings, so newcomers recognized and respected who was posting.
- Tactics he used:
  - Personally emailed a large share of signups to welcome them and give posting access.
  - Asked already-engaged users to CC one or two people they'd invite, like a friend bringing a friend to the party.
  - Sent lots of personal emails and tweets to build the initial strong cohort.
- The takeaway: people join products because of people, and the personal touch from a named founder goes a long way.

chunks.heading: What Weekend Fund looks for: insight, a why-now, and the right team
chunks.text:
- Weekend Fund invests across B2B and consumer. It looks for the technology shift or consumer behavior shift (emergent behaviors, generational shifts) that is new today, and asks what insight the founder has about it.
- A core question is "why now." Product Hunt's own thesis was that building would get easier, so more people would start companies and distribution would get harder. He says no-code and AI generation will magnify that, lowering the bar further.
- He assumes others have tried the idea before, so something must have changed to enable it today.
- Insight is the big signal: after a call he wants to come away thinking "I didn't know that" or "that's counterintuitive." He shouldn't know more than a founder about their space.
- Product quality: he's fine with products being ugly or broken early. He cares more about the decisions behind the product (why this onboarding flow, why this feature priority, how people use it).
- He identifies the biggest risks and checks the team can address them. Examples:
  - Strong insights but zero design or product skill is an orange flag.
  - A strong product and design team building something technically hard, like AI tooling, makes him cautious without strong technical talent.
- Traction helps. For pre-product or pre-traction deals, founder insight and ability to execute matter even more. Once there is consistent, non-spiky traction, the market is saying something and that weighs more.
- Different risks call for different lenses: a known problem in a mature market leans toward product execution, while a new idea leans toward whether a market exists.

chunks.heading: Pitching Ryan: be succinct, test for clarity, make it authentically personal
chunks.text:
- Easiest route is email (Ryan at weekend.fund).
- Be very clear and succinct. He sometimes reads a paragraph or two and still doesn't know what the company builds.
- Test the email on friends, and better, a stranger, and have them explain back in their own words what you build. Founders forget others have no context.
- Personalization should be authentic, not fake ("I see you invest in consumer apps"). Real effort creates reciprocity, so he's more likely to pay attention and respond.

chunks.heading: Deal structure, check size and how Weekend Fund supports founders
chunks.text:
- Weekend Fund is a small check writer that doesn't lead rounds. It usually targets about 2-3% ownership in the first check, enough skin in the game that each company could theoretically return the fund multiple times.
- Roughly 10-15% of the portfolio is outside the US (India, Europe, Brazil, Canada). Metrics are mostly evaluated the same way, but revenue potential differs by geography. For example, Indian consumer apps can grow fast, but average revenue per user is dramatically lower, so user counts aren't comparable to US apps.
- Terms: sometimes he helps set the cap early in a conversation; sometimes terms are already set and he takes them. He doesn't try to demand a better deal for coming late. Valuation is not a precise science.
- He also asks how much money the founder needs for 24 months or more, then works backward. Example: raising $2M at a $5M cap would be too much dilution and cause future problems, so a higher cap may be reasonable.
- A risk of writing the first check is that the founder can't raise enough, leaving only about six months of runway. He hasn't often run into that, but notes he's been in a bull market and considers holding a check until the round is large enough.
- Support model, positioned between two bad extremes (the investor who disappears and the naggy one who is extractive):
  - Read investor updates and take catch-up calls.
  - Use that context to be tactical: intros via the LP network, Twitter and LinkedIn; jamming on product for an hour.
  - Help close rounds, intro other investors, and avoid signaling risk since he isn't the lead. If Weekend Fund doesn't follow on in the Series A, it isn't a problem.

chunks.heading: Consumer social, lean teams, and where new opportunities may come from
chunks.text:
- Ryan jokes "don't invest in consumer social," but still can't help backing some. Conviction comes from the founder's insights and ability to navigate the nuances (he cites backing Alex Ma on TTYL, an early audio social network around AirPods, which led to Paparazzi).
- For consumer social, he wants very small, tight teams of generalists with strong product and consumer thinking and a low burn. A V1 needing 10 people is concerning; hiring the fifth or sixth person should come after some product-market fit.
- B2B usually has a clearer problem and market need. Consumer social is fuzzier, with "do people want this thing" unclear and more iterations needed. Post-traction, the hard question is whether metrics are sustainable, since consumers are flaky and churn around month six.
- On the future of social: it's hard to pull people from existing networks, so it needs a shift. Snapchat capitalized on a generational and behavior shift (ephemeral photos for younger users who didn't want permanent posts), not a technology shift. He thinks pure UX innovation on mobile is now much harder.
- He's more interested in new platforms or technology unlocks. He doesn't see any hardware (VR, AR glasses) reaching mainstream scale for a while, and sees AI creative tools as a possible source of new interaction modes, networks and identities, though he doesn't know the product.
- He likes founders who are scrappy and can get revenue early. Example: a thermodynamic computing company he backed already had a $2M LOI before building, and had a V1 that could make money soon alongside a long-term vision. He says revenue also shapes the product, since you build for one customer's specific workflow instead of a theoretical problem. He doesn't treat early revenue as a requirement, though, since over-prioritizing it has risks.

chunks.heading: Ryan's motivations and other asset classes he's exploring
chunks.text:
- The through line in his career is that he gets energy from creating, from childhood projects (a website, a Shreveport build) to Product Hunt. He's trying to scratch that itch at Weekend Fund with content and internal tooling, and is learning music production with a coach.
- He says having a teacher cut the friction of going from zero to one, and thinks adults should have more teachers and coaches.
- He's interested in alternative investing models beyond the traditional 2-and-20 VC fund: SMB investing, creators, buying small businesses, and micro-PE roll-ups. He isn't actively working on any.
- He's invested in some small funds as an LP (around $10K checks) for the experience, and in SMBs through revenue share, such as a hair salon or matcha shop. It won't produce a 100x return, but he's unlikely to lose his money.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains how Weekend Fund runs as a set of product experiments: a $21M fund with 360 LPs, a non-exclusive scout program, and Rolodexer for intros. He covers fund construction, winning deals as a small non-lead check, and backing founders with a secret or traction.

chunks.heading: Ryan's fund size and check-size strategy
chunks.text:
- Weekend Fund is on its third fund, $21 million, kept small by design. Ryan says the next fund won't scale much.
- Average check is about $350K, for roughly 2-3% ownership. He calls that small but meaningful because the target is decacorn outcomes.
- Plan is about 50 portfolio companies per fund, which he says is "very manageable" because the fund is not a lead investor and is not on boards.
- Ryan avoids being a lead and avoids the middle ground of being a non-lead who still has to write a $750K check to get meaningful economics. That is "really tough."
- A small check helps win deals. Even if a founder's allocation is tight, they can make room.
- Historically the fund avoided very small checks where a $10 million outcome doesn't return the fund. Small checks can also conflict the fund out of a better future investment. He is rethinking this as companies grow faster and more of them appear.
- Construction has to be realistic, so he works backwards: how many checks can be deployed, how many people he must meet, how many companies can be supported. He doesn't expect a 10% conversion from meetings to checks.
- Example outcome: a seed investment in Deel at a $10M cap, now a roughly $12B company, "almost a 400x outcome." Most investments won't be that, but one can return a 5x or 10x fund.
- He argues yesterday's unicorns are becoming tomorrow's decacorns because revenue growth is scaling fast and AI will eat more of the services side of GDP.

chunks.heading: Raising a fund from 360 LPs
chunks.text:
- The fund raised most of its capital from existing fund one and two LPs, some product investors from the Product Hunt days and some institutions. The rest was raised publicly.
- The strategy was to bring on "an army of operators and founders," from salespeople and designers to AI researchers. The aim was an extended family helping with diligence, investor intros and deal flow, not the money. The fund was already near its target.
- The fund was announced publicly under a 506(c) structure so it could legally take applications from LPs. Many LPs wrote very small checks.
- Applications included questions testing whether LPs understood early-stage investing. Ryan didn't want someone expecting their money back in two years.
- Results across 360+ LPs were mostly good. One LP asked for money back about two years in because they were becoming a monk, and it was a small amount that was resolved. One or two LPs had capital call issues.
- Hindsight: some LPs don't grasp that a commitment means future capital calls are not optional. The LPA lacked protection if an LP stops funding after capital was reserved for them, and he plans to add it in the next fund, "nothing aggressive."
- Small checks also meant no LP relied on the money for things like tuition, which reduces future headaches.
- Another fund's approach: put family offices and high-net-worth LPs into a more liquid six-year strategy before a 10-year fund. (This was the host's example; Ryan called it smart.)

chunks.heading: Productizing LP intros and an LP newsletter
chunks.text:
- Ryan runs a basic newsletter that reaches about 150 LPs who deploy roughly $50 million a year in total. Some are small $10K LPs who add value in other ways. Some are institutions writing $2.5M+ checks.
- The newsletter just shares what he is investing in. He has invested personally in over 30 funds, mostly small checks. Using his own capital is meant to be a signal.
- He started investing in funds about seven years ago. He doesn't mainly invest for returns. Motives: support fellow GPs, read their updates to see how they view the market, and occasionally get deal flow.
- Most of the funds he backs are under $30M. They are either narrow specialists or generalists who are highly connected, since generalists need to see a lot and be in the right places to spot spaces before any VC blog post exists.
- Fundraising "sucks" and many friends are doing it, which is why he helps with LP intros.

chunks.heading: Rolodexer: using a social following as a distribution tool
chunks.text:
- Weekend Fund built Rolodexer, a tool that searches Ryan's roughly 300,000 Twitter followers (he estimates about half are active, mostly tech).
- Use case: a company wants intros to early design partners or customers. Ryan asks for their target company list, say Ramp. Rolodexer finds followers who work there, and Ryan DMs them an intro.
- Conversion: "30 to 50% of people accept an introduction" from these outbound requests, much higher than email because the DM comes from someone they follow.
- Every portfolio founder gets access, which supports them "without requiring any of our time." Founders with their own following can search their followers too.
- It also helps win deals. Ryan will offer "tell us your B2B target customer list, let's go make some introductions," usually once a founder says it's a priority, and mostly after securing the allocation rather than before.

chunks.heading: Winning deals and being a non-annoying investor
chunks.text:
- Ryan lists the ingredients: access to see the company, a meeting with the founder, a small check that fits tight allocations, tools like Rolodexer, and references. His edge on access and meetings is Product Hunt (nearly 12 years old, roughly 100,000 makers launching per year) plus having "chewed glass" as a founder. He says there is no cookie-cutter template and it's customized per founder.
- Founders usually don't ask for references, but they may be doing them quietly, so reputation compounds.
- His approach: "We don't disappear and we don't bug them." Respond to every email, be proactive, and don't distract.
- "The worst thing you could do as a founder is bring on an investor who is net negative. And word gets around, reputation matters."
- When sharing useful info, he sometimes writes "no response needed" so the founder can archive it instantly.
- He describes a former Product Hunt COO's "piggy bank" idea: keep depositing small value into relationships, not as a transaction. It applies in venture because "everybody kind of knows each other."
- On SPVs and doubling down: LPs get first dibs, and they bring in strategic angels. Later-stage SPVs have been opportunistic. The game is early stage, and for competitive follow-on rounds it's relationship-driven: "have they been helpful? Do I feel like I owe them?"

chunks.heading: Scaling a small fund: scouts, tools and a two-person team
chunks.text:
- Ryan is an introvert who prefers working behind a computer and scaling through products. He does many quick Zoom calls (15-20 minutes for first meetings). His partner Jedica meets founders in person in San Francisco, so the two divide and conquer.
- The "weekend partners" scout program is non-exclusive. Scouts may scout for other firms, which suits the fund because it's small and early-stage, and Series A+ scouts can deploy earlier or gain access.
- Scouts get 25% of the carry on their deals, less than a16z or Sequoia scouts may get. Ryan says they are not doing it mainly for economics but to be part of the ecosystem. One scout has made 150 investments.
- Why scouts: tech changes fast and Ryan is a "product person, community person." He wants builders actively working in new areas, like a scout who is a founder in an upcoming YC batch and runs a hacker house in San Francisco.
- Transparency rule: scouts share deals in a shared Slack channel, not DMs, with the company, why they're excited, how they know the founder and other thoughts. Others can add views or founder connections. It creates more signal, and Ryan wants to see what everyone is looking at.
- He is building an investor workflow tool using LLMs and third-party data enrichment, "fun and frustrating," and says building it taught him what LLMs can do and where the holes are.

chunks.heading: Finding alpha: founder secrets, weird bets and lived experience
chunks.text:
- "A lot of what we're looking for is secrets." He backs a founder with a secret or with traction. Pre-launch: what do they see that others don't? Post-launch: if there's traction he doesn't understand, he digs into what he is missing.
- His view of the best alpha is lived experience with the problem a founder is solving. Example: he invested in Deel in 2018 because Product Hunt was fully distributed. He had seen the pros and cons and strongly believed remote hiring would grow, since recruiting in San Francisco was expensive and retaining talent was hard. This was before COVID.
- Invest in what you understand, though volume means many deals are outside his domain.
- He likes weird companies, especially weird consumer, though the fund invests in little consumer because it's very hard. Hot deals are often good, but only chasing them means playing the consensus game and missing weird companies. Backing a founder no one else would gives status and is "meaningful and important." Zeros are the nature of the game.
- The fund invests broadly, from "boring SMB tech to weird consumer stuff."
- Info diet: Twitter ("a fire hose," serendipitous) and conversations with founders and smart people. Conversations are "maybe the ultimate alpha" because they cover what people can't say publicly or haven't written. He used to blog from such conversations.

chunks.heading: Experiments, failures and early lessons
chunks.text:
- Weekend Build: an 8-week mini accelerator with no equity, run in Slack with weekly syncs, for people with side projects at big tech companies. Almost 1,000 applied and 10 teams were chosen. It failed because the thesis was finding venture-scale founders to back so they could quit their jobs, and none emerged.
- Why it failed: selection bias. People who had worked on a side project for over a year without leaving probably lacked traction, not just conviction or support. It would also need massive scale (about 100 teams, not 10) and is hard to productize. He says "most of them are complete failures."
- Advice to his younger self: he made zero investments before raising the first $3M fund in 2017, since investing as a CEO wasn't socially acceptable. He used to get too excited about the product and impart his own vision. He had to learn to ask what the founder's plan and the business are, a different muscle from "this is a cool product."
- Founder dynamic: he wants conversation, not lecture. If a founder agrees with everything he says, he's concerned.
- Introductions: he is strict about connecting people, and the host's double opt-in point was echoed only as a shared practice.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover traces his path from entrepreneur parents in Eugene to Product Hunt, then to investing via Weekend Fund. He covers validating a side project before committing, raising VC money only with a clear need, investing where you have an edge, and turning fund LPs into a community that helps founders.

chunks.heading: Early life and the entrepreneurial lens
chunks.text:
- Ryan grew up in Eugene, Oregon, in a middle-class family. His parents were entrepreneurs who worked together on "normal" small and medium businesses, not tech-enabled or VC-backed ones. His mom handled back-office accounting and operations; his dad was a problem solver and salesperson.
- His parents owned a video game store. At 14 he worked there for about $4 an hour, talking to customers and wiping down the glass counters.
- His dad's saying was "find the need and fill it". Ryan says this shaped how he sees the world: he can't help spotting business opportunities and problems solvable through entrepreneurship.
- As a kid he bought and sold on eBay, did some gray-hat projects (such as bonding Xboxes in high school), and built a website. These small projects scratched the entrepreneurial itch.
- He hates hourly pay. The incentive is misaligned: he could do the best or worst job and get paid the same. He prefers being paid on impact or output. He held hourly jobs in college (a call center, a pool store).

chunks.heading: How Product Hunt started: a side project, not a company plan
chunks.text:
- Ryan never woke up and decided to start a company. After studying at the University of Oregon, he interned at a video game company in Eugene, then moved to San Francisco in 2010 to join an early mobile gaming startup, PlayHaven (about employee number six). He did product there for about three and a half years.
- He followed his curiosity. He blogged about products (Snapchat's prompt design, Tinder's card stack that cues you to swipe more) and used writing "as a vehicle to express myself and learn".
- Product Hunt began as a newsletter aggregating products launched each day, sent to a few friends. He had little business thinking behind it; he just wanted to see if people liked it.
- Subscribers grew organically, which gave him confidence. He then turned it into a simple web app with his friend Nathan Bashaw in early 2014, built on the side over about four months.
- It grew quickly with no outside capital and no company. He paid a Heroku bill of roughly $500 a month and ran some advertising to cover server costs. Ryan Delk, then at Gumroad, Venmo'd him the first $5,000 the project made.

chunks.heading: Raising money for Product Hunt
chunks.text:
- Raising was "very, very easy" back then. The market was good (valuations lower than today), and Product Hunt served the tech community, so it already had investors' attention. VCs were courting him for coffee months before he decided to raise.
- He was cautious and delayed the decision for many weeks until he had conviction. His reasoning:
  - You can't just give the money back if you change your mind.
  - Raising VC capital means you have to go big; you can't aim for a $10 million exit.
- He says many founders get infatuated with the fundraising process without asking what they need the money for. His answer was simple: hire a team, since he had no money to build one.

chunks.heading: Product Hunt's mission and community
chunks.text:
- Over roughly seven and a half years, Product Hunt saw something like 200,000 to 250,000 products launched.
- Ryan says his motivation was not only VC-backed companies. It was encouraging people to build and giving them first users and self-confidence, such as a 14-year-old in the middle of nowhere launching a first app, Chrome extension or website.
- Users range from VC-backed startups to teenagers. Ryan says the global community helps people reach at least their first hundred, maybe thousand or tens of thousands, of users.
- Ryan stepped down as CEO in October 2020. Josh Buckley took over and the team has grown about 50% in recent months. Product Hunt was sold to AngelList; Ryan stayed about four years.
- On the cost of community: it is partly a support role, fielding issues every morning, and it is draining. Some long-tenured people stay (several have been there five to six years), but some community staff have burned out.

chunks.heading: Becoming an investor and starting Weekend Fund
chunks.text:
- He first considered venture in 2013, before Product Hunt. The only path then was an associate role, and as an introvert who didn't want to do a "bunch of coffee meetings", he passed.
- In 2017, AngelList launched venture funds, its first all-in-one fund management product after mostly doing syndicates/SPVs. On a walk-and-talk, Ryan asked Naval for advice on starting to invest. Naval suggested he start a fund.
- Ryan thought a fund was daunting and something he hadn't "earned the right" to do. He planned to raise $1 million and ended up raising $3 million for the first fund.
- Two motivations:
  - He was already doing similar work at Product Hunt (finding companies, building founder relationships).
  - He wanted to find out whether he was good at investing and start building that muscle as soon as possible.
- On rolling funds: the emerging-manager problem is that it's hard to predict how much you can raise. He aimed for $1M and raised $3M. The flexibility of not fixing fund size upfront lets you test the market.

chunks.heading: Investing philosophy and filters
chunks.text:
- He plays where he has an edge: private, early-stage technology companies. He has never bought an individual public stock and doesn't follow macro markets. His filter is "good product, good team".
- His advice to emerging managers is to be an expert in something and go deep. He admits he doesn't follow it: Weekend Fund invests broadly across consumer and B2B, avoiding hard tech and hardware, because it is introduced to many interesting emerging spaces.
- Deal flow comes from co-investors and his network, but also cold emails and proactive outreach after spotting something (for example on Product Hunt).
- On the biggest lesson: there is no formula for early-stage investing. Weekend Fund has passed on deals that failed its check boxes and that became billion-dollar companies a year or two later.
- On consensus: "where there's smoke there might be fire", so check out what everyone is talking about, but don't chase the herd.
- Crypto: he is not a token or NFT day trader because he lacks an edge. Weekend Fund invests in companies building things of real utility (DAOs, social tokens, tools that help communities organize and align incentives), not token projects as such. He believes this is where the internet is going.
- Examples he cited:
  - Deel: pitched as "Gusto for remote workers". Weekend Fund was a seed investor, and Deel later raised a Series C at a $1.25B valuation. The thesis in 2017 was that distributed and remote work would be the future, partly because Product Hunt itself was fully distributed.
  - Magic: a passwordless authentication platform. Weekend Fund did a $2M SPV. He likes it because it serves Web2 customers and revenue today while building for a Web3 future.
  - MiamiCoin (City Coins): he follows it as an opt-in, tax-equity-style idea in which 30% of purchases goes to a city-controlled wallet and the coin is programmable.

chunks.heading: Building a community around the fund
chunks.text:
- Ryan loves building and says community is often misused as a word. At Weekend Fund it means activating the 350+ LPs (operators and founders) who are excited to support early-stage companies and giving them a system to help founders directly, not only through the fund managers.
- The reasoning: founders have limited equity to give out, and each percentage point should buy high return. Founders benefit from as many capable, financially invested people around the table as possible.
- About 40 to 50% of people who invested through the community raise had never invested in a fund before. Some checks were as small as $2,000.
- Constraints: accreditation laws limit who can invest. He hopes laws change and has floated a future equity crowdfund, which has its own restrictions. If the community system scales, he says LPs could be far more helpful than the fund managers alone.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt began as a 20-30 person curated email digest, validated at ~400 subscribers, then became a site built in three weeks of weekend work with a friend. He covers seeding a community manually, designing for quality (invite-only, real identity), hiring and delegating, leaning on mentors, and why people should tinker.

chunks.heading: Why Ryan started Product Hunt as an email list and kept it a side project
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt began as a community-curated email digest of new apps, sites and products. Ryan was, in his words, a "manifestation of all the things I love": playing with new products and services.
- He built it with Linky Dink (by Makeshift), a service where invited people email in a link plus a sentence and it auto-sends a digest each weekday at about 5pm. He had no approval control over submissions.
- It started with about 20-30 contributors and 200-300 subscribers in the first week or so. It had about 400 subscribers when work on the site began, roughly three weeks in, with no marketing beyond tweets and a few posts.
- Validation was unprompted emails from readers saying they liked the list.
- Ryan is not an engineer. He asked a friend whether to learn Ruby on Rails or use Telescope. The friend, Nathan Basha (designer, product manager and engineer), offered to build it together over Thanksgiving.
- The first site cost no money, only time. It was a passion project with no business cards and no plan to start a company: "I just want to find cool new products and share them with friends."
- At the time he worked part-time (about 20 hours a week at reduced salary) while leaving a previous startup. That gave him time to experiment.

chunks.heading: Seeding a community with a small, connected group and doing things that don't scale
chunks.text:
- Early contributors were product enthusiasts in the tech scene (friends, investors, reporters), not "anybody in the world submitting anything." Ryan says this made it useful from day one.
- The first ~50 people were loosely connected, many knew each other or knew of each other. People he respected using it made others feel welcome to contribute.
- He grew it by email, one person at a time: ask engaged members "do you know two more people that you think would like Product Hunt and want to contribute?" He spidered out through degrees of separation.
- It was manual: many personal emails and lots of tweeting. He says people recognize a real human behind an email, unlike automated drip campaigns.
- He doesn't do this today because it doesn't scale, but "in the early days when you're just starting things up you have to often times do those things that are super laborious... seem really inefficient."
- He pushes for exclusivity early. Small invite-only groups are more intimate, and a shared bond (location, industry, loose network) gives a community its starting culture.

chunks.heading: Product design decisions that kept the community healthy
chunks.text:
- Ryan worried that opening up to everyone from day one would bring marketers and trolls, and he was the only community manager, with unmanned hours while he slept.
- Invite-only: the community invited others, so the system wasn't flooded with products.
- Twitter authentication: no email-only signups and no anonymous accounts. Companies still can't sign up under a brand name. The goal is to see the person's face and name for "real kind of direct interaction" and empathy. Identity curbs trolling, since "it's a lot easier to hate on someone when you're hiding behind a fake name." He notes pseudonyms work well for Reddit, so identity isn't right for every platform.
- Ongoing temptation: opening posting to everyone would likely give about 10x the products on the homepage and more engagement. But with 1,000 products, a product at 500th place gets lost. The goal is surfacing great products, so he manages volume against quality as the community scales.
- Culture is set by early members and is hard to change later. This is true of Reddit, 4chan and Hacker News too. Tone set in the beginning influences long-term direction dramatically.

chunks.heading: Earlier community experiments that informed Product Hunt
chunks.text:
- Ryan's background was product management, with no formal community-building job. Earlier side projects worked as retroactive practice.
- Startup Edition (with Nathan): a weekly email of blog posts. They emailed founders and CEOs a writing prompt (e.g. "how I built my team," "how I raised capital"). About 40-50 participants blogged on it, and the pair assembled the posts into a digest for subscribers. They also ran brunches of 8-10 people for in-person community.
- The model: give people a reason and platform to write, and curate the output for a broader audience.
- Pre-Product Hunt relationships mattered later. By the time he raised money, investors already knew him, and reporters he pitched had existing relationships with him. He didn't build them with the intent of extracting value, but they paid off.
- He built the network through curiosity: Twitter ("lightweight" and accessible for tech people), blog posts and writing, sharing his takes on products.

chunks.heading: Delegation, hiring and getting advice as a founder
chunks.text:
- A mistake he names: holding onto tasks. When it was just him he did everything (emailing, product wireframes, marketing). As the team grew he had to trust people to run with the job they were hired for.
- His reasoning: "you should be hiring people who are way better at all these things than you anyway," and his time and energy won't scale. He also doesn't have the best ideas, and teammates will make mistakes just as he does.
- Excessive control drives away the best talent.
- Two keys to giving people room: hire the right people, which is hard if you haven't worked with them, and make sure you're aligned on where you're going. Otherwise someone builds outside the vision and the founder takes the work back. He calls communication among teammates one of the most important things.
- Moving to mission-based initiatives rather than task or project assignment was a leadership process change prompted by board member Steven Sinofsky's input.
- Ryan leaned on experienced people: Josh Elman (Greylock) introduced the lawyer Josh Cook, who has handled incorporation and legal work since. Steven Sinofsky (board, a16z) advised him through the first time he had to fire someone.
- Fundraising is something most founders do rarely, so he talked to mentors and former founders. Lesson: "being okay with asking people for help."
- He values boards despite criticism of them: they keep a founder in check and flag pitfalls (legal, product direction, process) the founder doesn't know about.
- Backstory: early on, Naval (AngelList) was a seed investor. In 2017 Product Hunt joined AngelList, which focuses on fundraising, recruiting and now getting users. Both started as email lists (AngelList's was highly qualified investors receiving forwarded hot deals).

chunks.heading: Early tinkering, entrepreneurial roots and why passion makes it easier
chunks.text:
- At about 14, Ryan built a site after a friend made $100,000 from one. Operation Laugh (around 2002-2003) hosted jokes and comics and ran banner ads. He made about $70 and hosting cost about $60, so it was technically profitable after dozens of hours. He says the value was learning that making money online is hard and learning HTML and CSS.
- He hacked his Xbox as a kid (soldering in a modchip) partly to avoid paying $60 for games, and broke one doing it.
- His parents owned a video game store in the late '90s. He worked there at 13-14 and ran gumball machines, restocking and recording expenses and profits.
- He liked entrepreneurship because pay depends on output, not hours. Money is "a measurement of impact or value that you create."
- He used to dread public speaking but found pitching investors and giving talks easy once it was about something he was passionate about and knew well.
- Product Hunt's team hires for curiosity: curious people are open-minded, willing to experiment, and drawn to discovering new products daily.

chunks.heading: Ryan's stance: embrace tinkering and creation, and stop judging side projects
chunks.text:
- Ryan encourages tinkering and curiosity and loves seeing side projects launched on Product Hunt.
- He finds the startup ecosystem's negativity frustrating ("does the world need another gift app?").
- His argument: not every technology product is a company. Building an app, Chrome extension or website is increasingly "a creative expression," like learning guitar or drums. Nobody criticizes a kid whose first song is awful because he's learning.
- Conclusion: "we should embrace more creation... be less judgmental about people's products," because the kid tinkering could become "the next Zuckerberg" and build something meaningful.
- Product Hunt itself was an experiment, not a planned company.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains how he validated Product Hunt as a cheap email-list experiment, then grew it through writing-built credibility, Twitter login, a daily email habit loop, exclusivity, and building in public. He also covers personal outreach, community events, and why he avoids paid acquisition.

chunks.heading: Ryan's path from email-list experiment to Product Hunt startup
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt began as a simple email list built with Linky Dink, a tool for collaborative email lists. Ryan is not an engineer, so he did not try to build a full app to test the idea.
- He invited a few dozen people (investors, founders, friends) to submit cool new products and get a daily email of them.
- He had run many similar experiments before, such as an "Uber for laundry" landing page test. None had stuck. He treated Product Hunt as just another cheap, fun experiment.
- The email list had only a couple hundred subscribers. What convinced him to continue was qualitative feedback: people went out of their way to email or tell him in person that they read it every day.
- Stages as he describes them: experiment (email list), then side project (a website Nathan Bashaw built over Thanksgiving break, worked on together for about 3-4 months), then startup. He was still at PlayHaven, so there was no pressure to commit early.
- He considered a bootstrapped path (for example a $20,000-a-month business he owned fully) but chose to raise money and go bigger. He says self-funding is the right path for many people and most businesses.
- By the time of the interview, Product Hunt had over 200,000 monthly uniques and about 70% month-over-month user growth since January.

chunks.heading: Build an audience before the startup to de-risk distribution
chunks.text:
- Ryan argues the hardest part of a startup is not building the product. It is (1) figuring out what people want and (2) breaking through the noise to get attention.
- Building an audience first de-risks the second part before you have an idea, rather than starting from zero once you have one.
- His own audience came from about two years of writing on startups, growth, marketing and personal growth. He also helped Nir Eyal write *Hooked*. He calls it "not a huge audience" but enough credibility to run experiments to.
- Writing is not the only route. Podcasting and organizing events (conferences, brunches) work too. The point is to "provide value to some community of people."
- Advice for someone starting out:
  - Be curious and experimental. If writing doesn't go anywhere after a year, try something else like podcasting.
  - Pick something you will use and care about for years. He would not build a women's-fashion community because he isn't the right person for it.
  - Use your own product all the time, because the founder's behavior shapes the community culture.
- His motivation for writing was enjoyment and recognition, not a master plan. He admits the dots only connected in hindsight.

chunks.heading: Designing Product Hunt for habit and daily return
chunks.text:
- Email is central. About 50,000 people subscribed to the daily email at the time, and sending it makes site traffic spike. Featured products get thousands of extra visitors.
- Ryan's point: even if people like a site, they usually need an external trigger to return. Email is that trigger, and it also delivers value as a quick digest.
- For mobile apps, he says personal notifications and the app icon serve the same trigger role.
- Social re-engagement pulls people back too: when someone is mentioned or tagged, they get an email.
- "Day parting": the leaderboard resets each day. Unlike Hacker News or Reddit, which feel like an endlessly changing board of links and overwhelm visitors, a fresh daily list reinforces a daily routine.
- Login uses Twitter, for two reasons:
  - It was quick to build (no custom authentication).
  - It gives a consistent social graph (who follows whom), real names and handles, and a way to verify identity (for example a real Ashton Kutcher). It also gives another channel to talk to users. The Product Hunt Twitter account had about 20,000 followers.

chunks.heading: Incentives, sharing and community rules
chunks.text:
- Ryan avoids heavy sharing calls to action. There is only a tweet button, with no sharing walls. People already want to share cool new finds, and early adopters like looking ahead of the curve.
- Incentives are aligned: founders want upvotes and to reach the top of the leaderboard, so they share with friends and users. Some products got over 10,000 uniques in a day or two.
- Every participant must be a real person (no company Twitter accounts), so conversations feel human.
- Posting and commenting were limited to a whitelisted group at first. Reasons he gives:
  - Over 100 submissions per day never reached the home page (off-topic, duplicates, low quality).
  - Opening to everyone would bring self-promoters, and 60 products a day is already a lot.
  - Trolls and spam are hard to moderate with a tiny team.
  - Limiting early membership lets them shape the culture. He jokes that an influx of Justin Bieber fans would be "a different audience."
- Later, they began a recommendation system where members invite people they'd like to add. Early tests showed people like inviting friends, "like giving their friends a gift."

chunks.heading: Growth channels: word of mouth, press, user content, no paid
chunks.text:
- Word of mouth is the main driver. Everyone registers via Twitter and shares there.
- Press works unusually well for Product Hunt: TechCrunch, Next Web and VentureBeat readers are the same people who want to discover new products. Reporters use Product Hunt to find stories, so the relationships go both ways.
- Content marketing is done by the community. They ask the top 10 products' founders each day to write about their experience, then share it. Both sides benefit, and some of those posts did better than the original Product Hunt listing.
- Investors also discover companies on the platform, and a few products got funded, which completes the cycle of aligned incentives.
- No paid acquisition. He says paid is expensive, and he doubts it brings the best users, who are friends of existing community members.
- Custom boards work well: a board of every company in 500 Startups' batch 9 on demo day was a strong acquisition source. Other "collections" included GIF apps, a YC hackathon, and a nostalgia Flashback Friday.
- AMAs with well-known founders (Dennis Crowley, Mark Cuban, Jason Calacanis) bring in influential users because people ask them questions about their products.
- Tactic: check who is signing up. In the early days he put signup emails into Rapportive, spotted investors and reporters, and personally thanked them to start relationships. He calls it "a missed opportunity" not to do this, especially with reporters.

chunks.heading: Twitter and relationship tactics
chunks.text:
- Twitter is "arguably the most important product in my life" outside email. He used it to distribute writing and get feedback.
- Reply to everyone who shares your work, using their first name ("thanks Kyle"), because people appreciate that you typed it.
- He shared other people's blog posts via Buffer and always tagged the author. Over time, authors remember you, which leads to relationships (coffee, hiring, early users, investors, celebrity users).
- Advice: don't treat things as transactional, act like a human, and have fun. Individual interactions seem small but add up. There's a balance between being genuinely appreciative and "kissing ass."
- For email at volume: use Streak shortcuts and hotkeys for repeated answers, but stay human and add a relevant personal note (for example about a recent tweet). He once ranked first among about 150 startup people on an inbox-checkup app for emails sent.

chunks.heading: Building in public, podcasting and live events
chunks.text:
- Ryan shared wireframes and mockups with the first couple dozen users by email and asked specific questions. Later he put a site redesign on InVision and emailed it to the community, getting 100-200 replies in a morning. They changed things before building.
- His principle: transparency makes people feel part of the product, and "it's more important than anything for people to feel like they have a say."
- He cites Buffer as the most transparent company he knows (public metrics, investor updates, replying to everyone on Twitter).
- Podcasting: he started it partly because he enjoyed it, and also because it gives access to admired people and shows the human side. Hearing someone's voice builds more connection than Twitter or email. It's another engagement channel (iTunes subscribers).
- Live events:
  - Happy hours are easy: email a group with an event page. A New York one drew about 500 RSVPs.
  - Brunches of about 25 people are more intimate, and he enjoys them more.
  - Meeting in person builds more authentic ties, and people who meet this way become big supporters. Members have asked to run their own meetups elsewhere.
- Challenge he flags: keeping a high-touch support style while volume grows.

chunks.heading: Roadmap and team-size views
chunks.text:
- The iOS app (designed by David McKinney) was close to beta, with launch expected within a month. The mobile website was only semi-responsive.
- He expects the team to be the "face" of Product Hunt for the short-to-medium term, which won't scale long term.
- On company growth: PlayHaven went from 10 to about 110 people. He learned that the people who get you there early aren't always the right ones later, and process needs rise with size. He concluded he works best in smaller companies, and left to build a consumer product with a small team.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover joins Jason Calacanis and Sophia Amoruso to discuss emerging-manager fundraising, rising valuations, and how startup signaling has shifted to revenue and social reach. He shares how Weekend Fund decides follow-ons, why they sold part of a winner for early DPI, and why improving foundation models change how AI founders should think about timing.

chunks.heading: Weekend Fund's fund construction and check sizing
chunks.text:
- Weekend Fund is on its third fund. The first fund targeted $1M and closed at $3M, helped by former Product Hunt investors who became LPs.
- Ryan raised the first fund shortly after Product Hunt sold to AngelList. He stayed on as CEO for four years afterward. The current fund was raised in 2021, which he calls a relatively easy fundraising year.
- Historically the fund wrote about a $300K average check. The goal was that any unicorn or above in the portfolio could return the fund.
- Valuations are climbing. When the fund started, median entry price across seed and pre-seed was about $6.5M post-money. Ryan says that is far lower than today.
- He keeps some price awareness. The fund passes on deals when the valuation is very high, the company is pre-launch, and there are few objective proof points. He also doesn't want to miss the best companies, so he is rethinking strategy and deployment for the next fund.
- His optimistic framing is that today's unicorn is tomorrow's decacorn. AI is also eating into services spending, so some companies that used to cap out as unicorns may grow much bigger.
- He wasn't raising at the time of the episode. He says you only learn whether LPs will invest once you actually raise, since many ask "are you raising?" but don't write checks.

chunks.heading: Follow-on and recycling policy
chunks.text:
- Follow-ons and recycling are flexible at Weekend Fund. Nothing strict is written into the LPA.
- His follow-on test: "if we believe in this company, all things being equal, even if we're not an investor, would we invest in this company at this valuation today, knowing what we know now?"
- Recycling happens within a limited window. If a company shuts down or returns capital early, the fund recycles it.
- Around year five or six of a fund, the fund distributes returns instead of recycling. By then the team is usually raising or deploying a newer fund anyway.

chunks.heading: Taking liquidity from winners
chunks.text:
- Weekend Fund did this once, about 18 months before the episode. It had invested in a seed round at a $10M post-money valuation in the first fund. The last round was at a $12B valuation.
- The fund sold 14% of its position, enough to return the fund on paper. About 83-84% of the position remained, so a mistake would still leave a large stake.
- The sale happened below the $12B mark because the market was in a slump at the time. Ryan says the stock would now sell for more than 2x the sale price, but he still thinks it was the right call.
- Reasons for selling: LPs would be glad to see liquidity, since almost no one was getting any. It also put 1x DPI on the board. He still counts it as only paper returns until it is true DPI.
- He remains bullish on the company, both then and now.
- General rule: early-stage funds should start thinking about liquidity after roughly 5-8 years in a position, and take 20-30% off the table even when they are confident it keeps rising.

chunks.heading: Why founder-reported revenue is now the status symbol
chunks.text:
- Ryan says status signals in the startup world have shifted. Revenue is the new status symbol, ahead of raising capital. Brand-name investor backing still matters, but it is secondary.
- Public revenue numbers are also a leading indicator that gets investors interested. He admits that seeing founders post huge numbers on Twitter creates FOMO, for example companies claiming about $50M in revenue in their first 12 months.
- Press has been replaced by social reach as the way to get attention. Twitter has become a launchpad for new companies.
- Algorithm changes help unknowns. A no-name founder used to get little play from a post. The algorithm now heavily favors video, such as product demos, and surfaces them to people outside the poster's network.

chunks.heading: Building on improving foundation models
chunks.text:
- Ryan contrasts the AI shift with the move to cloud computing. Cloud was close to binary: you were on it or you weren't, and it made things a bit faster or cheaper without changing the underlying product.
- With AI, foundation models keep getting better, so a product built on them improves without the founder doing the heavy lifting. For some use cases the utility hasn't yet met consumer needs, but it will as models improve.
- The implication for founders: be in position and capture users now, so that when models become good enough to deliver what the product promises, the users are already there.
- He says building on top of these models is quite different from earlier tech waves because the underlying technology itself upgrades the product.
- On the number of builders: tools are getting better, so people like an accountant in the Midwest who understands a niche problem can ship at least an MVP. He acknowledges today's vibe-coded tools aren't production-ready, citing security problems at one product. He is confident the number of builders will rise sharply, though not all will be venture-backable.

chunks.heading: Revenue quality for fast-growing AI companies
chunks.text:
- On brittle versus durable revenue for AI tools, Ryan says churn and retention matter, and points back to improving foundation models rather than a metric-specific test.
- He sees the Lovable check as a case for thinking about this.
- He cites a team member who built a portal for the syndicate by vibe coding in Lovable, as a sign of how non-engineers can now produce software.

chunks.heading: Founder gatherings and portfolio support
chunks.text:
- Weekend Fund used to run small Zoom hangs for its portfolio, capped at roughly five to seven people. Founders talk about what they're working on and what challenges they have.
- Ryan argues the format works because there is more trust among peers. In front of a VC or their team, a founder has to look confident and can't be honest, and the same person acts differently. He calls it an environmental effect.

chunks.heading: Portfolio companies he highlighted
chunks.text:
- **Atlas**: Weekend Fund invested in the seed round, and the company has since raised a Series A and B. It helps Indian travelers apply for visas inside a mobile app, with tracking built in, instead of using clunky government websites. Ryan calls it a massive, overlooked market.
- At the start, founder Mohawk effectively built APIs on top of government websites through web scraping. Ryan says this was a clever "wrapper" around the whole experience, and he points out it began just before COVID hit.
- He also names the CEO, Mohawk, as a reason he likes the company, and says making travel more flexible and convenient is a net positive.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt began as a Linky Dink email list, was validated by unprompted feedback, then built as a simple Hacker News-style site over Thanksgiving. Growth came from personal one-to-one emails, an inner circle of early contributors, and founders sharing their own listings.

chunks.heading: How Ryan validated Product Hunt before building it
chunks.text:
- Ryan loves discussing products and how people build them. Offline, conversations with entrepreneurs always came back to "what cool apps are you finding" and "what's on your home screen."
- He wanted to move that conversation online. He found no community or destination dedicated to products.
- He validated with no code. He used Linky Dink, a simple collaborative link-sharing tool (he calls it "a collaborative email list"), created a group, and named it "Product Hunt," the first name that came to mind.
- He invited 20-30 entrepreneurs, founders and investors to submit products they found. A nightly digest was emailed to everyone.
- He posted once on Quibb and tweeted once. About 170 people subscribed in the first week without real marketing.
- The stronger signal was unprompted feedback. People emailed him or told him in person that they looked forward to the nightly emails. That convinced him others wanted it too, and that there might be an actual product.
- Linky Dink had no feedback mechanism for surfacing the best items. He wanted a Hacker News/Reddit-style community for products.

chunks.heading: Building the first version in four days
chunks.text:
- Ryan is not a technical founder. He can do some front-end work but has no backend experience, so he asked technical friends what to build it on. He considered Ruby on Rails and Telescope (Sacha Greif's app for building Hacker News/Reddit-style sites).
- Nathan Bashaw, a friend of about a year, offered to build it over Thanksgiving. He built the first version in roughly four to five days using Ruby on Rails. Ryan says Nathan had built similar social community products before (including General Assembly's Dash), so he wasn't doing anything new.
- They collaborated by phone and IM while both were at their parents' homes. Each sketched their own wireframes, then they aligned on a deliberately minimal V1 scope.
- Because the product was so simple, little back and forth was needed after the initial design. Ryan reviewed the first version (posts, no comments) and gave feedback.
- Their approach to speed: "making a decision quickly is better than stagnating." Ryan says it's better to ship something imperfect that people can touch and feel than to spend more time talking to users and refining the design.
- He agrees that the longer you delay putting something in front of real users, the more you're guessing. He reminds himself that his roadmap ideas, though he is confident in them, may not be what the community actually wants.
- On the partnership, there was no signed agreement and costs were informally split. Ryan relies on trust built over a year and says the two complement each other's skills. He admits it's "probably not the best way" and expects to sort out details later.

chunks.heading: Seeding the community with a private beta
chunks.text:
- For the first week, they re-invited the same contributors who had used Linky Dink, about 30-40 people. Nathan and Ryan emailed founders and product-minded contacts, asked for feedback, and asked them not to share it publicly. The group grew to around 50-60 by the end of the week.
- They showed these early members wireframes and upcoming features and asked for feedback. This served two purposes: feedback before building, and making them feel part of the process, "and realistically really they were part of the process."
- A public launch came after that first week.
