- Ryan says Product Hunt would not have worked as well nine months earlier. It was feasible because of the network he built over the prior year through blogging and projects like Startup Edition (a newsletter).

chunks.heading: Growth tactics: personal email, early-member loops, and press
chunks.text:
- Ryan's marketing strategy was email. His outbound email rose roughly 5-10x over three months. He did not use a mass-outreach tool (he mentions Tout App) because he prefers the personal touch.
- Each email used a base template describing Product Hunt, plus something relevant to the recipient, such as the last interaction.
- The goal was first to reach product-minded people likely to be good contributors, then get them to invite friends. Communities are more fun with friends.
- To make referrals easy, he included a ready-to-paste two-sentence intro so people didn't have to write the introduction themselves.
- He emailed the audience of Startup Edition (about 3,500 subscribers) only in week three or four, and it didn't drive much user acquisition.
- Results at the time of the interview: almost 5,000 subscribers, growing 80-150 new subscribers per weekday.
- Current focus was retention and engagement (people sticking around and coming back), with some user growth to keep momentum.

chunks.heading: The launch-day trick: tell early members first
chunks.text:
- Ryan had written for PandoDaily a handful of times and emailed reporter Carmel, whom he'd met once. They did an interview and she wrote about the project.
- The post drove only about 1,000-1,500 unique visitors. Its purpose was not user acquisition. It was to show the community that Product Hunt is real and get them excited.
- The night before, he and Nathan emailed about 80-100 early contributors saying the public announcement would run the next day, and followed up on that email thread with the link once it was live.
- People like being part of the behind-the-scenes process and wanted to read the article. They shared it, and per Carmel it became the second or third most popular PandoDaily post that day. Ryan credits that largely to emailing the contributors.
- He frames the strategy as making people feel included and giving them ownership.

chunks.heading: Word of mouth and the founder-engagement loop
chunks.text:
- Growth came from direct email recruiting, press, and word of mouth. He hasn't measured the split but sees dozens of tweets every week saying things like "I use this every single day" and "this is replacing Hacker News."
- Founders are a built-in distribution channel. When a product is posted, founders often notice via mentions or by monitoring their product name, join the thread, and bring in their own audiences to upvote.
- Upvoting requires logging in with an email address, so founder-driven traffic converts into sign-ups. Founders want to be at the top of the leaderboard, which grows more important as the community grows.
- The best discussions are when founders join to do Q&A or an AMA. Ryan says they encouraged this and that he personally likes talking directly with founders about product decisions.

chunks.heading: Background and path into product
chunks.text:
- He has been entrepreneurial from childhood (selling joke books at his dad's video game store, running a gumball machine).
- He started as an unpaid marketing intern at a video game company in Eugene and got hired after college. He migrated into product because he kept suggesting product features, and his VP of product made him a product manager. He says he didn't know what a product manager was six months before becoming one and was "a terrible product manager" in hindsight.
- After that company failed, he moved to San Francisco and ran product at PlayHaven for over three years, as the only product manager for the first year and a half.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt began as a no-code email list MVP, grew into a curated, invite-only community, and why a PM background and authentic social presence helped. He also covers early monetization via job posts, support via Twitter, and distribution value for startups.

chunks.heading: Ryan's path from side project to Product Hunt: start with a cheap MVP
chunks.text:
- Ryan started Product Hunt in late 2013 as an email list. He and his friends kept sharing new apps and sites in messaging apps and on Twitter, but there was no single place listing "new and cool today."
- He is not an engineer, so he had to find the fastest way to test whether people cared as much as he did. An email list needed zero engineering and took "an hour or half an hour" to set up.
- Several hundred people subscribed in the first week or so. He then watched whether they kept opening and engaging with the emails.
- He argues many startups begin as a simple email list. Six months earlier he had written a post called "Email for Startups." Its examples were AngelList, Sunrise (the calendar app) and Timehop, all of which started as emails.
- There was no single tipping point. It was a series of signals: more subscribers, unprompted emails saying "I like this email, it's really useful," and a steady pull from the startup community once the website launched.
- He ran it as a side project for roughly four to five months (early to mid 2014) before deciding whether to build a team.

chunks.heading: Deciding to turn the side project into a company
chunks.text:
- By early 2014 more founders and startups were launching on Product Hunt. The job board was already earning $4,000 a month (the transcript text reads "$44,000," which looks like a transcription error, so treat the figure as unclear). It paid his rent and he believed it could reach 10K to 20K fairly easily.
- He framed the choice as two paths: keep it a side project, or build a team and make it something much bigger.
- He got advice from Y Combinator partners (Gary Tan introduced him to Kevin Hale, Kat Manalac and Alexis Ohanian) before deciding whether YC was the right path.
- He made the call once he could answer two questions: could he see a path to it becoming a big and important thing, and would it be fun to work on for a decade? YC came out as the best route, and he went through it.
- He raised money leading into YC.

chunks.heading: Seeding a community: manual invites, a common bond, then productize
chunks.text:
- Ryan knew that opening the site to everyone would flood it with self-promotion, especially after the first press announcement. Early on they had little ability to detect fraud, and the feed can only hold so many items.
- In the beginning it was friends. Before any invite system existed, he emailed highly engaged people, asked if they knew a couple of others who would want to contribute, had them CC that person, and onboarded everyone by hand.
- The goal was people who would genuinely want to participate, not influencers or people over a follower count. Influence "wasn't even part of the criteria."
- On early community building, he wants "some sort of common bond." Not everyone must be friends, but it should feel like a cool house party rather than "a random mix of people all over the place that don't know each other."
- Once the manual process worked, they built an invite system so the community could invite others without him editing the database.
- Access later expanded: if you make a product that is on Product Hunt, you get access, because you need to answer questions and join the conversation.
- Opening the gates fully waited until certain product work was done.

chunks.heading: Why launching on a community works: Reset Plug and "unsearchable" products
chunks.text:
- Ryan says founders get unexpected results from Product Hunt in traffic, downloads, signups, sales, press and funding. Some investors found companies there and started a dialogue.
- Press uses the site too and sometimes writes about what it finds. "Ship Your Enemies Glitter" got extra press beyond Product Hunt, went viral, and the founder got more orders than he could fulfill because he was assembling the packages by hand.
- His favorite recent example is Reset Plug. You plug your router into it and it detects when the router has gone down and power-cycles it for you. Someone in the community posted it, and it got a lot of upvotes.
- Two days later the founder emailed Ryan: he had sold about 500 units in a couple of days, versus almost no website visitors before. The founder had not posted it himself, so it came as a surprise.
- The lesson Ryan draws: when you show a product to a community, people convert and buy. This is a product you would never search for, because you don't know it exists, even though everyone has had the problem.

chunks.heading: Why product management prepares you to be a CEO
chunks.text:
- Ryan says he could not have built Product Hunt successfully five years earlier, without his years of startup experience. He worked professionally in startups for about six years first, and he stresses there is no universal answer on whether everyone should do the same.
- He "accidentally fell into" product management at his first startup, loved it, and became Playhaven's first product manager in 2010.
- He calls it a unique role. You communicate across engineering (leading indirectly), design, sales and customer support, and you message both up to the CEO and down the org.
- Those communication skills transfer directly to being a CEO, at larger scale. The same people skills apply to sales, and to recruiting, where you are asking someone to quit their job and trust you and the company with their livelihood.

chunks.heading: Solo founder, and building a brand through personal social media
chunks.text:
- On being a solo founder, Ryan says there is no magic formula: solo, two or three founders can each work. He stresses he is just one piece of the product and that many teammates past and present got the company where it is.
- Product Hunt began differently from most startups. It was a side project, not meant to be a startup at first, and friends helped bootstrap it with enough data to prove people wanted it.
- He has no regrets about not having a co-founder and may or may not have one for whatever comes after.
- He was active on social media long before Product Hunt. His writing and Twitter connections were effectively "the MVP for Product Hunt": building an audience, trust and a brand that seeded the first community.
- He posts partly for professional reasons but mostly because he enjoys it (mystery package unboxings on Facebook Live, Snapchat). For the company, he says it matters that the brand feels authentic and human.
- He tries new social apps early and engages with the community there. He says he prefers Snapchat because it opens straight to the camera, and he won't post the same content to both Snapchat and Instagram Stories.

chunks.heading: Customer support: use Twitter, automate the obvious, keep it human
chunks.text:
- Ryan says Twitter is often faster and more responsive than a generic support email, and it feels more human than an anonymous inbox. He doesn't like being a jerk in public, so he often tweets a suggestion rather than a complaint.
- Example: he tweeted a suggestion to Uber about being charged $5 to cancel after a driver sat idle for 10 minutes. They responded, moved it to DM and gave him $10 in ride credit.
- He hates phone calls and avoids calling businesses. He would rather chat or solve the problem without a call.
- On bots, he says the aim is to automate obvious questions (for example "how late are you open today?") that a human shouldn't have to answer. People still want a human for big or complicated issues like banking.
- Product Hunt's support is run by community members, and the team takes pride in how fast they respond and in surprising and delighting people. He says the best outcome is someone arriving with a problem and leaving happy or having learned something.
- Because launches are a stressful and exciting time for founders, he thinks helping at that moment is what makes people feel passionately enough to send thank-you notes, stickers and gifts.

chunks.heading: Brand lessons from LaCroix and the Planet of the Apps opportunity
chunks.text:
- Ryan notes LaCroix, an old brand, took off in recent years. He doesn't claim to know if it was intentional, but points to what he thinks helped: many flavors, each person has a favorite, which creates personalization and competitiveness. He tweeted that he is "team coconut" and people argued back with their own flavors, which drives word of mouth and brand affinity.
- He also cites the retro, "normcore" look and rising health consciousness as factors.
- He joined Apple's show Planet of the Apps (via Gary Vaynerchuk's intro) partly for selfish reasons, to learn how the entertainment industry works behind the scenes.
- He sees a huge opportunity in mainstream interest in technology, and potentially large distribution for founders who appear on the show in a world where breaking out and getting attention is increasingly difficult.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Early (Feb 2015) interview where Hoover explains how Product Hunt grew from a curated email list into a voting community, via quick-and-dirty copying of proven patterns, a daily-habit email, and an open API. He stresses community over tech, habit triggers, and not being afraid to remind users you exist.

chunks.heading: Why Ryan started Product Hunt as an email list
chunks.text:
- Ryan likes talking about products. His conversations with friends often start with "what apps are you playing with" or "did you see that cool new app yesterday."
- He wanted a place to curate and share cool products with friends, so it began as an email list (a little over a year before this 2015 interview).
- The list was a true mailing list. He invited entrepreneurs and investors he knew, and anyone who found a cool product submitted it, which then emailed the whole group each day. He was not curating it himself at first.
- The list gained traction, and he saw that people love sharing technology products.
- A friend, Nathan Basha, built the first version over Thanksgiving in about five days on Ruby on Rails. It was quick and dirty.
- Ryan did not invent new mechanics. He took inspiration from Digg, Reddit and Hacker News, because tech people already understand upvoting and curation and don't have to learn something new.

chunks.heading: Why the daily email and daily rhythm drive retention
chunks.text:
- The email is the core experience. Each day it lists the previous day's top 10 products by upvotes, so it is an easy way to catch up on what's hot.
- The site is split by day on purpose, to encourage a daily habit.
- It goes out at 7:30 a.m. Ryan ran it himself every morning at the time of this interview.
- The email also carries editorial content and featured collections, such as on-demand delivery services, emoji products and gift apps.
- Its open and click-through rates were 2 to 3x the industry average, and the rates held up over time.
- Ryan says becoming part of someone's morning routine is the key to stickiness.
- He cites Nir Eyal (whom he helped with the book "Hooked") on triggers. Internal triggers are FOMO ("what's new, what's hot") and "I need a product that does X." External triggers are the daily email.
- He says many companies are afraid to spam users, and some do abuse email and push notifications. But "without reminding people you exist even if your product is awesome... people just don't remember to come back," so he thinks most should be more aggressive.
- The reminders must provide value. He gives the example of "Merry Christmas" and "happy New Year" emails with no value: "an excuse for me to unsubscribe."
- Marketing and sales only feel negative if you forget to put yourself in the consumer's shoes. Ask what information they would want and how you can deliver value that brings them back.

chunks.heading: How he got traction and approached Y Combinator
chunks.text:
- Ryan met Alexis Ohanian, Kevin Hale and other YC partners before he applied.
- He believes YC accepted Product Hunt because of the traction it already had. "Upvote cool products" is not an idea that obviously works on paper.
- Most YC companies already have something working when they join.
- YC lasted three months. He says the relationships, access to partners and office hours, and the alumni network continue afterward.
- Funding: Kevin Rose and Google Ventures invested in the seed round, and Alexis invested in the Series A. The total was $7.1M across the seed and Series A.
- Ryan used Alexis, Reddit and Hacker News moderators for advice on keeping the community healthy.
- Early on, it was an experiment and a side project. He debated bootstrapping it into a profitable business before taking money.
- He took the Series A to get a long runway. That lets the team focus on the product instead of short-term gains and fundraising, which he says is a huge distraction even when it's relatively easy.
- Funding does not change the team's intensity, but it adds pressure to succeed and return investors' money.
- Growth: Product Hunt grew well over 10x in monthly visitors in 2015 and the email list grew significantly. The team was 14 people.
- The site had no advertising, and Ryan did not see any coming for a while. Growth was viral.

chunks.heading: Community is the product, and the main risk
chunks.text:
- Ryan answers the question "how is this even a business" (a top Hacker News comment on the YC announcement) by saying the value is the community and the people who use it.
- Other "Product Hunt for X" sites appeared (health foods, niche categories). Most don't succeed. They build a working product but not the community, and the community is what makes it work.
- He says "we will either succeed or fail based on the community. It's not going to be a technical challenge."
- He watched Digg grow and implode, and keeps that in mind.
- Anti-gaming measures: voting-ring detection, spam-bot detection, sandboxing, and manual review. He says gaming is a sign of success and will be a constant fight.
- He also puts unusual focus on the internal team, finding community leaders who understand psychology and can build communities.
- Posts by makers promoting their own product are fine, as are posts by people who found something cool. The goal is to surface things people find interesting or useful, not who posted them.
- Makers often join the comment threads. Ryan says that direct dialogue between consumers and the people who made the product is what sets it apart from tech blogs.
- He worries every morning that he doesn't know what will be on the site or whether people will keep coming. During the 2013 holidays he feared users would not return, but they did.

chunks.heading: Metrics, data and platform strategy
chunks.text:
- Ryan's single core metric is how much traffic Product Hunt drives to the products listed. It shows the impact on the ecosystem. Founders also write blog posts about their own traffic from the site.
- Audience: about 4% is in the Bay Area and about half is outside the US, so it is not just a Silicon Valley bubble.
- The API was built after he saw spikes in real-time analytics from people scraping the site. He was nervous about opening it but decided it was the right direction.
- People built dozens of apps on it, including Android apps (Product Hunt had none of its own then), Alfred and Mac menu-bar tools, and Map Hunt, which maps products by maker location. He sees community-built hacks as a way to be led by what people actually want.
- He sees a longer-term platform and data play. "Related products" shows similar products when one launches, and the site gets more valuable as more products and makers join.
- Collections began as team-curated and became creatable by anyone about three to four months before this interview. Examples included emoji apps, Valentine's gift apps, helping hands, and a 2014 music collection that was an experiment launched that day.
- Long-term he has ambitions to expand beyond tech into other verticals ("there's no ceilings").

chunks.heading: Focus and product decisions
chunks.text:
- He started on the web, not mobile, for two reasons: limited resources (two part-time people) and content that suits desktop, since many listed products are landing pages built for full screens.
- He does not focus much on mobile yet, but sees mobile as the primary interface long term as they expand to different verticals.
- The site gets 200+ submissions a day, and not all reach the homepage. Even if all are amazing it would be overwhelming, so they are looking for the right balance.
- Voting helps users cut through a crowded space. In the GTD to-do collection, upvotes pushed a little-known app to the top.
- On risk: he is somewhat risk averse, yet loves entrepreneurship. He feels that no matter what happens he can't really lose, because he is learning and doing something he believes in.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt started as a small email list, then became a real product built in about five days with only the bare minimum features. He also covers how a pre-built audience seeded the community and how blogging, cold emails and cross-posting drove early distribution.

chunks.heading: How Ryan and Nathan shipped the first Product Hunt in about five days
chunks.text:
- Ryan describes himself as non-technical: he can do front-end work but can't build a Ruby on Rails app.
- Product Hunt began as an email list of roughly 20-30 founders and investors who each contributed cool products they'd found, with a daily digest emailed to the group.
- Subscribers grew and several people told him they looked forward to the emails, so he decided to turn it into a real product.
- He asked Nathan Bashaw (a "unicorn": designer, developer and product-minded) what to build it in. Nathan offered to build it over Thanksgiving break, and he took about four or five days.
- The goal was to build something quickly and get it to 20-30 early adopters for feedback as fast as possible. That meant being strict about cutting features to the bare minimum.
- v1 scope:
  - Post a product (link, name, short tagline).
  - Upvote.
  - Flat comment feed.
  - Twitter for authentication, so no auth system had to be built.
- Things deliberately missing at launch, such as the ability to hide posts. Inappropriate posts were hidden by editing the database directly.
- The model is "a Hacker News style" product, and Ryan says the first version "doesn't look much different than it does today."

chunks.heading: Seeding both sides of a marketplace with an existing audience
chunks.text:
- The initial email list was not marketed. Ryan posted about it on Twitter and Quibb, where he had built a following of entrepreneurs and founders.
- That produced about 150 subscribers and about 20-30 contributors. Some contributors came from direct outreach to people in their network.
- The list was then opened to more people, and there was more marketing at launch.
- He says that launching six or nine months earlier "wouldn't have been where it is today." Its success rests on the following, audience and trust he and Nathan built over the previous year or so, largely through blogging and connecting with others.
- He argues many products take long to grow because their founders haven't built that following first.
- Post-launch, the focus was engagement and retention rather than acquisition. Acquisition came mostly from word of mouth and press.

chunks.heading: Earning press through relationships and free content
chunks.text:
- Ryan got press from Pando Daily, including an interview with Carmel when Product Hunt was publicly announced. He also wrote three or four guest posts for Pando Daily or Fast Company on learnings from building Product Hunt.
- He says the interview worked because he had built relationships first: roughly four or five essays contributed to Pando, offered free, which earned him respect and a willingness to listen.
- He met Carmel once in person before she took the call, and notes that for reporters "it's all about timing too," so some luck is involved.
- Press that came from other writers covering Product Hunt added to this.

chunks.heading: Cold-emailing a publication for a guest post
chunks.text:
- His first Pando relationship started with a cold email to Sarah Lacy. He asked a friend who had guest posted there how he got in, and the friend said he cold emailed Sarah.
- The essay was "What product designers can learn from Phil's Coffee."
- His tactics:
  - Attach the full final draft. Pitching only a topic puts the publication at risk because they can't commit to something they haven't seen.
  - Add a short description of why it's important and relevant to their audience.
  - Make it specific to them. His subject line was "Love Pando Monthly," and the body praised the interview series, which he really did enjoy, and mentioned an upcoming interview.
  - Keep it short and genuine. He says "cold emails work" and that most people are too afraid to send them, though a warm introduction is usually most effective if available.
- Sarah forwarded it to Adam Penenberg, who published it and invited more essays in that domain.

chunks.heading: Distributing writing across multiple platforms
chunks.text:
- Ryan posts on his own blog first (hosted on Tumblr at the time). The next day or so he cross-posts to Medium, Svbtle and sometimes Quora.
- The purpose is distribution. He says it's easy to copy and paste, and "if it's relevant to the community... then why not post it everywhere."
- Some topics do better on certain platforms. An essay can flop on his own blog and take off on Medium; Medium suits topics like writing.
- On the SEO risk of Medium outranking his own site, he posts to his own domain first so Google tends to treat it as canonical. He hasn't analyzed it closely and judges that the upside of more distribution outweighs the risk.
- He broadcasts each post on Twitter and Quibb, but hasn't pushed people from those channels into Quora.
- Even on platforms that don't allow custom pop-ups, he ends essays with calls to action: his Twitter handle (spelled out) and a link to subscribe to his blog or email list. He gets few subscribers this way, but it is "always worth doing."

chunks.heading: Planned improvements and why community engagement mattered
chunks.text:
- Next priorities were monitoring engagement and adding missing features:
  - Comment upvoting, because he wanted to give someone a pat on the back for a good comment without posting "awesome post."
  - Basic comment threading.
  - Search.
  - A better, more scalable home page.
- Founder AMAs (Q&As with the makers of products) were already running, and the flat comment feed made them hard to follow, so upvoting and threading were meant to make discussion richer.
- Over the next few months the plan was to build culture in the community and improve the product based on feedback.
- Makers join in because "people like to talk about themselves." Ryan reaches out to makers when their product is posted, and others find it via Google alerts or Twitter mentions.
- He flags founders bringing in dozens of people to upvote as gaming of the site to address later, calling it "a high class problem to have."

chunks.heading: Why founders value Product Hunt traffic
chunks.text:
- Ryan's example: the founder of Appcues had his brand-new product posted by someone else and it topped the leaderboard that day. The product had little prior feedback.
- He jumped into the comments, got over 100 signups that day, and engaged with the audience.
- The next day he created a special landing page and sign-up for "Product Hunters," giving them priority access to the beta. Ryan praised this as capitalizing on the traffic and giving back to the community.
- Ryan describes the audience as people who like talking about products, who readily give feedback and who want to help founders, with a "pay it forward" mentality common in startups.

chunks.heading: What makes blogging worthwhile to Ryan
chunks.text:
- He has no binary success metric; you never know which post will do well. He admits to liking seeing many people read and share his work.
- He also values a single reader whose perspective or actions change.
- Example: he wrote a post about leaving PlayHaven, a company he worked at. It did well on page views and shares and drew a lot of direct emails, about 70 by his count, from people in the same position.
- Even one email like that makes several hours of writing worthwhile; the human connection is the value.
- He worries about giving bad advice, so he has written about reading everything with context: advice may not apply to you.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains why vertical job marketplaces (Pattern, Marketer Hire, Toptal-style) are a big opportunity. He shares how he evaluates startups: find the biggest risk, solve the hard side of a marketplace first, avoid paid-acquisition dependence. He also defines what a real community is and why it scales better than an audience.

chunks.heading: Ryan's lens on the biggest opportunity: vertical job marketplaces
chunks.text:
- Ryan wants more people to find work that fits their skills and that they enjoy. He says "too many people hate their job."
- The gig economy already gave millions more flexibility. He cites Uber as having employed millions of people with more freedom than a typical 9-5.
- He sees vertical job marketplaces as the next big shift.
- General-purpose job boards will stay valuable. But a company built around one specific vertical can serve both talent and employers better than a horizontal board.
- He finds the category impactful for people and also potentially very lucrative.

chunks.heading: Pattern: a vertical marketplace for hourly workers
chunks.text:
- Ryan is an investor in Pattern. He first met the founder, Wilson, when Wilson asked him for feedback on his YC application.
- Pattern is a marketplace for hourly workers. It started with hospitality.
- Example he gives: an event needs two bouncers, waitstaff and a few cooks, all arriving at the same time, with the right skills, and reliable. Assembling that crew is a hard logistics problem.
- Pattern uses software to assemble the people, qualify them, and give a signal of quality. The alternative he names is hiring off Craigslist.
- He says revenue has grown significantly over the past year or so, but he doesn't give numbers.
- The industry gets little attention from tech. Hourly work covers warehousing, hospitality and cleaning, and is less top of mind for most entrepreneurs.
- On market size, he says hourly hiring is massive: people are always hiring, and these industries have a lot of turnover. He says it could be a multi-billion dollar company, though not "tomorrow or next year."
- He has also spoken to truck-driving staffing marketplaces, which he calls massive too.

chunks.heading: How Ryan sizes a new market
chunks.text:
- He looks at who else is building in the space or has tried it. Comps with real scale are some evidence that a market exists.
- Early first-to-market players often create markets or prove they exist.
- He also looks at adjacent old-school industries (for example, staffing) and does the math on the number of people employed and the value of contracts.
- For brand-new categories this is hard. His example is Clubhouse, which he sees as talk radio plus podcasting plus a bit of Twitter, a massive market, but one it is partly defining as it goes.

chunks.heading: Finding the key risk in a company
chunks.text:
- Ryan asks what the big risk in a company is.
- He assumes everyone has already tried everything. So something must have changed, such as a consumer behavior shift or a technology shift, and the team needs a unique ability to solve the biggest risk.
- For Product Hunt, the big risk was the community, not the tech. He says "it's not hard to build Product Hunt from a technical perspective."
- Once you build the community, establish the brand and get the flywheel going, the product can work and grow.

chunks.heading: Marketplace strategy: solve the hard side first
chunks.text:
- A marketplace has two parties: people who hire and people who want to be hired. He tries to work out which side is harder and solve for that first.
- His warning: if you focus on the easy side, you never get the hard side, and you are "almost like delaying failure."
- He gave Pattern as an example. Without detailing how, he says it found a balance of high-quality talent and demand, then scaled both.
- In freelance marketplaces like Marketer Hire and Advisable, he assumes talent is the harder side. His reasoning: with high-quality talent, companies will come, especially for distribution help, which is hard right now.
- He prefers companies that aren't reliant on paid acquisition. If you pay for talent, you run into hard CAC vs LTV problems, which get thrown off if Facebook changes its algorithm or a funded competitor enters.
- Example: AngelList has essentially free talent. People sign up and create profiles, which is unusual for job marketplaces.

chunks.heading: Challenges and upside of freelance marketing marketplaces
chunks.text:
- Marketer Hire, Indispensable-style and Advisable-style marketplaces are hard businesses. He names two problems:
  - Keeping people on-platform. Clients may take a marketer off platform and hire them full time.
  - Retention. Project work means churn after 3 to 6 months.
- He is still attracted to the opportunity of overcoming them.
- Why he likes hiring marketers by contract or project at early-stage companies:
  - There are many channels (TikTok, SEO, Facebook ads, Instagram ads) and a small team can't be expert in all of them.
  - An expert can both do the work and teach the company.
  - A generalist hire is probably not as good, and may not fit once you know which channel to focus on.
- If he were building a new company and needed marketing help, he would look to these platforms first.

chunks.heading: What makes a vertical marketplace attractive
chunks.text:
- Industry shifts: pick the industry going through the biggest shifts, or the one that would benefit most from technology and software. Many haven't been reshaped by software yet.
- Low trust: he likes markets where there is no good way to verify a person's abilities today. A marketplace can build trust through verification.
- That trust also helps retention. If talent builds identity and reputation on your marketplace, which helps them get more jobs or money, they stay.
- He said he hadn't thought deeply enough to name a specific vertical.

chunks.heading: Community: how Ryan defines it and why it matters
chunks.text:
- He recommends community-driven strategies. Starting with a community, even before you know exactly what the product is, gives you an audience for launch and insight into what to build for those people.
- His three-part definition of community:
  - People in it interact with each other. By definition, it isn't a community unless they do.
  - A sense of belonging. His examples are church and religion, and swag such as Hustle or Trends merch that ties a person's identity to the brand.
  - Utility. This is not strictly required, but he thinks it's important: members must get real value, such as learning what's next.
- He rejects treating a Twitter following as a community.
- Why communities are powerful: they scale and let you reach people you couldn't create content for personally. An audience stops growing when you stop posting. A community doesn't.
- Product Hunt example: he barely posts to Product Hunt himself and intentionally does so rarely, and it still runs.
- He says he never read about community building, so for him it was intuitive and hard to teach. He adds you can teach anyone anything, but some people pick it up more naturally.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains how he built Weekend Fund from a $3M first fund to a $21M third fund using a diversified, non-lead, small-check strategy. He also walks through his three-stage LP fundraising sequence, when to start deploying and when to start raising the next fund.

chunks.heading: Fund 1 construction: small, diversified, non-lead
chunks.text:
- Ryan's first check was a fund investment, not an angel check. He avoided angel investing while running Product Hunt (a signaling risk as CEO, plus a loose "teammates shouldn't invest" policy). After the AngelList acquisition he raised Weekend Fund in 2017, as AngelList was rolling out its funds product.
- He targeted $1M and raised $3M from product investors he had known for a long time. At that size (even sub-$10M), check size doesn't make deals harder to get into.
- His early decisions: a more diversified fund, no leading deals, and not 100 companies in two years, since he was still CEO and part-time on investing.
- Why non-lead: he treats the fund like a product sold to founders. Checks are meaningful to the fund but leave room for co-investors. Not elbowing others out of rounds attracts more deal flow, because investors bring deals to each other.
- Why diversified: "it's power law," so a fund needs enough shots to find the one or two companies that drive returns. In fund one, a $75K check at YC/seed represents well over 90% of portfolio value (he's unsure of the exact figure, 90 or 95%).

chunks.heading: Evolution of fund size and strategy
chunks.text:
- Fund sizes: $3M, then $10M, then $21M for the latest. He may never raise a larger fund for first checks.
- Reason: once checks pass roughly $500K, you need to be in the conversation earlier. If a founder is 90% committed, fitting a $500K check means "cramming people down," which he doesn't want to do.
- Leading is a different game: one player competes for the lead slot, and not taking pro rata in the next round can signal badly.
- Scrapped idea: about 2.5 years ago, while planning fund three, he modeled a separate pool for small checks (e.g. $100K) into pre-founders. The model assumed higher failure rates, so it needed low entry prices and high volume.
- Why it died: the market got frothy and entry valuations over about $2M broke the model.

chunks.heading: How he raised LPs: three stages
chunks.text:
1. **Own network.** Build a spreadsheet from LinkedIn, Twitter lists and email; brain-dump every possible LP (high net worth individuals, funds, family offices). Early commitments from reputable people create social proof, since raising your first dollar is hardest. Most people can't raise a full fund from first-degree contacts.
2. **Referrals from existing LPs.** Ask specifically: "can you introduce me to one or two people who are like XYZ," and supply a ready-to-forward blurb to cut friction. Existing LPs are the best referrers. Most introduced one to three more LPs, and well over 50% of those meetings converted. He jokes about an "LP K-factor."
3. **Community round (Fund 3 only).** With about $18-19M of a $20M target raised, they structured it as a 506(c) so they could discuss it publicly. They took applications for $2,000 to $10,000 checks (capped at $10K). About 700 accredited investors applied; they accepted 180, bringing total LPs to about 370. The goal was not money but a network of operators and founders for deal flow, diligence and portfolio help.

chunks.heading: Pitch deck and positioning to LPs
chunks.text:
- Basics: who you are, your focus, your fund construction strategy, and your track record (angel investments and their results).
- Different LPs weigh different things. Institutional LPs ask about portfolio construction, mechanics, and whether you're building a multi-decade franchise. High net worth individuals care more about your niche and how you win great deals.
- Through-line for everyone: how you get access to the best deals and how you judge them, because there are so many funds.
- Positioning: a founder sells equity, so the investor should deliver more value than the equity taken (e.g. "if you're selling 10% of the company you better deliver 10% or more equity value"). Weekend Fund pairs small checks with outsized value from many co-investors.
- Their own strengths are product and community building. Outside that (enterprise sales, data science) they route founders to LPs, which scales beyond their own skills and time. LPs have a financial and emotional interest in helping.
- A known founder helps: the first conversation is warm.

chunks.heading: When to close and start investing
chunks.text:
- No fixed rule. He suggests not deploying until you've raised at least 25% of the target.
- Risk: raising 10% (e.g. $1M of $10M) and writing $150K checks leaves about six companies if the rest never arrives, versus a model of 35-45.
- Smaller early checks distort position sizes versus the final construction.
- He is "a pro small funds" person. Raising $50M as a first fund (a friend's plan) means needing deep-pocketed LPs or institutions, which take long and often want your second or third fund. Better to raise small, deploy for a couple of years, then raise a larger fund. "We're not starting a fund to raise money from LPs. It's a means to an end."

chunks.heading: LP follow-up and timing the next raise
chunks.text:
- Institutional LPs who pass on fund one: add them to your LP updates. It costs nothing, gives them data points on how you operate and communicate, and keeps the relationship warm. Some also like a catch-up every 6 to 12 months. He admits Weekend Fund hasn't prioritized this because it isn't aiming for a massive fund. Early touchpoints still matter because institutions rarely invest before seeing you operate for months or years.
- Next-raise timing: depends on how fast you can raise. Public raises can lock commitments within a month, with about two more months for wires, and they create urgency. His own rule: start conversations about six months before needing money to deploy, not a year ahead.

chunks.heading: Follow-on and reserves
chunks.text:
- He says he hasn't figured out when to double down, calling it one of the most heavily debated decisions.
- Spectrum: some funds hold zero reserves and write the biggest check upfront. Weekend Fund leans that way, sizing initial checks assuming they may never get to invest again.
- Non-lead downside: even with legal pro rata, a big incoming lead may pressure the founder to cut others' allocation, and they don't want to be a difficult investor.
- They passed on some pro ratas a few years ago when companies were marked up 3-5x in under six months with similar risk. Test: "would we invest in this company if we weren't investors today, at that price?"
- Hindsight caveat: some passed Series A rounds would have returned many millions more to LPs, but "hindsight will kill you."

chunks.heading: Signature Block newsletter
chunks.text:
- It targets fund managers and investors (just under 9,000 subscribers), who manage billions in aggregate. It gives Weekend Fund a channel to current and future co-investors.
- Goal: evergreen content on managing and raising a fund, inspired by Venture Hacks (Naval and Nivi's content for founders). Content is crowdsourced from more experienced investors, including portfolio construction, pitching LPs, and questions to ask founders. They also published a post on LP decks.
- Next: subscribers want community, meeting co-investors by sector (space tech, ESG, consumer social); direction undecided.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt grew from a 20-minute email list experiment into a company, and why building in public, prioritizing by metric impact, and hiring specialists matter. He also gives career advice: create things online, join communities, skip over-planning, and ask for help.

chunks.heading: Start with an experiment, not a business plan
chunks.text:
- Ryan frames Product Hunt as an escalation ladder: experiment, then side project, then startup. It began as an experiment to see whether people liked the idea.
- At the side-project stage he worked on it about 30-40 hours a week while still employed part-time elsewhere.
- The seed was his own interest: he downloads many apps just to explore how others build, "almost the same way that like maybe an art connoisseur loves to look at paintings."
- His friends already shared apps in private group chats. He asked why there wasn't a single email list of cool new products, and that email list was the first version of Product Hunt.
- It grew into a website and a community of makers, founders and early adopters.
- He warns against overthinking: "You can't write a 20-page business plan and think your way into a company. You really just need to build and create."
- He advises building something useful and fun for yourself, because you will be more motivated to push through when it gets difficult.
- He tinkered with other projects too, and many went nowhere. He found the process itself fun.

chunks.heading: Building in public
chunks.text:
- Ryan credits Joel Gascoigne of Buffer as the influence. Buffer shared even sensitive data such as team salaries and revenue numbers.
- He sees two benefits. It is strong content marketing, because people thirst for authenticity. It also builds a connection between customers and the team, so they feel part of the journey.
- Product Hunt adopted the same approach early: share what you're working on, which creates buy-in and gets feedback before anything is built.
- Example: the team put feature mock-ups on InVision, a tool meant for internal design feedback, and shared them publicly with the community by email. Within the first day there were hundreds of annotated comments.
- The comments ranged from tactical confusion ("I don't really understand what this thing does here") to new feature ideas. All of it arrived before any code was written.
- The team also hosted a podcast early on. Ryan thinks hearing someone's voice is a more intimate experience.
- The format was a conversation about technology rather than a typical interview, as if the community were "a fly on the wall" chatting with well-known innovators.

chunks.heading: Prioritizing feedback and features
chunks.text:
- A product community gives easy feedback because it is full of makers with opinions. The downside is that everyone has an opinion, so you have to filter.
- He argues you need your own vision and direction. If you rely 100% on user input you only iterate on features and never reach the next slope of growth.
- For social and community products he thinks in systems: how each feature or change affects the rest of the experience. He admits this is hard to put in a catchy one-liner.
- For each feature, identify the one metric it is primarily meant to move. Most features move several, but focus on one.
- Estimate the impact by working backwards from the metric. For revenue, back into an estimated number. It will never be exact, but it lets you cross items off the list.
- Example: if a feature will raise revenue about 5% "if we're lucky," it is probably not worth investing in.
- In early-stage startups, he says not to invest in marginal 5% improvements unless they take about five seconds. Work on things that probably won't work but might have a 2x, 3x or 5x impact.
- He says deciding what to prioritize is the hardest part, because there are a million things you could do.

chunks.heading: Closing skill gaps: hire, and ask for help
chunks.text:
- His biggest answer to skill gaps is hiring. He says there are other ways, but building a team is the biggest leverage.
- Early on the team was generalist, and it is still only about 20 people. Over time you should hire specialists in areas where you are not an expert.
- He says the real purpose of raising venture capital was to pay salaries, since he had little money in the bank. There were other benefits, but that was the main one.
- He is not an engineer, so engineering was the first need. Andres joined as CTO and built the engineering org.
- Rebecca Wilson (her name is garbled in the transcript, so omit it here) is not named; the point is that a CEO with over a decade at Microsoft brought operations, team building and finance experience he lacked.
- He also hired a community lead because Product Hunt was so community-driven.
- Method: ask which holes the business has, then find the best people who share your values and want to hustle hard.
- Looking back, he thinks he could have done better on personal growth. He learned everything on the job as problems arrived, rather than proactively reading or seeking guidance.
- He wishes he had used his investors more. Steve Newcomb-style advice is not claimed; he says board member Steve Anderson (name unclear in the transcript) came from Microsoft and had seen companies scale, and he still looks up to him.
- His conclusion: "I don't think I asked for enough help," and he says that is a common pattern among founders. Asking someone who knows can beat searching for the answer in a book.

chunks.heading: What Ryan looks for in founders (Weekend Fund)
chunks.text:
- Weekend Fund invests very early, sometimes pre-product, so there is little data to go on.
- He looks for founder-market fit: is this the best team to solve this particular problem? That may come from personal experience or past work that gave them an insight few others have.
- He looks for companies built on a consumer behavior shift or a technology shift that makes something newly possible. His reasoning is that so many people build companies that something must have changed, or the founders must see something no one else sees.
- His favorite diligence question: "You could be building a million different things, why are you building this?"
- He listens for whether they just want to build a company or are authentically passionate about the problem. Founders in the first group worry him, because they may give up when things get hard.
- For hiring, he looks for the highest-skilled person for the specific role who also shows the qualities and culture you want.

chunks.heading: Advice for starting out in a career
chunks.text:
- Step one: create something on the internet, such as a podcast, website or newsletter. Pick whatever makes you curious, don't overthink it, and keep shipping.
- Step two: join online communities such as Product Hunt, Twitter, Reddit or Indie Hackers.
- He hates traditional, transactional networking. Participating in communities creates serendipity that may pay off only in year three or four, for example by introducing a future co-founder, investor or insight.
- Step three, if you want to join a company: decide between big and small. Small companies give you many hats and exposure to different roles. Big companies make you a specialist but give you a bigger network and a view of building at scale.
- For a big company, aim for one on a rocket-ship trajectory. He got this advice from Josh Elman around 2012, when Ryan was leaving PlayHaven: join Pinterest or something similar.
- Elman's own path went through Facebook, LinkedIn, Twitter, Robinhood and Apple.
- He calls creating things online and participating in communities "table stakes" if you want to grow and eventually become a founder.

chunks.heading: Skeptical of college, bullish on real-world experience
chunks.text:
- Ryan is "pretty bearish on college." He has a business degree with an entrepreneurship focus and says it was irrelevant and even negative for his founder journey.
- He says following that playbook (a 20-page business plan, talking to many customers) would have meant Product Hunt never existed, because the real first step was an email list that took about 20 minutes.
- He finds four years very inefficient and the cost too high. He feels sad for graduates with $100,000-$200,000 in debt and few marketable skills.
- He says college has value for relationships and personal growth, and he is not totally against it.
- He prefers hands-on experience with people who do the job today, rather than textbooks and professors who haven't built companies. This is the appeal of Acadium, in which he is an investor.
- He says the missing piece when learning online is community and network, which is why he recommends joining communities as a supplement.

chunks.heading: Remote work, onboarding and the startup "levels"
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt was distributed from the start. It once had a San Francisco office with about a third of the team, and now the team is spread across places like India, Canada, France and Bulgaria.
- Benefits he cites: you can hire anyone in the world, and there is no "facetime culture." Output matters more than hours, and he says he doesn't care how many hours you work if performance is good.
- Hiring only locally limits you to a tiny slice of the talent pool. He expects more companies to go remote because talent demands it.
- He cites a friend at a big, well-known company who said he would take a third of his salary to stay in his state instead of moving to California.
- Remote doesn't mean never meeting. Product Hunt met in person twice a year, summer and winter, for example in LA, SF and Tahoe. He values dinners and shared activities for getting to know each other.
- Onboarding tactic: in the Monday all-hands call, a new teammate introduces themselves with role and location, and shares "a product that they use and love that very few people know about." He calls it basic but an effective icebreaker.
- Other onboarding tactic: connect new hires one-on-one with the right people, in some cases four to six people while they get to know the team.
- Startups are like a video game with levels. Things go great, then you hit bumps where what worked before stops scaling.
- He thinks no company has had one playbook that scales from zero to a billion, so you must keep reinventing.
- The easy part is the admin that paralyzes young founders: legal setup, taxes, recruiting. He says it is well documented, and a mentor can connect you with the right lawyer and accountant. It "shouldn't stop you from starting."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover shares lessons from his early PM mistakes and from building Product Hunt. He covers involving the community before building, designing growth as a flywheel, spotting opportunity in platform and behavior shifts, adding structure to startup teams, and launching with plain messaging instead of selling the vision.

chunks.heading: Ryan's early product-management mistakes and what he does differently
chunks.text:
- Ryan became a product manager at about 22, coming from a marketing internship. Looking back, he calls his early work embarrassing.
- He spent weekends alone writing specs and wireframes, believing he was helping the company by working hard.
- He now sees that as a huge mistake. He was "living in my own box", not talking to customers or the team.
- Handing a team a finished sheet of "here are the things to build" doesn't build buy-in. People don't invest in a product they had no hand in shaping.
- His fixes: talk to customers, get the team's input early, and build the product together.

chunks.heading: Using the community in the product-building process
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt's success depends entirely on its community: without people posting products, voting and commenting, it has nothing. Ryan says involving the community in building works as a tactic even for products that aren't community-based.
- Tactic: share mockups before building. The team sends an InVision mockup to the community with context and asks for feedback and ideas.
- InVision lets people annotate anywhere on the mockup with red dots. A few hours after sending one out, the page was covered in dots, and the team had feedback before building anything.
- Contributors feel more involved because they are shaping the product, and they are.
- The team doesn't share everything it designs, only some things, and does it early and often.
- Don't build everything people suggest. Work out why they suggest it: the idea may be the wrong solution, but the problem or goal behind it is worth understanding.

chunks.heading: Using metrics, KPIs and fake-door tests
chunks.text:
- Every product and initiative at Product Hunt should move, directly or indirectly, three core KPIs: general user growth, revenue, and community contributions (a measure of community health).
- Example of a cheap test: login was only via Twitter and Facebook. The hypothesis was that some people, especially those logging in for business, didn't want to use social profiles.
- The team put a Google login button on the login page without building the login and counted clicks. This was a "Wizard of Oz" test.
- About 40-45% of clicks went to Google login, which justified building it.
- Ryan says data suits optimizations like this. For something brand new there's often no data, so you rely on gut and knowledge of the audience.
- Product Hunt has also surveyed its community about motivations and goals to inform product decisions.

chunks.heading: Flywheels as a growth framework
chunks.text:
- Ryan recommends dissecting a product as a flywheel. Product Hunt's flywheel wasn't designed up front; it emerged organically.
- The loop: someone finds a product and shares it on Product Hunt, which introduces it to the maker. The maker shares it with their audience, which includes other makers, so more posts lead to more makers, more people and more products.
- The less friction between each step, and the more people who do each action, the better the system works and the more users arrive.
- Method: map your product's steps (step 1, 2, 3...) and find the one with heavy friction or failure. Fixing it can complete the flywheel and drive growth.
- Example: early on there was no system to tag makers or notify them. Makers only noticed when they saw odd traffic in Google Analytics.
- Product Hunt then let the community tag makers. If you know a maker's username, tagging notifies them on Twitter or by email if the team has their address.
- Ryan's next step is automating this so every maker gets tagged efficiently. He says it is hard but worth solving.
- He cites the AngelList talent platform as another flywheel: free job postings attract candidates, which produce matches, which attract more companies.

chunks.heading: Trends: use them without forcing them
chunks.text:
- Ryan has watched trends on Product Hunt: anonymous apps (when Secret was popular), on-demand startups for everything, and now blockchain/crypto and AI. Some "AI" products just sprinkle it on for marketing.
- Trends can be a trap. People force blockchain or AI onto a problem that isn't native to them.
- He stresses founder-market fit: the best founders solve a problem for themselves or have a unique advantage. His own example of a poor fit: he would be the worst person to build an automated laundry service.
- Trends are still valuable as a new opportunity. Ask what blockchain or AI makes possible today that wasn't possible yesterday.
- Two framings he likes beyond trends: platform shifts (smartphones and mobile enabled Instagram and Snapchat) and behavior shifts (e.g., a younger generation not wanting to share on Facebook with family, which Snapchat used).
- Timing example: Dailybooth was a roughly decade-old desktop product for a daily webcam selfie, reaching millions of users but ultimately failing partly because the platform was wrong. Launched five years later and focused on mobile, it might have worked.
- Incumbents like Facebook and WhatsApp are susceptible to platform and behavior shifts, which are holes in their armor that startups can exploit. Ryan says timing is hard to predict, and being too early is also a risk.

chunks.heading: Voice, audio and blockchain social networks
chunks.text:
- Ryan is most interested in voice and audio. People are shifting from tapping screens to audio interfaces and forming new habits, such as saying "OK Google, play..." out loud.
- He cites 40-60 million US homes with an Alexa or Google Home device.
- Exercise for finding opportunities: list behaviors people repeat daily that suit voice better than typing. His example is asking for the weather while getting dressed.
- He also suggests B2B voice use cases, since B2B more often has a direct revenue or efficiency impact and is a better business than hard-to-win consumer.
- He has invested in a couple of audio companies, calling it an early bet on an audio-based future.
- He also finds blockchain-based social networks fascinating. Traditional social networks are centralized, and the people who create the value earn none of the revenue. A token model could change that, which is why Facebook built a team to explore it.

chunks.heading: Team structure: hierarchy and titles help
chunks.text:
- His most counterintuitive lesson, learned recently: startups are often told to be flat, with no titles and everyone wearing many hats. Ryan found a lack of titles and structure can be bad.
- Product Hunt moved to giving people domain ownership and creating team leads. Before, everyone reported to him, which doesn't scale.
- Results: people are more motivated and clearer on what they are responsible for. Hierarchy and titles exist in most companies for a reason.
- The team is distributed: about 3 people in San Francisco and about 14 elsewhere (Bulgaria, Paris, Toronto, New Zealand, India). Over half the community is outside the US and less than 2% is in Silicon Valley.
- He rejected splitting Product Hunt into regional versions (Europe, India, US), valuing the diversity of what people build worldwide. He notes products from Paris are consistently beautifully designed.

chunks.heading: Launching advice
chunks.text:
- There is no single launch. You are always shipping and launching, whether it's a first version, a second version or a new feature.
- Common mistake: selling the dream (the vision and five-year plan) instead of the product you built today.
- Describe what the product does and how it's useful. For a video conferencing app, "the future of remote working" tells people nothing, while something like "super fast way to video chat with your co-workers" says what it does. Visitors lack your context and don't care about your vision.
- Test messaging by showing your landing page or tagline to people who aren't your friends and know nothing about the product. Ask for impressions, and if they don't get it, rework it.
- Talk to people, but have a perspective. Customers inform your decisions about what to build; they shouldn't tell you what to build.
- Brand note: the Product Hunt cat with Google Glass came from an illustrator named Jesse who offered free t-shirt and flag art early on. Ryan liked it because it felt "friendly and welcoming and a little bit silly", and it now reflects the culture. He says it wasn't strategic or data-driven.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover recounts learning product management on the job at Playhaven and what skills mattered: empathy, humility, verifying assumptions with data and customer talks, and over-communicating with engineers. He also argues side projects and blogging are the best way to prove product skill without a PM title.

chunks.heading: Starting as a product manager without a roadmap
chunks.text:
- Ryan's first PM role was at a PC gaming company called Interaction. He was doing marketing strategy, his boss was VP of Product, and he moved into product management "learning on the job" with no idea what he was doing.
- He then joined Playhaven, a mobile gaming tools company, where he was the first PM. He says he was only a PM for about a year before the move.
- The job came through a relationship: a former colleague (the CEO at Playhaven) knew he wanted to be a PM and gave him a shot.
- He notes that colleges rarely teach product management, since the role is vague and varies by company.
- His takeaway: opportunities come from connections, so treat people fairly and keep building your network. A large share of Playhaven's early hires came from referrals, including eight to ten people from the previous company.

chunks.heading: Empathy and humility as the core PM skills
chunks.text:
- Ryan names empathy as the recurring theme for any PM: understanding what people want, how they feel, and how they react.
- It matters most when building a product for someone else. At Playhaven he built tools for mobile game developers and was not a mobile game developer himself.
- To close that gap he had to understand their day-to-day, their challenges and how they were measured. He found this out by observing behavior and talking to developers.
- He pairs empathy with humility: "your assumption is probably not correct as confident as you are." Be confident, but verify assumptions by talking to customers and looking at data.
- He also says communication is probably the most important PM skill, and that empathy for engineers and designers is what makes it work.

chunks.heading: Combining product data with customer conversations
chunks.text:
Ryan's process at Playhaven combined intuition, data and interviews:

- **Intuition:** you can't talk to customers about every decision, so you use judgment on how an interface should look and work.
- **Usage data first:** the dashboard had many features, so he looked at which tools people actually used. For example, of ten tools built, why were two unused? Possible reasons: no use for it, too confusing, or output that can't be measured.
- **Form hypotheses, then validate:** he took those hypotheses into customer conversations.
- **Vary the sample:** he visited big companies like Glu Mobile and spoke with VPs and producers about the product and their personal goals. He also phoned indie developers, some of them one person working on a game alone.

Order of work: research the data internally, then talk to customers to validate and add context, so you aren't unaware of how they use the product.

chunks.heading: Customer interviews and usability testing
chunks.text:
- **Don't pitch the idea.** Starting with "here's this cool idea, aren't you going to love it" is a bad way to learn what people need.
- **Explore the problem space first.** For a hypothetical feature to increase engagement, ask how they measure engagement and how users currently engage with their products, and pull out themes.
- **Introduce the idea late.** Toward the end, show wireframes, a prototype, or let them use it while you sit back and watch.
- **Usability tests are very helpful, but not too early.** Watching someone struggle with your prototype is painful but you learn a lot.

chunks.heading: Working with engineers and designers as a team grows
chunks.text:
- **Role varies by team size.** At about 10 people, Ryan was the only PM with a few engineers and no designer, doing wireframes and general PM work himself. At around 100 people there were multiple PM teams, a UX designer and a visual designer.
- **Tradeoff:** the small setup moves fast with few people, but the product may be worse because a non-professional is doing the UX. The larger setup brings more resources, research and fuller features, but needs more process, planning and communication.
- **Top tip for working with engineers:** over-communicate rather than under-communicate.
- **Don't drop requests on engineers.** Asking "can you build this thing" without thinking ahead can break their train of thought and frustrate them. Give them some warning and lead time.
- He says the same applies to designers, but is "even more prevalent" with engineers because of how they like to work.

chunks.heading: Tools and wireframing habits
chunks.text:
- **Tooling:** no special PM tools. Playhaven had an internal data analysis tool, used Pivotal for project management and moved to JIRA when teams grew. Otherwise Gmail, Google Docs, pen and paper, and whiteboards, which he says are often the best for collaboration.
- **Wireframing:** he likes OmniGraffle because he knows the shortcuts and has stencils. Others use Balsamiq or go straight into Sketch.
- **Force yourself to go analog.** He sometimes uses whiteboards or Post-it notes instead. Because it's constrained and can't be edited, it forces ideas to be succinct and quick.
- **Mistake to avoid:** in digital tools he becomes a perfectionist and spends time making wireframes pixel perfect. Early on that is a waste of time.

chunks.heading: Launching a feature or tool
chunks.text:
- He says the answer depends on context: a new feature for an existing audience versus a brand new product are very different.
- For a new tool shipped to an existing audience at Playhaven, communicate what it is, what it does and why it matters, framed around the customer's goals and how it helps them do their job better.
- **Channels:** email, the product itself (the dashboard), and internally.
- **Internal enablement:** Playhaven had account managers and salespeople, so they needed to understand what the tool does and how to talk about it externally. Sales education on new features is part of the launch.

chunks.heading: Hiring PMs and breaking in through side projects
chunks.text:
- **Best hires:** people he has already worked with or who come through referrals.
- **Evaluating strangers:** he looks at what they have actually done. He checks them online, including Twitter and whether they have a blog and what they write about.
- **Blogging:** a PM doesn't design or code, so there's no profile to point to. A blog is a good way to communicate how you think.
- **Side projects:** he encourages them, and wrote a post called "Anyone Can Ship". Examples:
  - an email newsletter (how Product Hunt started)
  - meetups in your city around a topic
  - a podcast
  - a product idea you want to try
- A side project is a way into PM when you can't get a PM job without experience. It demonstrates your process and ability to execute.
- You don't need to code. Figure out how to build something simply, measure it and get feedback on whether people care.
- **Technical depth:** it depends on the company. Some PM roles require being an engineer to communicate what's being built. Others are design-centric and need strong UX sense but little technical knowledge.

chunks.heading: What carries over to founding Product Hunt
chunks.text:
- Ryan says he struggles to name specific skills. The soft skills dominate: learning to speak with designers and developers, and understanding how different people work.
- Hard skills he mentions include looking at data and deciding what to measure.
- The main thing is "learning on the job", being creative and curious, and a mindset of experimentation. Product Hunt "was not the first experiment" he did; he ran many and learned from each along the way.
- His summary: the right frame of mind is openness to experimentation and curiosity, practiced continually over time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover argues founders should build an audience before (or alongside) building the product, via blogging, podcasting, newsletters or meetups. He says an audience helps with recruiting, user acquisition and research, and that his own writing and newsletter became the seed of the Product Hunt community.

chunks.heading: Audience-first startup building
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover's core advice for founders who lack a team or traction: build an audience before building the company. He gave this feedback to someone asking how to find a technical co-founder for a startup idea: "Build an audience yourself first."

chunks.heading: How to build the audience
chunks.text:
Ryan lists the channels he considers viable:

- Blogging
- Podcasting
- Starting a newsletter
- Hosting meetups

He cites Casey Neistat as an example: Neistat, co-founder of beme (acquired by CNN) and a prominent YouTube star, started his vlog to build an audience for his company. Ryan quotes him: "I originally started the vlog two years ago so I could share with an audience, my company beme. What it meant to start a company, to maybe build an audience that might be excited about what I was doing[…] And that worked and it was awesome."

chunks.heading: Three benefits of audience-first
chunks.text:
Ryan names three things an audience helps with:

1. **Recruiting.** Pre-product and pre-traction, it is difficult to convince anyone, technical or not, to join. An audience gives a founder credibility and a pool of people to draw from.
2. **User acquisition.** Acquisition is hard both before and after launching a product. The sooner a founder de-risks it, the better.
3. **Research.** Audience-building feeds customer development and a better understanding of who the founder is building for.

chunks.heading: How it played out with Product Hunt
chunks.text:
Ryan says he took this approach unintentionally when building Product Hunt. In the years before Product Hunt started, he wrote a lot:

- He blogged about product design, marketing and startups in general, inspired by observations and conversations while working in tech.
- He wrote 150 essays in 2013.
- He guest authored on Fast Company, Pando, The Next Web and other tech publications.
- He hosted small brunches with founders.
- He started an email newsletter called Startup Edition with Nathan Bashaw.

chunks.heading: The audience as a seed community
chunks.text: These projects built relationships and an audience that became the seed of the Product Hunt community. Ryan notes it was relatively small but established a platform, and argues that "without this, Product Hunt would have been DOA."

chunks.heading: How big the audience needs to be
chunks.text: Ryan's takeaway on scale: "Sometimes you just need 1,000 true fans to get started." The audience does not have to be large; it has to be engaged enough to supply early users, recruits and feedback.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan describes prototyping Product Hunt with an existing link-sharing tool instead of building an app, gaining 170 subscribers in two weeks. He argues an MVP exists to learn and test assumptions, and gives a three-step framework to run before writing any code.

chunks.heading: Validating Product Hunt with a 20-minute, no-code MVP
chunks.text:
Ryan's origin story for Product Hunt: he had the idea (a community for product people to share, discover and discuss new products), but building even a basic Ruby on Rails version would have taken him weeks of nights and weekends. He wasn't willing to spend that on something nobody might use.

- Instead he looked for the fastest way to test the hypothesis.
- He remembered Linkydink, a link-sharing tool by Makeshift. You create a group, invite people to share links with other contributors and subscribers, and each day's posts are emailed to the group.
- In about 20 minutes he created a group, invited a few startup friends to contribute, wrote a quick blog post, announced it on Quibb and tweeted.
- His summary: "Within 20 minutes, I had an MVP."

chunks.heading: What an MVP is for
chunks.text:
Ryan argues an MVP is a learning tool, not a thing you must build.

- "The purpose of an MVP is to learn, to validate and invalidate assumptions."
- "Entrepreneurs often assume an MVP needs to be 'built.'" He says there are almost always faster ways to validate than building a product.
- The Linkydink MVP let him validate assumptions and watch real user behavior "without a single line of code."
- "An MVP is Not a Product." Once the idea had traction, the next step was a real product, but he still sought something fast to test his next set of assumptions.

chunks.heading: A three-step process before writing code
chunks.text:
Ryan's checklist for any new product or startup idea:

1. **Identify your assumptions.** What must be true for the product to succeed? How do you identify your audience?
2. **Test your assumptions.** Take the riskiest assumption and brainstorm quick ways to validate or invalidate it. His examples: landing page tests, Wizard of Oz experiments, customer interviews, and other ways to get feedback from the target audience.
3. **Learn and iterate.** If the assumption is invalid, reevaluate the idea and the target audience. If it holds, test the next riskiest assumption.

He says this lean approach was used to birth Product Hunt and guide its ongoing development.

chunks.heading: Early results and what counted as traction
chunks.text:
- Within two weeks, over 170 people had subscribed to product discoveries from 30 hand-picked contributors (startup founders, VCs and prominent bloggers).
- Early feedback was strongly positive. Ash Bhoopathy (Sequoia Capital) called it "the PM / growth dude's best replacement for 'Dribbble' for collecting inspiration." Andrew Weissman (Union Square Ventures) liked that "all kinds of VCs" were subscribed. Talton Figgins (Disqus) wrote the idea off at first, then got "hooked" after seeing the recommendations.
- He weighted unsolicited emails and in-person conversations expressing love and support as encouraging signals.
- This came despite the minimalism of the MVP and his "(intentional) lack of marketing."

chunks.heading: Honest caveat: the audience was earned
chunks.text:
Ryan notes he didn't launch from a blank slate.

- Years of blogging, relationship building and projects like Startup Edition gave him an audience and network of supporters.
- "The term 'startup' is deceiving. Successful companies don't start up overnight; they are founded upon years of experience and help from others that must be earned."

chunks.heading: Choosing the "real" build: pick the fastest option
chunks.text:
After the MVP gave him confidence, Ryan researched how to build a full product.

- Engineering friends suggested Sinatra or Ruby on Rails, but he had no experience with either and was still working with many hypotheses about what the product could be.
- He wanted something sooner to test his next set of assumptions, so he looked at Sacha Greif's Telescope, an open-source app for creating your own Hacker News or Reddit-style community.
- He asked designer/developer friend Nathan Bashaw, who built the first version over Thanksgiving break.

chunks.heading: Launch sequence for Product Hunt
chunks.text:
- Telescope decision to launch took eight days.
- November 26 (2013): began seeding the community with a few select founding contributors.
- One week later: formal launch in the press (a Pando article), which brought another healthy spike of adoption and feedback.
- Ryan framed it as the first post in a series on the strategies, tactics and surprises of building Product Hunt.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover argues that launching a startup as an email product is a lightweight way to validate an idea. Email is fast to build, forces focus, creates habits, reaches everyone, and later feeds web or mobile offerings. He cites Timehop, iDoneThis, Thrillist, AngelList and Sunrise as examples.

chunks.heading: Why Ryan favors email-first startups
chunks.text:
Ryan describes the "email-first startup" as a less common launch strategy, chosen after weighing product, market, team, timeline and competition. His claim is that email, as the starting medium, lets a startup validate a business and gain traction "with relatively minimal investment."

His six reasons:
- **Validate ideas quickly.** An email-first product is generally faster to build than a full website or mobile app. The sooner it reaches customers, the sooner you learn what does and doesn't stick.
- **Fake it 'til you make it.** Email is largely asynchronous, so manual processes can stand in for missing functionality (Wizard of Oz experiments).
- **Force focus.** Email "doesn't afford feature-creep." Email-first products are limited, which forces a succinct focus on one use case.
- **Create habits.** People check email several times a day, so a well-done email product can become part of a daily routine.
