- **Be ubiquitous.** Everyone uses email, and it doesn't discriminate against devices or operating systems.
- **Transfer to other mediums.** Up-selling or cross-selling to web or mobile products is easier when a reliable communication channel already exists.

chunks.heading: Examples of startups that began as email products
chunks.text:
Ryan lists these as having started email-first:
- **Timehop** began as 4SquareAnd7YearsAgo, which emailed Foursquare check-ins from exactly one year earlier.
- **iDoneThis** was created over a weekend. Users email the tasks they accomplished that day, and the next morning an email goes out to their team.
- **Thrillist** was a hand-made email newsletter on men's lifestyle.
- **AngelList** narrowly focused on a curated list of angel investors, delivered by email weekly.
- **Sunrise** sent a morning email with the day's schedule: "Simple. Useful."

He notes that all of them have since expanded into web and/or mobile applications. Email is where they were born, and it let them validate their business cheaply.

chunks.heading: When to choose an email-first strategy
chunks.text:
- His rule: "If your product and market fits the medium, consider an email-first strategy."
- Good fits, from his examples, are products that deliver one narrow, useful piece of information on a schedule (a daily digest, a weekly curated list, a recap of past activity).
- He treats email as a starting channel, not the end state. The plan is to validate with email, then move users to web or mobile once there is traction.

chunks.heading: Using email to run lean experiments
chunks.text:
- Because email is asynchronous, a founder can do the work by hand behind the scenes (curating, compiling, sending) before building automation.
- This lowers the cost of testing demand. The Thrillist example, a hand-made newsletter, and the iDoneThis example, built over a weekend, both reflect it.
- The goal is learning what sticks with customers early, before investing in a full product build.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains why Product Hunt delayed monetizing to focus on community growth, then launched three revenue lines (Ship SaaS, Deals, Promoted Products) that booked over $250K in weeks. He stresses focus, charging for things that fit the community, and reinvesting revenue to keep building.

chunks.heading: Product Hunt's mission and why monetization came late
chunks.text:
- Ryan says people have asked "How will you make money?" since Product Hunt's beginning.
- He argues there's "no right way to startup," but every team needs a focused goal early on, because everything on a startup's to-do list takes the place of something else.
- Product Hunt's mission: "surface awesome products and help makers find an audience."
- The team stayed focused on growing the community and on new ways for makers and consumers to share and discover products, rather than charging on day one.
- Some experiments failed completely; others had big community impact.
- By the end of 2017 Product Hunt hit new milestones in user growth and products discovered, and earned its first real dollar.
- Footnote: in 2014 the team made nominal revenue from job postings and t-shirt sales, only to pay its Heroku bill for a short period.
- After the first dollar, Product Hunt booked and collected over $250K in revenue, and half of that came in the final three weeks before the post.
- The 2018 aim was profitability, "a milestone few startups achieve."

chunks.heading: Ship: a SaaS toolkit as the first revenue line
chunks.text:
- Ship launched September 14, 2017. It's a toolkit for makers, inspired by community feedback and by what the team learned supporting thousands of product launches each year.
- It uses a SaaS model with free and paid versions.
- It's integrated into the core Product Hunt experience but is essentially its own product with a small, dedicated team.
- Early stats:
  - 600,000+ email subscribers
  - 2,800+ upcoming product pages created
  - hundreds of paying startups
- The goal for a February update: make Ship a core part of product development and "the best tool to talk to users, build a community, and develop a real connection between the makers and users of a product."
- Product Hunt also used Ship internally to announce new projects and collect community feedback.

chunks.heading: Product Hunt Deals: monetizing behavior that already existed
chunks.text:
- Makers were already posting exclusive discounts for the Product Hunt community in the comments of their launches.
- The community welcomed these, and the discounts often drew more interest and adoption.
- Ryan's team wanted to encourage that behavior and give the community access to discounted and exclusive deals.
- The paid offering lets makers host and promote deals directly on Product Hunt.
- The pattern: find something users already do for free, then build a paid, better-supported version of it.

chunks.heading: Promoted Products: building what makers kept asking for
chunks.text:
- For years, makers asked how to get more exposure after they'd already launched.
- That demand inspired the third revenue line, Promoted Products.
- How it works:
  - It resurfaces popular products on the Product Hunt homepage and in the newsletter.
  - Each is marked with a "PROMOTED" badge.
  - It's only for makers already part of the community, and not for brand-new launches.
  - It's limited to popular past products, measured by upvotes from the community.
  - New launches remain free: "All makers are welcome to post their new product launches as they normally would without charge."
- Ryan describes beta testing it quietly for a few weeks "amidst overwhelming demand from makers."
- January and February were sold out, and reservations for March were open.
- He says the team monitored community feedback closely, and that it remained supportive.
- The beta partners included Intercom, InVision, HubSpot for Startups, Appcues, GitKraken, Front Chat, Shopify's Draggable and Lonely Planet's Trips, among about 30.

chunks.heading: Diversifying revenue while protecting the core product
chunks.text:
- Ryan says that although Ship was growing nicely, the team understood "the importance of revenue diversification," so they added Deals and Promoted Products.
- Revenue wasn't the sole focus. The team kept working on:
  - increasing product discoveries
  - driving maker engagement
  - encouraging positive contributions from the community
- He calls all of these important to "a growing, sustainable, and healthy platform."
- Non-revenue projects in progress:
  - a rebuilt mobile app
  - Sip, an experimental mobile app delivering infrequent tech news updates
  - Maker Goals
  - Team Profiles
  - the Golden Kitty Awards
- Ryan's stance: it's important to be thoughtful about what you charge for and to ensure Product Hunt "continues to be valuable for makers of all kinds."
- Paid features were designed so the core experience, including free launches for new products, stayed intact.

chunks.heading: Why profitability matters and building in public
chunks.text:
- Ryan calls Product Hunt "my baby," a community and platform he hopes will thrive for decades.
- His argument: "If done right, generating revenue and achieving profitability will ensure that we can continue building forever and ultimately lead to a better product as we reinvest capital into the platform."
- Product Hunt has a culture of building in public.
- He cites that culture as part of his motivation for sharing the revenue numbers and the 2018 profitability goal.
- He was also open that one reason for the post was to raise awareness of the paid initiatives.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan tells how he was turned down for an Entrepreneur-in-Residence role by Shaan Puri, stayed in touch, and two years later partnered with Shaan's team (Blab) to launch live video on Product Hunt LIVE. The lesson is about relationships, transparency and reframing "no".

chunks.heading: Rejection can seed a better relationship than acceptance
chunks.text:
- In mid-2013, after 3 years at PlayHaven, Ryan wanted a new startup challenge. Incubating new consumer products was his "dream job."
- Shaan Puri, CEO of Monkey Inferno, invited him to lunch, then back a second time for product feedback, then offered a "Trial by Fire" test for an Entrepreneur-in-Residence role.
- Ryan's work: over a weekend he researched, built wireframes and a deck as if he were product leader of their Q&A platform, Boya. He pitched it with no access to data.
- Shaan rejected him, but with a long, transparent, constructive email explaining the reasoning. He ended by hoping to "stay in touch."
- Ryan treats this as a model for how a rejection should be handled. Most employers don't give that much detail.

chunks.heading: Never burn a bridge: the rejection became a partnership
chunks.text:
- Ryan stayed in touch with Shaan. When he started Product Hunt, he asked Shaan (Product Hunt user #15) for feedback, and Shaan stayed supportive.
- Shaan emailed days before Product Hunt LIVE launched, offering help. Monkey Inferno was building Blab, a platform for live video conversations.
- After the public launch, they met to use Blab's tech to make Product Hunt LIVE more intimate. The first Blab-powered LIVE Chat was with Matt Mazzeo, on the day of the post (October 19, 2015).
- Ryan's lesson: "it's important to never burn a bridge in Silicon Valley (or anywhere, really)." The partnership happened "because we stayed in touch and genuinely liked each other."
- Takeaway: relationships built through a failed hiring process can pay off years later as distribution or product partnerships.

chunks.heading: Product Hunt LIVE: text Q&A first, then video
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt LIVE launched in August 2015 as "a place to chat with the world's most interesting makers," starting with text-based discussions.
- Within about two months it had hosted Q&As with over 150 guests, including Amanda Palmer, Aileen Lee, Ashton Kutcher, Ben Horowitz and Tony Robbins. Ryan did one too.
- The plan from the start was to eventually expand into livestreaming video to make it "even more intimate and fun."
- Ryan frames the mission as connecting the community directly with their favorite makers in an authentic conversation. Video is "the closest thing to meeting someone face-to-face" and lets people "sit in the room" with founders, investors, artists, authors, game creators and entertainers.
- Approach: validate the format in a simple medium (text), then partner for the richer one (video) rather than building it from scratch.

chunks.heading: Reframing "no": rejection as a sign of ambition and a path to better outcomes
chunks.text:
- Ryan quotes Chris Dixon: "If you aren't getting rejected on a daily basis, your goals aren't ambitious enough."
- He argues "sometimes 'no' is good." He was disappointed by the rejection, but "Product Hunt wouldn't exist if I got the job."
- Practical advice for people facing rejection: respond graciously, keep the relationship warm, and stay open to where it leads.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan argues "community" is an overused buzzword and that founders chase it before they have a product people actually need. Drawing on Product Hunt's early community building, he says utility is what brings people in, and community is what retains them and spreads word of mouth, but only after utility exists.

chunks.heading: Utility comes before community
chunks.text: Ryan argues "community" is a buzzword that audience-builders have misappropriated because it sounds more valuable than "users" or "followers". Founders who chase it before they have a clear, useful product fall into what he calls the community trap.

chunks.heading: What a real community is
chunks.text:
- A true community is not a prescribed label. It is about belonging, shown through the actions of a group of people.
- He treats the difference between a label and actual behavior as the test of whether a community exists.

chunks.heading: Product Hunt's early community building
chunks.text:
- Community building was foundational to Product Hunt from 2013.
- The team built a global audience of makers and founders excited about the future and technology.
- The audience produced hundreds of meetups, from 1,000+ person events in San Francisco to local gatherings in Amsterdam.
- Members wore Product Hunt swag, including forehead tattoos (temporary), and supported each other's launches daily.

chunks.heading: Community is secondary to utility
chunks.text:
- Ryan states: "But community is secondary to utility." He says this was true for Product Hunt then and now, and for every other company.
- "No one wants to join a community. They want utility – something that solves a problem or provides clear value to their life."
- Product Hunt's utility for makers: spreading the word about a new product, acquiring first users, gathering feedback, and earning status by reaching the top of the daily leaderboard.
- Product Hunt's utility for consumers: following the latest tech trends, getting inspired, and connecting with likeminded tech optimists.

chunks.heading: Sequencing: utility first, then community
chunks.text:
- "Utility brings people through the door, while community keeps them at the party, inviting their friends."
- Done well, community drives word of mouth, increases retention and creates a sustainable brand.
- This must come after utility.
- Ryan says many founders ask him how to build community before they have figured out utility, meaning the specific problem they are solving and for whom.
- Even though he advocates community building, he says focusing on it without clear utility is a trap.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan argues that building products has become cheap and easy enough that one person can out-ship a team, which shifts the bottleneck to getting feedback and standing out. He maps maker communities by focus (vertical, role, demographic, general) and spots opportunities in underserved audiences and mobile.

chunks.heading: Why maker communities are emerging now
chunks.text:
Ryan argues that building has become radically cheaper and more accessible, which creates a new problem: getting feedback and standing out. Maker communities are the response.

- Spinning up a simple web app "used to require months of development, a team of people, and tons of capital for (physical!) servers."
- Today "a single person can build more than a team of ten in a weekend." He says he sees this daily on Product Hunt.
- "No code" tools and decades of progress have made turning an idea into a product easier than ever.
- People now use technology to build and express themselves "the same way a musician dabbles on the drums."
- Side effect: it is harder to get feedback and to break out from the noise.
- He sees "increasing demand" to connect, learn, and collaborate with other makers, and new spaces keep appearing.

chunks.heading: How Ryan defined and mapped the maker community landscape
chunks.text:
In November 2018 he asked Twitter which communities to include in a map of the maker ecosystem, then compiled the results with further research.

Inclusion criteria:
- The primary interaction is user-to-user or UGC: users share, connect, or collaborate with each other.
- The focus is on making something tangible in tech (an app, logo, DIY project, podcast, etc.), directly or indirectly.
- Broad social platforms like Twitter and Reddit are excluded. They serve makers but it isn't their primary purpose.
- Hundreds of small maker Slack teams and Facebook groups are skipped in favor of larger communities.

chunks.heading: A four-part taxonomy for maker communities
chunks.text:
Each community is categorized by its area of focus:

1. **Vertical:** a specific industry or craft (crypto, DIY hardware, bootstrappers).
2. **Role:** a job function or skill (design, engineering, writing).
3. **Demographic:** a gender, location, age, or identifying trait (women, POC, high school students).
4. **General:** broadly serving makers of all kinds.

He notes the categories aren't perfect, since some communities span several dimensions.

Examples he lists:
- General: Product Hunt, Pioneer, Buy Me a Coffee, Patreon, YC Bookface (private to YC alumni), Prototypr.
- Vertical: Kickstarter, Stripe Atlas, Indiegogo, Substack, Indie Hackers, Nomad List, MegaMaker, Instructables, Make.
- Demographic: Girlboss, Tech Ladies, The Wing, Hack Club, Women Make, Afrotech, Elpha.
- Role: Hacker News, GitHub, Glitch, Dev, Codepen, Makerlog, Stack Overflow, freeCodeCamp, Dribbble, Behance, Designer News, MakerPad, Product Manager HQ, CMX, and others.

chunks.heading: Ryan's observations on gaps and opportunities in maker communities
chunks.text:
- **Many audiences are underserved.** Engineering-focused communities are relatively abundant, which he says fits how the internet evolved. That leaves room for others to serve different types of makers.
- **Most communities are young**, which he reads as a growing desire to build community for every niche.
- **Most are web and desktop focused.** That makes sense for people working at a desk, but he suggests there may be a bigger opportunity for mobile.

chunks.heading: Product Hunt's tie to the maker community movement
chunks.text:
- He frames the trend as something Product Hunt sees firsthand, through the volume of products makers launch there.
- Product Hunt is listed in the General category, and he discloses he is building "something new" for makers at Product Hunt, inviting readers to sign up for early access.
- He discloses he is an investor in Girlboss, and invites readers to suggest communities he missed via comments or Twitter.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover shared unfinished Product Hunt comment-system mockups and got 50+ annotated pieces of feedback within 24 hours. He argues most startups, especially those building a community, gain more than they lose by involving users in the design process. He names three benefits (buy-in, early feedback, excitement) and points to companies like Buffer, Quibb and Assembly as examples.

chunks.heading: Why Ryan thinks startups should build their product in public
chunks.text: Ryan argues that most startups, especially those building a community, have more to gain than lose by sharing unfinished work and involving users in design. He says there are legitimate reasons not to be this transparent, but "the majority of startups, especially those building a community" should do it. He wrote this in April 2014, after sharing incomplete mockups of an improved comment system for Product Hunt.

chunks.heading: What happened when Ryan shared Product Hunt mockups early
chunks.text:
- He shared mockups of a new Product Hunt comment system even though the design "wasn't perfect" and "wasn't even complete."
- He used InVision for annotated feedback.
- Within 24 hours he received over 50 annotated pieces of feedback from the community.
- The feedback sorted into what users liked, what was unclear, what was concerning, what was broken, and new ideas to make Product Hunt better.
- One user's sorting suggestion (from Geoffrey) made it into the final design.
- The result made him wonder why more startups don't do this.

chunks.heading: Three benefits of building in public
chunks.text:
1. **Increase buy-in.**
   - People want to be heard, and their investment in the product rises when their feedback is acknowledged.
   - When their ideas are incorporated, they feel a sense of ownership (he cites the ownership bias), which drives engagement and loyalty.
2. **Get feedback early.**
   - Designers close to a product miss usability issues, so fresh perspective helps.
   - Feedback is best gathered before design is committed to code, which gives a better product and less waste.
   - Caveat: people don't always know what they want, especially for products driven by emotional needs. The best product designers know what to listen to, what to ignore, and how to identify useful feedback.
3. **Excite people.**
   - People love sneak peeks. He compares it to fans paying a premium for a backstage pass, and Kickstarter backers paying top-tier prices for behind-the-scenes early access.
   - The excitement captures consumer attention and creates evangelists for the product.

chunks.heading: Examples of companies building in public
chunks.text:
- **Monkey Inferno / Bebo:**
  - After reacquiring Bebo, the team skipped the traditional approach of building a product and revealing it months later.
  - They built Bebo Insiders, a mobile app giving their audience a preview of what they were building.
  - Users got a push notification soliciting feedback as the team iterated, and could chat in real time with CEO Shaan Puri.
- **Buffer:** Ryan calls it possibly "the most transparent startup around." It publishes employee salaries, employee equity options, monthly financials and culture principles.
- **Quibb:** Editor-in-Chief Sandi MacPherson, known for authenticity and personal touch, announced a friends and family round in January 2014 that let the community invest. His take: "Is there a better way to get users invested in the product than having them invest their own money?"
- **Assembly:**
  - A crowd-building platform where users submit product ideas.
  - Ideas with enough support are designed and built by the community.
  - Each project's feature ideas, roadmap, contributions and financials are public.
  - Builders receive equity as compensation.
  - Ryan calls it "crazy ambitious and potentially very disruptive."

chunks.heading: Tools that make building in public easier
chunks.text:
- **Funding:** Kickstarter, Crowdtilt, Patreon and Alphaworks let businesses raise money directly from their audience.
- **Communication:** Intercom, Customer.io and Olark give direct access to users. Twitter is "arguably most impactful" for removing barriers to engage and broadcast personally.
- **Storytelling:** Medium makes it easier for founders to share their story.
- **Marketing:** Thunderclap assembles fans to spread news on Facebook and Twitter in coordinated "crowdmarketing" events.

chunks.heading: Ryan's own practice and view on limits
chunks.text:
- He says not every startup can or should build in public.
- He has found tremendous value in Product Hunt community feedback, and says sharing Product Hunt's story in public has positively influenced community-building.
- He planned to keep sharing Product Hunt's story and experimenting with new ways of building in public.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan argues that generative AI will challenge incumbents who built content libraries, since on-demand media can be personalized, niche and unlicensed. He sees the innovator's dilemma at work and says real-human networks are the more durable moat, leaving room for new startups to rethink media.

chunks.heading: Generative AI disrupts media incumbents through change and the innovator's dilemma
chunks.text:
Ryan opens from a core startup principle: "Successful startups are born from change." Regulatory updates, cultural movements and new technologies create vulnerabilities for incumbents that fail to adapt, and generative AI is one of those big changes.

- Ryan notes that wildly impressive demos of AI-generated videos, songs and memes go viral on Twitter daily, and results keep getting better fast.
- He says it is hard to predict how things will play out, but incumbents that spent years building content libraries "will be challenged."
- He frames the dynamic as "a classic case of innovator's dilemma." Incumbents can use the technology too, but if it interferes with their business model or existing stakeholders, they may struggle to adapt.

chunks.heading: Why on-demand generative media can beat static content libraries
chunks.text:
Ryan argues that for many use cases, on-demand generative AI media will deliver better results than the incumbent's solution.

- Unlike traditional static media, generative AI media adapts in real time to the user's requests, preferences and context.
- It can appeal to the smallest niche.
- It works without licensing restrictions or costly human labor, and can do so infinitely.
- Ryan's implication for defensibility: a content library's moat is at risk when synthetic content is just as good (or better) and available at a fraction of the cost.

chunks.heading: Examples of reimagined media products
chunks.text:
Ryan sketches how new products could replace incumbents by generating instead of curating:

- **Music (Spotify competitor):** generates entirely new music matching the user's query, not limited to existing catalogs, producing personalized and novel sounds. Suno is an early example.
- **Image inspiration (next Pinterest):** generates house renovation inspiration on the fly, adapted to the user's home, budget and style. Catbird is exploring this.
- **Fiction (future Wattpad):** writes fan fiction instantly, possibly including the reader's friends or relatable experiences for a more engaging story. Storybooks does this for children's books.

chunks.heading: How incumbents get trapped by their stakeholders
chunks.text:
Ryan explains why incumbents struggle even though they can adopt the same tech: the new model undermines the people who currently supply and pay them.

- **Spotify:** artists and major labels won't be pleased if a large portion of the audience shifts toward royalty-free music.
- **Ecommerce on Pinterest:** merchants will be upset if discovery of their products collapses as attention moves to synthetically generated images.
- **Wattpad:** writers won't be happy if sales of their werewolf romance stories drop as readers seek AI-generated novels.

Ryan's footnoted ways incumbents could adapt:
- Spotify could let artists and rights holders opt in to use of their likeness and sound for generating new music, earning a cut of revenues.
- Pinterest could present merchants' products inside synthetically generated images, driving more attention and higher conversion rates.
- Wattpad could help storytellers and IP holders create more content for their fans.

He concedes Spotify, Pinterest and Wattpad "may thrive in this new world if they can adapt," but until then there is an opening for startups "to reimagine (literally) media consumption."

chunks.heading: Which content libraries are more or less defensible
chunks.text:
Ryan distinguishes libraries by timeless, cultural relevance rather than treating all as equally threatened.

- Spotify's vast music network "will always be relevant and desired by listeners." His personal example: he will never stop listening to Porter Robinson's *Worlds* album.
- Pinterest's image database has less timeless, cultural relevance, so it is more exposed to synthetic alternatives.
- The rule of thumb: libraries tied to emotional attachment and culture hold up better than libraries that are functional inspiration or reference.

chunks.heading: Moats built on real humans
chunks.text:
In a future where media is abundant and cheap (and "humans are synthetic"), Ryan says he is "increasingly bullish on companies that establish a moat with real humans."

- People will keep desiring human connection, both professionally (LinkedIn) and socially (Instagram).
- AI companions like Replika and Character.ai will succeed at satisfying the primal desire for entertainment and play, but he sees them as "not a complete replacement" for the personal connection and opportunities gained from other people.
- Status matters: "people are status-seeking monkeys" and need other humans to see them flex to feel acknowledged (referencing Eugene Wei's "Status as a Service").
- Takeaway for founders: as content becomes a commodity, defensibility shifts toward networks, identity and status among real people.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan argues the build-for-yourself advice also works for investing: he gets most excited about founders building products he'd personally use. He lays out five themes he wants to back (distributed living, edge health, people investing, new work, weird consumer), each from his own life as the customer.

chunks.heading: Why Ryan invests in products he wants as a customer
chunks.text:
- Ryan's startup advice: build for yourself, as he did with Product Hunt. He says there is "no right way to start a startup", but solving your own problem has three advantages:
  - It is easier to empathize with the audience and know what to build when you are the customer.
  - It is more convincing to future hires and investors when you can speak firsthand about the problem.
  - It is more fun.
- He applies the same approach to investing.
- Every morning he gets a flood of startups to potentially back. At Weekend Fund they avoid imposing too much of their own opinion on what the future looks like. That leads them down many rabbit holes, from AI-powered litigation tech (Justpoint) to "boring" payroll software (Deel).
- Personally, he gets most excited talking to founders building products he wants. He says this leads to rich jam sessions and, he hopes, better input from him as the potential customer.
- He closes by inviting founders in these spaces to email him, joking that he might give them money "as an investor and customer".

chunks.heading: Distributed living and Edge Health: two themes drawn from his own life
chunks.text:
**Distributed living**
- Ryan believes that despite the pendulum narrative back to in-office work, distributed work is here to stay and adoption will only increase.
- He lives in multiple cities and prefers it: he sees more friends, finds inspiration in new scenery, and expands his experiences.
- The pain points he lists:
  - Where to stay.
  - Whether to rent out his place while away.
  - Which friends are in town.
  - Whether to pause gym memberships.
  - Whether to pack four weeks of supplements.
- With kids, he notes, everything becomes dramatically more complicated.
- An EA (he mentions Athena) can handle logistics, but most people don't have one.
- Example he cites: Mozie, a private network for meeting up with friends, focused on sharing future travel dates.

**Edge health**
- In his mid-30s, five years ago, he realized he was mortal and became more proactive about health. He has experimented with peptides, regularly gets bloodwork drawn, and occasionally gets IPL/microneedle treatment.
- The problem is a dizzying number of potential solutions. Some startups treat specific things (low testosterone, hair loss), but he argues people need to evaluate their health as a whole.
- What he wants: a continuous, holistic understanding of his health in a closed-loop system that gives clear guidance, plus the agency to educate himself and pursue treatments at the forefront of science.
- Example he cites: Function Health, which tests over 120 biomarkers to identify potential issues and help optimize health. He gets his blood drawn there.

chunks.heading: People investing: a new asset class aligning individuals with long-term goals
chunks.text:
- At Weekend Fund, Ryan says they invest in companies but much of the decision criteria is based on the founder(s).
- His view of venture: despite its flaws it is "a beautiful system that enables risk-taking". But it is limited:
  - Few people can access it (technology founders, typically pursuing audacious $1B+ outcomes).
  - The economics are tied to the company, which can misalign incentives. What's good for the company may not be good for the founder(s).
- The opportunity he sees is a new asset class that aligns people with their long-term goals and capitalist incentives.
- Example he cites: Humanism, which lets you invest in someone's future over multiple decades. It was started by the Liberman brothers, who have been dogfooding the model themselves.

chunks.heading: New work: rethinking talent matching and the economics of work
chunks.text:
- Ryan's thesis: work used to be limited to the traditional 9-to-5. Some people prefer that, but many want more flexibility and financial and intellectual diversification.
- In knowledge work, time invested isn't always correlated with value created. This is increasingly true as AI gives significant leverage to people with good ideas.
- Fractional work (freelancing, contracting) is very inefficient. Some people spend half their time sourcing and selling clients, and hiring is laborious and drags on productivity.
- He is interested in platforms rethinking the talent-matching and economic system of work. He expects it probably doesn't involve human recruiters, lengthy interview processes, or hourly pay.
- Examples he cites:
  - Bountycaster, a crypto-native job marketplace. Each bounty has a clearly defined deliverable and reward, and in some cases no approval is needed to start and complete a task and get rewarded.
  - Assembly, an attempt at a similar mission over a decade ago.

chunks.heading: Weird consumer: backing novel products built for emerging behaviors
chunks.text:
- Ryan has always been drawn to novel consumer products, especially those that build for emerging behaviors. His rule: "The more weird and counter-intuitive, the better."
- He predicts "consumer tech is about to get weird", driven by AI:
  - An explosion of new forms of UGC.
  - Shifting human-computer interaction (he expects far more talking than typing).
  - Cross-media translation (books becoming movies with one click).
  - A greater understanding of ourselves.
- Examples he cites:
  - Rosebud, a Weekend Fund portfolio company, for self-understanding.
  - Friend, a necklace pendant that records your conversations 24/7 to deliver feedback and act as a "friend". He says he loves experiments that question social norms.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan explains why he has backed about 30 venture funds over 8 years: learning, deal flow, supporting fellow investors, and (lastly) returns. He focuses on small pre-seed/seed funds, connected generalists or deep specialists, and investors who take the job seriously.

chunks.heading: Why Ryan invests in venture funds as an LP
chunks.text:
Ryan has quietly backed 30 funds over 8 years. He ranks his reasons in this order:

1. **Learn.** He loves reading quarterly LP updates, where investors highlight new investments, explain their view of the market and share the results of their experiments.
2. **Get deal flow.** He is often introduced to new companies that spark his interest. Fund managers are often happy to make an introduction when there is allocation available, and sometimes between rounds.
3. **Support fellow investors.** "Fundraising, especially today, is hard!" Besides his "tiny check," he often introduces other LPs to the fund.
4. **Make money.** This is the lowest priority because his checks are so small, not because he doubts the funds will do well. He says this will change once he has more liquidity to tie up for 10+ years.

chunks.heading: Which funds Ryan backs
chunks.text:
Most of his fund investments are in managers he has known for many years. He names these LP positions: Earl Grey, Factorial, HF0, Founders Inc, Hustle Fund, Julian Capital, Prototype Capital, Spice Capital and Thales, plus several others.

He focuses on three criteria:
- Small funds, ideally sub-$30M, investing in pre-seed and seed.
- Highly connected generalists with unique access, or deep specialists in one vertical.
- Investors who take the job seriously.

chunks.heading: Why Ryan prefers small funds (sub-$30M, pre-seed and seed)
chunks.text:
- Small funds have historically delivered better returns on average. He points to Carta's 2024 VC fund size performance data and SVB's H2 2024 State of the Markets report.
- Fund-size math: a $300K check into an early-stage opportunity can be a multiple-fund returner for a small fund.
- Larger funds ($250M+) must invest far more capital to capture meaningful ownership and outcomes, which is "almost always far more difficult."
- Those large funds often need to lead rounds. They must beat a growing number of competing investors, including multi-stage behemoths with massive teams and scout networks.

chunks.heading: Generalists vs specialists in his LP portfolio
chunks.text:
- **Generalist funds** help with deal flow because they align with what he typically invests in at Weekend Fund.
- **Specialist funds** help with diversification. They give him more exposure to industries he doesn't invest in, such as biotech, deep tech and climate tech.
- He wants generalists with unique access, or specialists with real depth in one vertical.

chunks.heading: Backing investors who take the craft seriously
chunks.text:
- He sees "managing other people's money" as a responsibility.
- He wants to back investors who are "thoughtful, disciplined, and committed to the craft."
- Because most of his LP checks go to managers he has known for years, he can judge this firsthand.

chunks.heading: How he helps funds he backs
chunks.text:
- Beyond his own small check, he introduces other LPs to the fund, because fundraising is hard.
- He invites others who want to invest alongside him to reach out via a form.
- For people trying to break into venture, he points to an article he and his team wrote on the topic at Signature Block.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover announces Weekend Fund, a $3M angel fund backing founders at the earliest stage. He argues many of the biggest companies began as side projects driven by curiosity, and that the next big thing is probably being built on nights and weekends right now. He also notes Product Hunt itself started as a side project.

chunks.heading: Weekend fund: a $3M angel fund for nights-and-weekends founders
chunks.text:
Ryan Hoover announced Weekend Fund on September 21, 2017. It is a $3M fund to support founders at the earliest stages. He frames it as backing the people who are building the next big thing in their spare time, and he keeps Product Hunt as his number one focus. He describes the fund as his own nights and weekend hustle, like the startups he plans to invest in.

- The fund runs on AngelList's new Angel Fund platform.
- AngelList handles back office, legal, and many of the logistical headaches of setting up a venture fund, at a fraction of the cost.
- Ryan calls Angel Funds "a potentially great option for operator angels", meaning people like him who work full-time at their startup. He admits he is biased.
- He offers to connect anyone interested in setting up an Angel Fund with the right people.
- His LPs range from seasoned entrepreneurs to experienced investors to leaders in entertainment.
- He invites people to follow the portfolio through his infrequent email newsletter.

chunks.heading: Product Hunt as the origin story for side projects
chunks.text:
Ryan uses Product Hunt as his own example of a side project that became a company.

- It started nearly four years before 2017 as a side project while he was transitioning from another startup.
- The goal was simple: share and discover interesting new apps and products with friends.
- He worked nights and weekends, and friends joined to help build the community. He says that without them Product Hunt wouldn't exist.
- It began as a simple email list among friends. Momentum then built quickly and unexpectedly, and the opportunity became clear.
- By 2017, more than 30,000 entrepreneurs had launched a product on Product Hunt, leading to more than 100M product discoveries.
- It grew into a platform to discover products and help makers reach an audience.

chunks.heading: Thesis: the next big thing is built on nights and weekends
chunks.text:
Ryan argues that Product Hunt's upbringing isn't unique, and that many of the most transformational companies began as side projects driven by curiosity and an eagerness to build something new. He says the next Facebook is being built on nights and weekends right now, and that these curious, creative founders are who he wants to support.

He cites Chris Dixon: "What the smartest people do on the weekend is what everyone else will do during the week in ten years."

chunks.heading: Examples of companies that started as side projects
chunks.text:
Ryan lists these as evidence for the thesis:

- **Facebook:** "Thefacebook" launched in 2004 on Harvard's campus.
- **BuzzFeed:** Jonah Peretti started it while working at Huffington Post, curious about why and how people share content online.
- **eBay:** Originally AuctionWeb, it was created over Labor Day weekend in 1995 alongside other sites by its French-born founder.
- **Imgur:** Alan started it as a personal project in college. Asked if he expected it to get so popular, he said "Never... I just stuck with it."
- **Tattly:** Tina Roth Eisenberg built the temporary tattoo company after working on various other projects.
- **Craigslist:** Craig started it in the mid-90s as an email newsletter to keep friends up to date on events around San Francisco, and incorporated two years later.
- **Gmail:** Paul Buchheit was given autonomy to build something new after finishing the first version of Google Groups. He was unhappy with existing email services and created Gmail.

He notes that side projects can also come from inside existing companies, as Gmail did. He also points readers to a separate post with tips for finding inspiration for a next side project.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover describes the mental toll of founding (a threatened lawsuit, an internet mob, near-bankruptcy) and why founders hesitate to start a second company. He splits the anxiety into three fears (past pain, reputation, "my next thing has to be huge") and argues second-time founders are still better equipped if they start small and act.

chunks.heading: Why second-time founders feel more anxiety than first-timers
chunks.text:
Ryan argues that starting a company the second time can be harder than the first, even though second-time founders are better equipped. He wrote this on October 17, 2023, and says he has felt all of these anxieties himself.

- Entrepreneurs self-report dramatically higher rates of depression, ADHD, substance abuse, and bipolar disorder (he cites a study). He notes this doesn't prove causation, and it's unknown whether the mental health challenges or the company came first.
- The "really bad stuff" founders face is rarely shared in public.
- Founders can develop debilitating anxieties. "The body doesn't want to go through it again," so many become hesitant to swing again.
- He sees a growing, silent wave of company shutdowns amid macro difficulties, and invites second-time (or third, fourth) founders working on something new to reach out.

chunks.heading: The founder's hidden struggle: the smile versus the internal monologue
chunks.text:
Ryan shares challenges he faced building Product Hunt, most of which he couldn't share at the time:

- A large company threatened to sue before the company had raised a dime.
- An internet mob attacked the company and his character.
- The company almost ran out of money after a "sea of investors told us 'no'."

He calls the hardest part maintaining a smile and instilling confidence with his team, investors, and the community while his internal monologue was filled with doubt and dread. "The dissonance between the internal emotions and external mask is agonizing." He adds that other founders have had it much harder than he did.

As an investor, he says he has admiration for founders who bring something new into the world and put in the work, even when it doesn't work out, because he knows the sacrifice required. When a founder the firm backed texted him that they were shutting down the company, he took the call and treated the founder with that respect.

chunks.heading: Anxiety 1: "UGH! That really hurt" (scars and lost naiveté)
chunks.text:
- First-time founders are gifted with naiveté. They may have heard how hard it is, but they haven't felt it. Like a child unafraid of daring stunts on the playground, they lack painful memories that introduce hesitation. That lack of fear of failure empowers them to try bold ideas.
- Second-time founders have scars. They know how hard it is, so they make excuses not to pursue ideas or bow out of entrepreneurship entirely.
- Ryan's advice: ask yourself how you would feel 10 years from now knowing you didn't try to bring your idea to life.

chunks.heading: Anxiety 2: "Everyone's watching" (reputation pressure)
chunks.text:
- First-time founders have less to lose reputationally. Expectations are lower, so fewer people in their community are watching and judging (or so it's perceived).
- Second-time founders have a reputation to uphold. The more successful they were before, the more pressure they put on themselves to achieve even more.
- Ryan's advice: most people don't care about you, and the people who truly do care about you for you, not for your startup success or lack thereof.

chunks.heading: Anxiety 3: "My next thing has to be huge" (paralysis by ambition)
chunks.text:
- First-time founders are OK solving "small" problems. Many simply want to build something people want without overthinking the grand vision.
- Second-time founders can over-intellectualize into paralysis. They focus on systems design and potential TAM instead of solving a specific problem for a specific set of people, "i.e. the basics."
- Ryan's advice: there's no right way to start up, and it's fine to dream big, but not at the cost of starting. "It's OK to start small because even the smallest nudges can lead to an avalanche."

chunks.heading: Why second-time founders still have the edge
chunks.text:
- Data point he cites (Ali Maseb, author of Superfounders): nearly 60% of CEOs and CxOs who founded a startup valued at $1B+ have past founder experience.
- Second-time founders have more experience building, recruiting, raising, selling, and scaling. They've met challenges that were invisible and unknowable to people without the experience.
- Their network is larger, opening doors to potential customers and future hires.
- They have more credibility in the market, even if their previous venture failed. "There's a reason VCs pay a premium to back second-time founders."
- His message to them: recognize your edge "with humility."

chunks.heading: Ryan's own return to building
chunks.text:
- He admits he hesitated to get back to building, often over-thinking or using prior commitments as an excuse not to act.
- A few months before writing, he started a couple of projects that solve his own problems, and says he's "having so much fun." The projects relate to Weekend Fund and investing.
- Unlike with Product Hunt, he is not building in public this time, despite acknowledging the benefits of doing so.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan argues that Easter eggs (hidden features or inside jokes) are a powerful, cheap form of marketing. They get people talking, bond users who share the secret, and build a memorable brand. He cites Snapchat's B&W filter, Siri's jokes, Lyft's pink mustaches, and Google's "do a barrel roll".

chunks.heading: Easter eggs as a marketing channel
chunks.text:
Ryan argues that Easter eggs (hidden features or inside jokes) are a powerful form of marketing even though they cut against the usual advice that apps should be intuitive and accessible. He calls this "the nature of Easter eggs is an oxymoron": hiding functionality violates user expectations, and that violation is what makes it work.

He credits Easter eggs with three marketing effects:
- **Get people talking.** People love knowing secrets but like sharing them even more.
- **Bring people together.** Shared secrets separate people "in the know" from outsiders, which forms a bond among holders of the secret and strengthens a community.
- **Build a brand.** Easter eggs are fun and produce a "WOW!" effect, creating a memorable connection between brand and user through a shared understanding not privy to everyone.

He recommends considering how to build Easter eggs into any product or service to increase engagement, establish a community, get people talking and build a memorable brand.

chunks.heading: The Snapchat black-and-white filter example
chunks.text:
- Ryan received a black-and-white Snapchat from a friend and asked when Snapchat had added filters.
- The friend proudly explained that typing the caption "B&W…" activates a hidden black-and-white filter.
- Ryan immediately sent a dozen B&W Snapchats to friends, anticipating their curious replies "because I knew something they did not."
- The lesson: the secret spread person to person because each recipient wanted the thrill of being the one who knows. Knowing a secret creates the urge to share it and to watch the other person's reaction.
- The filter is one of many hidden Snapchat Easter eggs.

chunks.heading: Apple Siri: hidden answers as free marketing
chunks.text:
- When Siri launched, Easter eggs "bombarded the internet." People couldn't get enough of Siri's unexpected, witty answers to hidden questions and phrases.
- Blogs, TV shows and social networks exploded in discussion, and websites dedicated to Siri's Easter eggs sprang up. A Google search for "siri funny questions" returned over a million results.
- Ryan argues the free marketing from these Easter eggs was "arguably more impactful than Apple's multi-million dollar advertising budget."
- Mechanism: the secretive, clever nature of the eggs pushed users to explore the product to uncover its secrets. Users who cracked one got bragging rights and shared the discovery with friends. As a result "Siri became a celebrity as people promoted her wit."

chunks.heading: Lyft's pink mustache: hiding the brand behind a mystery
chunks.text:
- Ryan overheard people on Howard St. in San Francisco asking, "What are those pink mustaches for?", and saw two other groups ask the same question that week.
- Lyft decorated its fleet with furry pink mustaches instead of plastering its brand name on the side panels. The mustache acted as an Easter egg that caught attention and got people talking.
- After seeing half a dozen mustache-sporting cars, "one is bound to resolve the mystery." When people asked friends or searched online to understand it, Lyft became more memorable.
- Why it matters: in competitive markets, recall and top-of-mind awareness determine which transportation service someone turns to the moment they need a ride. Lyft stood out from competitors by hiding its brand behind an Easter egg.

chunks.heading: Google: playful surprises and hidden search terms
chunks.text:
- Google replaces its logo with Google Doodles for holidays, special events and anniversaries. Examples Ryan cites include an interactive synthesizer (Robert Moog's 78th birthday) and a zamboni mini-game. Rotating doodles spur conversation and give people a reason to visit the homepage to see what others are talking about.
- Less obvious but "arguably more impactful" are hidden search terms. Typing "do a barrel roll" into google.com makes the screen rotate. Released in 2011, it was still spreading in 2013, with hundreds of tweets about it that week.
- Ryan's point: even as a multi-billion dollar corporation, Google shows playfulness and charms users with surprises. Easter eggs add no value to the core offering, but they give the brand a personality and get users to market the product by forwarding it to friends.

chunks.heading: Why the tactic works (summary of the mechanics)
chunks.text:
- Hidden things reward exploration, so users engage with the product beyond its core use.
- Discovery gives users bragging rights, which turns them into distributors who share with friends.
- Spread is word-of-mouth and often self-sustaining: the barrel roll kept circulating two years after release.
- It is cheap relative to paid advertising (the Siri comparison), and it works for physical products as well as software (Lyft's mustaches).
- Ryan ends the essay with the tactic applied to the reader: "now that you know the secret, don't you want to share it?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains why YourStack, a product-recommendation spin-off from Product Hunt, failed after a decent launch of 15K signups. The causes were an infrequent use case, too-broad scope, web-first instead of mobile-first, overbuilding before launch, and founder burnout. He still believes in the thesis that trusted recommendations drive product adoption.

chunks.heading: Why YourStack existed and what it was meant to do
chunks.text:
- In 2019 Ryan carved a small part of the Product Hunt team out to build YourStack. It had its own brand and domain, separate from producthunt.com, and was built from scratch using five years of Product Hunt lessons.
- Product Hunt is about what's new: a firehose of the latest tech launches. YourStack was about the products you use and love, regardless of age.
- The goal was to go beyond tech and help people discover and buy products recommended by people they know and trust. It used a follower model instead of a daily-launch leaderboard, to personalize the feed and widen the products surfaced.
- The thesis: "People will try and buy products from people they trust." Longer term, the aim was a new product graph, a data set of products people actually use and endorse.
- It launched in early 2020 and got 15K signups in the first week. Ryan calls that "not crazy, but a great start". It still failed.

chunks.heading: Product discovery is not a daily habit
chunks.text:
- Ryan's first reason for failure: "Product discovery isn't a daily or even weekly activity." People rarely seek new products to buy.
- Most consumer social products need frequent engagement, or no habit forms. External triggers like push notifications can bring people back, but the internal trigger (a desire to discover or buy products) was infrequent.
- Designing for DAU then means fighting "the natural state of what people want".
- Contrast with Product Hunt, which is designed for the DAU. Its internal trigger is staying up to date on what's new in tech, following trends and getting inspired by what people built. It has a clear flywheel that drives adoption and re-engagement.
- A DAU experience can be forced by steering engagement toward tangential use cases, but that changes the product's underlying goal. His example: surface product recommendations while the core loop centers on financial management.

chunks.heading: Too broad: niche down first
chunks.text:
- YourStack deliberately aimed beyond tech gadgets, SaaS and apps. Ryan now says: "sometimes niching down is the best way to start."
- A narrower focus makes it easier to build the ideal experience for that use case or interest.
- It also clarifies the target audience, which simplifies messaging and the GTM strategy for reaching those people.

chunks.heading: Mobile-first for consumer products
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt started on web and desktop (2013), which fit its audience, team skills and era. YourStack carried that web focus forward, which Ryan calls a mistake.
- His rule: when building for a wide consumer audience, especially one that demands frequent engagement, mobile should probably be the priority.
- A mobile app started post-launch was confined by what had been designed for web. It also split the team's focus and made it harder to iterate on the core model across both platforms.

chunks.heading: Overbuilding before launch
chunks.text:
- Ryan says they should have launched YourStack, or a version of it, much sooner to test the core interaction model and assumptions.
- Instead they "got too cute and fell into the midwit trap". Before launch they built:
  - a product Q&A experience
  - a scraper to ingest product recommendations from Twitter
  - user-created tips on how to use specific products
- The extras pushed back the launch date, split engagement and added more surface area to maintain.

chunks.heading: Founder burnout and the iterations needed for PMF
chunks.text:
- By launch Ryan was nearing 7 years as CEO of Product Hunt and losing motivation. He says that in hindsight it is clear what he should have changed to avoid burnout, but once he "caught the bug" it was hard to sustain the stamina needed to iterate toward product-market fit.
- He argues founders underestimate how many iterations it takes to build something people want, especially in consumer social, where "the smallest changes can make a massive difference". "The first version is never it."
- After launch he knew what they had wouldn't work, and he knew the commitment required to reach PMF.

chunks.heading: What Ryan still believes and where the opportunity is
chunks.text:
- He still holds the thesis: "The best way to drive product adoption is through an authentic recommendation from a trusted person." It looks even more obvious now, given influencer marketing and creator-led brands.
- YourStack aimed to let everyday consumers "influence" their micro networks, lengthening the tail of product discovery and elevating products people actually use. The key is that recommendations are authentic and relevant to the recommender's background.
- Social recommendations may be the best route to serendipitous discovery. When people know what they want, they go to Amazon, Google or YouTube. Social recommendations can pull them toward products they didn't know existed.
- As the cost of bringing products to market falls, more options will appear and the need for curation grows.
- The winner may not tackle product discovery head-on and may enter "through a backdoor". Example: TikTok (and Musical.ly before it) isn't designed for music discovery, yet has done more to break artists and shape culture than any music discovery platform in the last decade.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover lists eight practical ways to find side project ideas, from reflecting on your own day-to-day to exploring emerging platforms, Product Hunt, GitHub and hackathons. He argues side projects make you a better builder and can grow into real businesses, as Product Hunt did.

chunks.heading: Where Ryan looks for side project ideas
chunks.text:
Ryan (writing in November 2016) is a big fan of side projects. He calls them "a great vehicle for expression," similar to how an artist communicates through their art. He says they can make you a better engineer, designer, marketer or salesperson, and they can turn into a business: Product Hunt started as a side project.

His view is that it's "difficult to manufacture a truly great idea in a whiteboarding session." Ideas are often serendipitous, triggered by stories and changes in the world, so he lists places to look for inspiration rather than a brainstorming formula.

chunks.heading: Mine your own life and your friends' lives for pain points
chunks.text:
- **Reflect on your day-to-day.** Ryan says the best ideas often come from your own experiences. Write a detailed diary of everything you do in a typical day, then identify things that could be improved.
- The problem can be important (for example, what tasks to prioritize in your day) or small (for example, deciding whether to bike or take an Uber to work).
- **Ask your friends.** Run the same exercise with them and look for frustrations or pain points that could be eliminated.

chunks.heading: Build on emerging platforms
chunks.text:
- Ryan worked in video games when Facebook's games platform was on the rise. He combed through Facebook's API and developer docs to find new, creative things to build on the platform.
- His principle: "As platforms emerge and evolve, new opportunities arise."
- As of 2016, he said he might explore Google Home, Alexa or Facebook Messenger.

chunks.heading: Browse what other makers are building
chunks.text:
- **Product Hunt.** He admits he's biased, but argues "great ideas are often built off each other." Products created today will inspire the next Snapchat, directly and indirectly.
- **Kickstarter and Show HN** are two more places he suggests for browsing new products.
- **GitHub.** Even non-programmers can use it for inspiration. Browse trending repos for new ideas or projects to join.
- **Hackathons.** Hackathons are designed for side projects and give you a motivating place to share ideas with other enthusiastic makers.

chunks.heading: Turn a feature into a standalone product
chunks.text:
- Look at favorite apps, sites or products and ask whether you can repurpose and improve one of their features as a standalone product.
- His example: Medium created an elegant way to share and present comments inline. Other people might want that functionality on their own sites. He notes this side project already exists.

chunks.heading: Read the internet
chunks.text:
- Reading the news and blog posts increases the chances of discovering new ideas.
- Ryan treats this as an ongoing habit. Stories and changes in the world are what trigger serendipitous ideas.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover adapts the venture "right and non-consensus" framework to founders: obvious problems with obvious solutions rarely win, while non-obvious problems offer less competition and a shot at owning a new category. He uses Calendly and Deel as examples and lists questions for finding non-obvious problems.

chunks.heading: Framework: obvious vs. non-obvious problems
chunks.text: Ryan sorts startup ideas on two axes: whether the *problem* is obvious, and whether the *solution* is obvious. He borrows the logic from early-stage venture investing, where the best outcomes come from being right and non-consensus. In his words: "I've seen a ton of startups from my time building Product Hunt and now investing in early-stage opportunities at Weekend Fund." He says most founders pursue obvious problems, and he is most interested in founders who tackle non-obvious ones.

chunks.heading: The venture analogy behind it
chunks.text:
- Investing in a company that is wrong loses money, whether the bet was consensus or non-consensus.
- Investing in a company that is right and consensus makes outsized returns harder, because the market already priced in the potential when the check was written.
- Investing in a company that is right and non-consensus is the most likely path to outlier returns, because the market hasn't priced in what you saw early.
- Ryan notes outliers exist, and that this is the nature of early-stage investing.

chunks.heading: Obvious problem, obvious solution: unlikely to succeed
chunks.text:
- There is likely a graveyard of similar attempts that failed for legitimate reasons.
- Dozens of competitors may chase the same idea, making it hard to break through the noise and attract customers.
- Example: an app to meet up with friends (obvious problem) where the user broadcasts their location (obvious solution). Ryan says Product Hunt has dozens of products that tried this over the years.

chunks.heading: Obvious problem, non-obvious solution: might succeed
chunks.text:
- The solution may only be possible now because of technology or cultural shifts. It may be the first time the problem can be solved, or a dramatically better answer to a long-standing problem.
- It can also come from an "earned secret" or insight from the founder's past experience.
- Downside: fast-followers chasing the same obvious problem. Once the solution is known, competitors can replicate it and sell into their existing, highly relevant customer base.
- Example: calendar scheduling is an obvious problem. Calendly introduced a clever UX pattern in 2013 that flipped scheduling workflows into a simple booking system, dramatically reducing friction.

chunks.heading: Non-obvious problem (obvious or non-obvious solution): the blue ocean
chunks.text:
- Far less competition, and the potential to be the leader of a new category.
- Target customers are less inundated with solutions and likely more receptive.
- Non-obvious problems are often driven by a change in the world: a new problem, a problem affecting a growing market, or a problem becoming more painful.
- Example: Deel (a Weekend Fund portfolio company). In 2018 it focused on remote payroll for globally distributed teams. At the time this wasn't seen as an obvious problem and was discounted as too "niche". The market later exploded, partly because of COVID and cultural shifts in how people live and work.
- Ryan's conclusion: "Perhaps the biggest blue ocean opportunities are in non-obvious problems."

chunks.heading: How to find non-obvious problems
chunks.text:
Non-obvious problems require a unique insight or rare perspective. Ryan's prompts for founders:

- What unique problems have you faced in your personal life or work?
- Which problems seem to be getting worse?
- Have you hacked together a solution to a problem few people have identified?
- Do you have a strong view of the future, and what problems would emerge if your prediction is right?
- Are you seeing recurring complaints from people in your network or communities?

He adds the caveat that startup success still depends on solving a real problem with the right solution, and that founders should place their idea along these axes.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan argues that GUI-based "no code" tools are cutting the time, cost and expertise needed to build software, much as cloud hosting replaced racking servers. He expects more makers, more MVPs built without code, and growing demand for maker communities and monetization tools.

chunks.heading: Why "no code" is inevitable: Ryan's case for the rise of no-code tools
chunks.text:
Ryan's core claim is that "no code" tools are collapsing the time and skill needed to turn an idea into something people can use, and that this will widen who gets to build. He ties it to his own start: he built his first website in Dreamweaver as a 15-year-old with only basic HTML and CSS. It was ugly and didn't take off, but he calls it "a gateway drug to creating things on the internet."

- Earlier WYSIWYG tools (Dreamweaver, FrontPage, Flash) cut the barrier to creation sharply, and he says their impact on today's tech ecosystem is understated.
- He sees a new wave of tools that make creation more accessible and change how things get built for the internet.
- Once, only a small group of engineers (self-described "webmasters") built on the internet, often after months of learning to code.
- In December 2018 he tweeted that powerful "no code" tools are entering the market, that he was speaking with 3 startups raising in voice, mobile and web app creation, and that "the time and cost to build software products will drop by another 10x." He called this part of Product Hunt's thesis.

chunks.heading: The no-code stack Ryan lists (as of January 2019)
chunks.text:
He says that in under an hour, anyone can now build:

- A CMS-driven responsive site with Webflow.
- An ecommerce shop with Shopify.
- A Facebook Messenger bot for a shop with Octane AI.
- A web app with Bubble.
- A mobile app with Thunkable.
- A voice app with Voiceflow. He built a joke bot in 10 minutes and discloses he invested in Voiceflow.
- A complex web app combining Zapier and Airtable.
- A single-page site with Carrd.
- A paid newsletter with Substack.
- An AR/VR/3D browser experience with Scapic.
- An online magazine with Readymag.
- A website from a Google Sheet with Sheet2Site.
- Internal dashboards and tools with Retool.

He also points to no-code resources: Zeroqode, NoCode and MakerPad.

chunks.heading: Everyone becomes a maker
chunks.text:
- Building is no longer limited to the "<1% of engineers that can code," which he expects to cause "an explosion of ideas from all kinds of people."
- You no longer need to become a programmer to build on the internet, which brings in makers from different backgrounds and perspectives.
- He says Product Hunt sees no-code projects often, including a Golden Kitty award winner.
- Making things accessible was part of Product Hunt's thesis when it started five years earlier.

chunks.heading: Answering the critics
chunks.text:
- Ryan expects people to criticize and judge no-code users. He grants there are tradeoffs, but says it is "inevitable" that more products will be built, or at least MVP'd, without code, including by programmers who can code.
- Example: a VP at a Series A startup told him they use Salesforce and Zapier for sourcing B2B leads. The company has an engineering team and could build anything, but chose no-code because it was faster to build and easier to maintain.
- His diagnosis: "We often perceive things that are hard to do as better." Sometimes that's true, but as no-code tools advance, "it will be silly to do it the old way."

chunks.heading: The hosting analogy
chunks.text:
- Ryan compares no-code to hosting. Putting a site online once meant buying expensive physical servers and heavy dev ops work, and a feature on Yahoo's homepage could crash the site.
- Now AWS, Heroku and Google Cloud make this easy, and even the most experienced dev ops engineers use them to start and scale.
- He says it would be foolish for them to spend time racking their own servers, and he expects the same shift for building software.

chunks.heading: Where opportunity follows: maker communities and tools
chunks.text:
- As more people become makers, there is "an even greater thirst for community" to give feedback and support along the way.
- He predicts maker communities will become increasingly popular as everyone becomes a maker.
- He also expects growth in tools that help makers monetize, find side-project buddies, and get the word out, and says those tools might themselves be built without code.
- He says he is very interested in tools for makers and creators and is looking to invest in the space. He notes Product Hunt was building something new for makers, freelancers, remote workers and side-project builders.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover reflects on five years of building Product Hunt, sharing the mistakes and learnings from running a venture-backed company. Topics include org structure, repeating your mission, hiring, distributed teams, avoiding pointless redesigns, and planning for fundraising and acquisition early.

chunks.heading: Org structure, communication, and the founder's voice
chunks.text:
- Ryan ran Product Hunt with a very flat structure for years, aiming to encourage autonomy and mutual respect. It backfired: the lack of structure and clear ownership produced the opposite effect, and 15+ direct reports didn't scale.
- His conclusion: "Org charts and titles aren't evil."
- He says a CEO should feel like they're repeating themselves. When a teammate asks "What are we building? Why?", it's the founder's fault for not communicating mission and strategy clearly and frequently enough to people who are heads down on one part of the business.
- A founder's word carries heavy weight, during their tenure and after they leave. The ideas a founder promotes or shoots down can shift the team's focus and motivation, for better or worse. He points to a Jason Fried post on this.

chunks.heading: Hiring and letting people go
chunks.text:
- He calls "Bad hires might kill your company" a startup cliche because it's true.
- Startups inevitably hire people who aren't a good fit. Ryan has let go of a few people at Product Hunt.
- It wasn't because they were bad people. Sometimes the person simply isn't right for the product, culture, or stage of the company at that time. In most cases, he says, they know that too.

chunks.heading: Distributed teams
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt has been distributed since the beginning. The team spans seven timezones: UK, France, Bulgaria, India, Canada, New Zealand, and the U.S.
- Benefits: it can hire talent from anywhere, not just the <1% who live in or can relocate to San Francisco. It also gives the team a global perspective that mirrors its global community.
- Limits: he says distributed teams "won't work for everyone," especially companies that scale to hundreds of people, although he notes a few seem to have figured it out.
- His headline view is that distributed teams are the future, but not for everyone.

chunks.heading: Why redesigns almost never work
chunks.text:
- Ryan says "Redesigns" almost never work. Product Hunt wasted a lot of time redesigning its homepage.
- The trap for someone proud of the product they ship is making it look better and fiddling with pixels without questioning the impact.
- Questions he says to ask first:
  - "Is this actually going to change how people use the product?"
  - "Will it meaningfully impact our metrics?"
- His rule: don't let ego get in the way of prioritizing what's right for the business and users.

chunks.heading: Investors: build relationships before you need them
chunks.text:
- Many advise founders to avoid investors until it's time to fundraise. Ryan recommends limiting the number of "coffee meetings" because they can be a major distraction.
- Even so, he stresses that investing is largely relationship-driven: the more investors trust you, the easier it is when you raise.
- Choosing the right investors matters because once they're on the cap table, it's difficult to get them off.

chunks.heading: Plan for acquisition and keep optionality
chunks.text:
- Acquisitions, like fundraising, are often relationship-driven, maybe more so.
- Ryan says founders tend to pridefully claim they'll never sell without giving a single thought to who might buy the company. His advice: map out potential acquirers early and start planting seeds, because "optionality is key."
- Example: he says that if Naval hadn't invested in Product Hunt's 2014 seed round, he's not sure AngelList would have acquired Product Hunt.

chunks.heading: Context on the lessons
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt started in November 2013 as an experiment announced via a tweet, and Ryan applied to Y Combinator (S14) with a video. The team was invited to join the S14 batch.
- He says much of this advice is specific to building a venture-backed business. Bootstrapped SaaS may look very different, and "there's no right way to startup."
- His broader reflection: starting a company and raising money is abnormal, and founders learn on the job. A 20-page college business plan taught him mostly what not to do.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover argues that the traditional VC edges of sourcing and picking startups are eroding because public signaling, discovery tools and AI make every deal visible and evaluable by everyone. What remains is winning the allocation, which depends on helping founders and earning access.

chunks.heading: Why sourcing and picking stop being an edge
chunks.text:
Ryan argues that an investor's job is four things: source promising startups, pick the right ones, win an allocation, and help founders. Investors take pride in sourcing and picking, built on years of coffee meetings and pattern-matching. Ryan says that edge is "deteriorating and will increasingly lead to false confidence."

- Many investors are exceptional at both today.
- The risk is that confidence in these skills outlasts their actual advantage.
- His conclusion: "there's no edge in sourcing and picking in the near future. All that matters is winning."

chunks.heading: Everyone will see every deal
chunks.text:
Deal flow already travels fast through investor catchups and deal-sharing networks. What is new is public signaling by founders, plus tooling that surfaces them.

- Signals that a founder is preparing to raise: launching on Product Hunt, getting loud on X (often with a hockey-stick chart), and following VCs on social.
- Tools that use public data to find newly minted founders and opportunities: Signa, Harmonic, Landscape, Tracxn, plus internal systems many VCs have built.
- Ryan expects these tools "will only get better," so sourcing advantage narrows as visibility becomes near universal.

chunks.heading: AI will pick better than humans
chunks.text:
Ryan expects AI to out-select human investors, and not only on objective metrics.

- It can comb through data rooms more thoroughly than any person, instantly evaluating comps, the market, and the team's background.
- Examples he cites: En Verite is productizing this, and firms like ADIN have internal systems to help pick.
- It will also evaluate founders: automating reference checks and analyzing nuanced signals in a pitch captured via Zoom plus Granola.

chunks.heading: Winning the allocation is the game
chunks.text:
With sourcing and picking commoditized, Ryan says earning access and winning allocations becomes the most important part of investing.

- He admits he is "being slightly provocative" but stands by the point.
- Exception: investors with truly proprietary, non-public data may still have alpha in sourcing and picking.
- Reputation, which is earned by helping founders, is what wins deals. Brand is shaped by perception, "for better or worse." He grants that brand-building and "thread boi maxxing" will still serve a purpose.

chunks.heading: Why this is good for founders
chunks.text:
Ryan frames the shift as positive. Investors spend less time deal-hunting and arduously analyzing opportunities, and more time helping founders. Helping founders is the core input into their ability to win the next deal, so the incentive to be useful grows. "And that's great for founders."

- Implication for investors: invest in being genuinely helpful and in reputation, since that is what wins allocations.
- Implication for founders: signaling publicly gets you seen by everyone, so choose investors on how much they help, not on access to them.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover argues that vibecoding turns software creation into entertainment and self-expression, which threatens the durability of many consumer utilities. When features are easy to clone, defensibility shifts to social graphs, distribution, licensing, data moats and hardware, and the strongest products combine several.

chunks.heading: Vibecoding as self-expression
chunks.text:
- Ryan and his fiancée used Lovable to build an event site to collect RSVPs, even though Partiful, Paperless Post, or dozens of other tools could have done it in about 10 minutes.
- They spent a few hours prompting, tweaking, and laughing at weird outputs, and ended up with something that "felt like ours."
- The result was functionally inferior to a polished event platform, but more meaningful and more fun to make.
- His takeaway: "software creation itself is becoming the product." Vibecoding is a form of self-expression, creating software went from tedious to fun, and it is "as much entertainment as it is function."
- As a result, he argues the durability of a large class of consumer software is in question.

chunks.heading: Why consumer utilities are more exposed than B2B
chunks.text:
- Ryan notes the chatter about the "death of SaaS" mostly focuses on B2B and its decaying moats, but he thinks consumer utilities may be even more exposed.
- B2B software selection is constrained by trust, security, integration complexity, and organizational inertia. Consumer is different.
- For many consumer use cases, the job to be done is no longer just functional; it is emotional and expressive. Demand shifts from utility to self-expression and entertainment.
- Software stops being purely a time-saving device and starts becoming a time-spending activity. "The value isn't only in the output. It's in the act of making it."
- This isn't entirely new. He cites people who rebuild the same habit tracker in Notion, constantly redesign link-in-bio pages, and craft hyper-personalized workout planners in Google Sheets instead of downloading a tracking app.
- What changes is that vibecoding expands software-as-self-expression to far more use cases for the masses.

chunks.heading: What stays defensible in consumer software
chunks.text:
