Ryan's premise: if vibecoding makes software easier to create, feature advantages collapse even faster. He lists what remains defensible in consumer utilities:

- **Social graphs.** LinkedIn is at its core a simple online resume, but the real value is the network and the assumption (correct, at least in tech) that most professionals use it to research people.
- **Distribution.** More than 12 years after its founding, Product Hunt's distribution flywheel keeps spinning. Its core product, a daily leaderboard of product launches, "could be vibecoded in a weekend but the value isn't in the code."
- **Licensing and regulations.** Spotify succeeded by securing licenses with major labels and aggregating the world's music in one place. Replicating that is incredibly difficult and time-consuming.
- **Data moats.** Waze is useful because it collects data from millions of drivers daily to estimate traffic, flag construction routes, and more.
- **Hardware.** Physical products are getting easier to build but remain relatively hard compared with pure software. "You can't (yet) vibe code an Oura Ring."

He adds that the most durable products will combine more than one of these.

chunks.heading: Software painting and the original Product Hunt bet
chunks.text:
- When Ryan started Product Hunt, the bet was that software creation would become more accessible and increasingly serve as a form of self-expression. He says that has "never been more true today."
- His closing framing: "We're all software painters now. What have you made?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover argues that resumes poorly communicate ability, and that blogging does what GitHub does for developers: it shows how you think. He shares how a year of writing built a network that produced job offers and seeded the Product Hunt launch, then lists the caveats of blogging.

chunks.heading: Blogging replaces the resume as proof of how you think
chunks.text:
- Ryan argues resumes are crummy: an 8.5x11 sheet can't communicate a life's accomplishments or skill set, and he questions whether anyone reads them.
- In his view they only weed out obvious "hell no" candidates.
- Hiring managers lean on trusted recommendations and on tangible things an applicant has accomplished.
- Ryan's example of a good resume is GitHub for software developers. Public repos, breadth across languages, open source work and side projects show what someone has built, so it "shows" rather than "tells".
- For non-technical roles (product managers, UX designers and similar) his GitHub equivalent is a blog. His thesis: "Blogging is new resume."
- A blog shows expertise, personality and above all thought process. How someone thinks signals ability and culture fit, which a resume lacks entirely.

chunks.heading: How blogging opened doors for Ryan
chunks.text:
- He started actively blogging about a year before, writing 1-3 essays a week.
- He wrote for fun and to learn, on startups, product design, UX and psychology. The research and reflection sharpened his expertise, and the more he wrote, the better he wrote.
- Early pieces hit the front page of Hacker News (for example "Email-First Startups" and "Stop Using NoReply"). His Twitter following grew and he gained attention in tech and blogging communities.
- His writing was featured in PandoDaily, FastCo and Forbes, and on Andrew Chen's and Nir Eyal's blogs.
- When he announced he was leaving PlayHaven with no plan, he was nervous. The network he built through blogging reached out with support, and several followers offered him jobs and introductions to founders.
- He credits his professional experience as instrumental, but says blogging "amplified peoples' interest in me and helped market my expertise."

chunks.heading: Blogging as an evergreen resume, even at low volume
chunks.text:
- Ryan says not everyone needs his level of dedication. Regardless of exposure, a blog is a vehicle to share ideas, expertise and interests, "an evergreen resume."
- His example is Lenny Hu. Ryan first met him through a post, "LetsLunch Landing Page", where Lenny redesigned the homepage and explained his thought process.
- The post stayed memorable a year later because it showed proactiveness and ability.
- Lenny kept writing product deconstructions and product design thoughts. Despite a small following and infrequent posting, he built a strong, long-lasting resume.
- It paid off: Lenny messaged Ryan that he'd been hired as a short-term consultant for a stealth startup who "saw my blog."

chunks.heading: Blogging to build a product and seed a community
chunks.text:
- Ryan and Nathan Bashaw launched Product Hunt, a site to share and discover products.
- They seeded the community largely through relationships formed via his writing, inviting several dozen well-respected startup founders, investors and product people to participate.
- After a private release they announced it in the press (Pando) and to his audience, gaining another 1,000 users over the next week.
- He says none of this would have been feasible 12 months earlier, before he had built a network of supporters through writing.

chunks.heading: Six cautions before you start blogging
chunks.text:
- **Enjoy it.** It's hard to sustain without intrinsic motivation, and you'll quit. Frequent writing isn't mandatory, but the more you put in, the more you get out.
- **It's a long-term investment.** Your first, second, third or 50th post is unlikely to go viral. Accept that most people don't care what you think and that quantity leads to quality.
- **It's not about you.** Readers don't care how awesome you are. An occasional humblebrag is OK, but constant self-promotion about you or your startup's successes turns readers away.
- **Write about your passions, not trends.** Don't write about growth hacking because it's in vogue; write about it only if genuinely passionate. Topics without mass appeal are fine because others share the interest.
- **You don't know everything.** Have conviction but humility. When criticizing people or startups, remember you lack full context; they may have specific reasons or data outsiders aren't privy to.
- **Don't let it become a distraction.** Once you have an audience and habit it's hard to stop, but blogging shouldn't substitute for the important, less enjoyable work in your startup or life. His advice: "Do 'shitty' work."

chunks.heading: Using writing in place of a resume
chunks.text:
- When startups ask about his background and expertise, Ryan replies with a brief bio and a few select articles relevant to their situation.
- His logic: if you read his writing you know how he thinks. If you agree with his analysis and recommendations, you'll trust his product decisions. If you disagree, "then we shouldn't work together anyway."
- He says resumes fail to communicate any of this, and he hopes never to touch his resume again.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan argues founders gravitate toward their own craft (coding, wireframing) because it feels like progress, while neglecting unglamorous but critical work like talking to customers and acquiring users. He shares his PlayHaven wireframing mistake and a simple fix: ask "why" about every to-do item.

chunks.heading: Prioritization means doing the unglamorous work, not your craft
chunks.text:
Ryan argues that startups succeed or fail on what founders choose to do and not do, and that "not everything on the to do list is fun. Sometimes you have to do 'shitty' work."

- Typical startup to-do list he cites: support emails, bugs, newsletter, pitch deck, blog post, homepage design, Twitter ads experiments, new on-boarding flow, marketing events.
- Successful startups "require attention in all areas." Even without a marketing title, someone has to figure out how to acquire users.
- Prioritization is paramount because speed is a startup's most valuable asset. He quotes Paul Graham: "What's important about startups is the speed."
- Building a successful product and startup is "all about knowing what to do and what not to do."

chunks.heading: Founders gravitate to their craft because it is comforting
chunks.text:
Ryan's core diagnosis: people prioritize what they like to do over what they should do.

- Coders like to code, salespeople like to sell, designers like to design.
- "We prioritize our craft because it's comforting. It's what we're best at." But the craft is not what the company needs at all times.
- Example he heard from a solo founder of an early social product: he built the product in a few weeks, but four months later still hadn't figured out getting users. His words: "I don't enjoy marketing. I just want to code."
- Ryan says he has made this mistake himself and hears this pattern often.

chunks.heading: Wireframes to nowhere: his own PlayHaven mistake
chunks.text:
Early at PlayHaven, as the sole product manager, Ryan was responsible for designing new product concepts.

- He spent nights and weekends on high-fidelity wireframes, agonizing over text field alignment and copy that "didn't matter one bit at the time."
- One wireframe took days for a consumer app discovery concept the company never built. He says they should have validated market need and business feasibility instead of "pixel shifting for a product no one wanted."
- What he should have done instead:
  - Talked to customers before designing features he only thought they wanted.
  - Gotten engineering input on feasibility and tradeoffs before jumping into design.
  - Sketched first and used paper prototypes to bring ideas to life in less time.
- Many wireframed concepts were never built, or had to be adjusted after talking to engineering and customers. He concludes that doing the less fun, important things first would have saved the company time.

chunks.heading: Fake progress: why craft work feels like winning
chunks.text:
Ryan calls this the "delusion of progress." Wireframing was fun and the results were rewarding, so it "felt like progress," and the wireframes became "a trophy" for late nights.

- A founder friend described the same sensation with code: "It's incredibly satisfying to build a product... Each GitHub commit feels like progress. So I keep coding even though I know I should be focusing on marketing."
- Why code is seductive: it is responsive and predictable. Write `alert('Hello World!');` and the app responds with "Hello World!" immediately.
- Why marketing and sales are less rewarding: people are "unpredictable and non-responsive," and their tastes, expectations and context keep changing. That means less certainty and delayed reward, which reduces motivation to invest in these "non-rewarding" activities, especially if you don't enjoy them.

chunks.heading: How to combat fake progress
chunks.text:
Ryan's remedy is self-accountability through a daily "why" check.

- Each morning when reviewing your to-do list, ask why for every item.
- Example questions: Why should I create wireframes for a new landing page? Why should I add Facebook integration? Why should I attend the Lean Startup Conference?
- He says this simple, honest question "may have saved me a lot of time and effort."
- The goal is to spot work that feels productive but isn't what the business needs right now, and to do the shitty-but-important work instead.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains why he left a well-paid, growing startup role after nearly three years. His top priority is learning, and he'd lost passion for the market. He closes with three questions he uses to evaluate his next opportunity.

chunks.heading: Why Ryan left a good job at PlayHaven in August 2013
chunks.text:
- Ryan left a full-time role at PlayHaven by choice, in San Francisco. He was paid well, the company was growing, and he worked with friends.
- His stated reason: "my #1 priority is to learn." He grew most during periods of discomfort, when he was challenged the most.
- His test for staying: if you look back at yourself six months earlier and don't feel embarrassed by your naiveté, you're not learning or growing. He credits this idea to his friend Nathan Bashaw.
- Telling his boss and friend was hard. He could barely say "I'm leaving" and cried, but he knew it was the right move for him.

chunks.heading: Signals it's time to move on
chunks.text:
Ryan's signals, from his own experience:

- **Role narrowing.** As the company grew, his role became more specialized and moved away from his generalist roots. A UX designer was hired to take over many of the responsibilities and "(fun) challenges" he used to handle.
- **Lost passion for the market.** He lost passion for the industry, and a two-week vacation (his first in a long while) three months earlier did not bring it back.
- **Personal interest faded.** He grew up obsessed with games (Starcraft, Team Fortress Classic, Halo), but now rarely plays even casual iPhone games. He spends his time on reading, writing, and side projects/experiments.
- **Telling omission.** He never writes about gaming, the industry he works in. He says this "is very telling."
- **Not a builder in the space.** He is not a game developer and has no motivation to become one.

chunks.heading: Build products you consume
chunks.text:
- Ryan argues people who build products for themselves have a "tremendous advantage" because they are their own user.
- They don't have to "get inside the user's head" to understand the problem.
- Their perseverance is strengthened by the motivation to solve their own problems.
- He states a strong ambition to build a product that he is the consumer of.

chunks.heading: Questions for evaluating the next opportunity
chunks.text:
Ryan uses three questions to evaluate new opportunities:

1. Is this really what I want to do?
2. Am I (strongly) passionate about the product, market, and vision?
3. Will I be challenged, learn, and grow to my full potential?

chunks.heading: How PlayHaven started and what he learned
chunks.text:
- He joined PlayHaven as employee #10 nearly three years earlier, drawn by Silicon Valley and the chance to work with founder Andy Yang in mobile gaming.
- Early on the product had traction, but revenue and adoption were nearly stagnant. Cash reserves dwindled and layoffs came; the company downsized and six people remained.
- The team scrapped nearly all existing code and rebuilt the product around a new vision. Ryan was the sole product manager working with five engineers. He defined the user experience and wireframed the new dashboard, learning on the job.
- They set a goal of a private launch at Casual Connect in July 2011.
- With no QA person, Ryan (a mostly non-technical person) set up a local environment of the dashboard and fixed bugs himself. The night before a demo with a large client, he tested the product until 2 A.M. He calls this "incredibly unscientific", but they had no time for "process" and "just had to Get Shit Done." The product shipped in a usable state and landed their first big client.
- By 2013 the team had grown to 85, with several thousand customers and multi-million dollar revenues.
- Lessons he lists from the experience:
  - Methodologies for discovering what people really want.
  - The importance of building the right (minimal) features.
  - Processes for bringing an idea to market.
  - How to scale a company.
  - The criticality of hiring the right people and building an aligned culture.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ryan Hoover explains how Product Hunt grew from a simple email list into a community, crediting years of blogging and relationships for the initial 300 subscribers. He covers early growth via press and word of mouth, the hardest parts of running a company (firing, momentum), and his advice to build an audience before you launch.

chunks.heading: Starting with a hole to fill
chunks.text:
- Ryan grew up in Eugene, Oregon, with entrepreneurial parents who owned a video game store. As a kid he bought and sold on eBay and made video game handbooks to sell in that store.
- His dad's advice: "Find a hole and fill it." Ryan uses it to pick projects that solve problems he has or sees.
- Product Hunt began as one of many experiments, started because he wanted the thing to exist. He had no plan to make money and no plan to turn it into a business.

chunks.heading: Where Product Hunt came from
chunks.text:
- Ryan and his friends were already swapping cool products over SMS and group chats ("What's on your home screen?", "What are you playing with?"). He argues people like to talk about products the way they talk about movies or music.
- No place on the internet was dedicated to that conversation. Twitter and Facebook are general-purpose networks and aren't built for discovering new products.
- There was also no single list of new products launching each day. Tech publications mix products with other news and have no community.
- The first version was a simple email list of the most interesting new products of the day, launched in November 2013.
- Writing fed into it. In 2013 he published 150 blog posts, nearly one essay every two days. He used writing to learn about products, such as teardowns of early Tinder that asked why it was compelling and which cognitive biases and design cues it used.
- He hated writing in school because the topics were assigned. He took to it once he wrote about things he cared about.

chunks.heading: Build a following before you build the product
chunks.text:
- Ryan's top advice for some entrepreneurs is to build a following. He means an audience in a similar interest space, not Twitter vanity.
- Product Hunt started with about 300 subscribers on day one. That was possible only because of years of blogging and relationships with notable people who became core early community members.
- He says "The hardest thing is distribution for any kind of product, and even just getting beta users can be really difficult." An audience that cares about your work gives you people to launch to and support you immediately.
- He says Product Hunt wouldn't have worked without at least some following.

chunks.heading: How Product Hunt grew in year one
chunks.text:
- Ryan says two mechanisms drove growth in the first year.
- **Press:** Product Hunt was a new source for finding products and the people behind them, so reporters used it. TechCrunch sometimes found a product there and linked to Product Hunt. That sent relevant readers to a small user base, and the people who clicked through found value.
- Ryan calls this a rare case where early press worked as an acquisition strategy. For most companies, he says press misses the real target audience and is more of a vanity metric.
- **Sharing and word of mouth:** People like Ryan shared finds on Twitter, Facebook and elsewhere. Makers also shared their product pages, and discussion happened on those pages.

chunks.heading: Team, momentum and morale
chunks.text:
- The hardest personal challenge is letting a teammate go, especially when teammates become friends who made sacrifices to join. He says "If you're not letting someone go, and you haven't ever fired anyone, something's probably wrong."
- On the business side, he says every company must keep up momentum. Early excitement fades, every company hits some stagnation, and every company tries things that don't work.
- The harder part is keeping the team pumped and working hard when things aren't going great.

chunks.heading: The AngelList acquisition
chunks.text:
- Product Hunt was acquired by AngelList in 2016. It's the only acquisition Ryan has been through.
- From the start, his aim was to keep autonomy, brand and voice. The team and community stayed relatively intact.
- He says acquirers often kill a product or merge teams and integrate products. He wanted to keep ProductHunt.com and the kitty mascot, and AngelList agreed, understanding the importance of the community and brand.

chunks.heading: Moving to profitability and what he was building (2018)
chunks.text:
- Ryan says Product Hunt intentionally avoided focusing on revenue from the start. Experiments began around September and October of the prior year.
- Goal for the year: reach profitability. Last month, the company covered more than half its expenses, up from $0 six months earlier. He didn't share specific numbers.
- **Ship:** a toolkit for startups and makers to communicate with users, acquire beta testers and understand customers. It pulls together tools people already use, such as surveys, landing pages and email marketing.
- **User growth:** SEO was producing strong results. He was also trying a new place for makers to share what they're working on and get help from others, and early feedback from that small community was good.

chunks.heading: What motivates him and how he works
chunks.text:
- Motivation: thank-you notes from makers, and the drive to make a bigger impact and move a number (revenue or users) from x to y. He likens building products to a giant strategy game.
- His favorite part of the role is building new products and experiences, even though not all of them work.
- Time management: he says he has no great process. He jumps between product, marketing and team work, which he enjoys but which makes long focus blocks hard.
- What helps most lately: at the start of each week, he writes down three things that must get done. If only those happen, the week is still a win. This keeps lesser tasks from eating the week.
- He is routine-driven. He spends at least a couple of hours each morning at Philz Coffee, where Product Hunt itself was started.
